# Building the Future: Backing Auckland to succeed

Source: <https://www.national.org.nz/news/261014-simonwatts> (New Zealand National Party (national.org.nz)). Main article/policy content only; site navigation, footer and 'More policies/Latest news' lists removed. Text is verbatim.

## Full text

## Building the Future: Backing Auckland to succeed

14 October 2026

·

Simon Watts

·

Chris Bishop

## Building the Future: Backing Auckland to succeed

Today National is releasing its plan for Auckland, which will continue to get Auckland moving, unlock its potential and make it a city where people and businesses can get ahead.

“Over the past three years National has focused on fixing the basics; building roads, investing in public transport and major events, cutting red tape, and making it easier to build the homes and infrastructure our biggest city needs,” National’s spokesperson for Auckland Simon Watts says.

“Thirteen Fast-Track projects have been approved in Auckland, including the Auckland Port expansion, creating thousands of jobs and billions of dollars of investment. We have progressed major transport routes like SH1 Warkworth to Te Hana and opened the City Rail Link.

“We’ve backed major events and removed the restrictions at Eden Park, helping Auckland attract events like next year’s State of Origin match. We have 400 new classrooms built or under construction and secured land in Drury to build a new hospital.

“Auckland has had a challenging few years following the prolonged Covid lockdowns, but National is turning things around.

“Under National our economy is growing faster than the UK, the US, Canada and Australia. Exports are up $20 billion; inflation is down from a 32-year high and 220,000 new jobs will be created - so we want to help Auckland capitalise on that opportunity,” Mr Watts says.

A re-elected National government will:

- Plan ahead for Auckland’s future, working with Auckland Council through the Auckland Deal to align housing, infrastructure and economic growth.

- Build the infrastructure Auckland needs to grow, including SH1 Warkworth to Te Hana, stage one of Mill Road, the Eastern busway, 296 new classrooms, and further progressing a new hospital in Drury.

- Back Auckland families with the cost of living, by growing the economy, supporting more housing and keeping pressure off household costs.

- Keep driving crime down, with more visible Police, including on public transport, tougher consequences for serious and repeat offenders, and safer neighbourhoods and public spaces.

- Keep lifting health and education performance, so patients are seen and treated sooner, more children are in school, and more young Aucklanders leave with the skills and qualifications they need.

In a further move to make Auckland commuters and residents’ lives easier, Chris Bishop says National will also abolish the blanket ban on minimum car parking requirements in city and district plans which were introduced in 2020.

“The blanket ban on minimum car parking requirements has not worked. The economic theory behind it did not account for the reality of New Zealand’s suburban streets. Many streets, especially in Auckland, are clogged and hard to get through, and people are now parking on berms and footpaths.

“Aucklanders know all about the access and safety issues this policy has created. Some people are having to walk 10 minutes or more to get home from where they’ve parked.

“We will fix that. Our changes will give councils the flexibility to require car parks in suburban and other areas – outside locations identified for intensification in the new planning system,” Mr Bishop says.

“If Aucklanders want a city to be even more proud of, they should stick with the plan and party vote National.

“The alternative is a Labour Government propped up by the Greens, Te Pati Māori and Opportunity, planning nine new taxes and more of the wasteful spending and lack of ambition Labour showed last time.”

# Plug-in solar for Kiwi homes next year

Source: <https://www.national.org.nz/news/261015-simeonbrown-1> (New Zealand National Party (national.org.nz)). Main article/policy content only; site navigation, footer and 'More policies/Latest news' lists removed. Text is verbatim.

## Full text

## Plug-in solar for Kiwi homes next year

15 October 2026

·

Simeon Brown

## Plug-in solar for Kiwi homes next year

Shops will be able to sell plug-in solar panels off the shelf within the first six months of a re-elected National Government, supporting more households to lower their power bills, National’s Energy spokesperson Simeon Brown says.

“Making your own power should be as easy as plugging in a toaster,” Mr Brown says.

“Kiwis should be able to walk into Bunnings, Mitre 10, IKEA, or The Warehouse, pick up a plug-in solar panel, take it home, plug it in, and start generating their own electricity.

“Right now, they can’t. Plug-in solar is used safely overseas, but our electrical safety rules were never written with it in mind. That means Kiwis are missing out on one of the easiest and most affordable ways to cut their power bills, especially people in rentals and apartments who have been locked out of solar.

“Since we announced in April that plug-in solar was coming to New Zealand, our Government has been working on new safety rules to protect households, the power network, and line workers before panels go on sale. Government agencies are developing them right now, and we’ve teamed up with Australia on shared rules.

“A re-elected National Government will finish the job, so shops can sell plug-in solar panels off the shelf next year.

“Plug-in solar is just the start. Rooftop solar can save the average household $1,000 or more a year on power, and National’s Home Energy Fund will put it within reach of more homeowners.

“The fund will cover the upfront cost of rooftop solar, batteries, insulation, and heat pumps. Homeowners then pay it back alongside their rates over time, at a low interest rate. We’ll also let homeowners put solar on their roof without needing a consent.

“Together, plug-in solar and the Home Energy Fund will help more Kiwis make their own power, save money, and become more self-sufficient.

“This builds on what we’ve already delivered. Over the past three years, National has:

• Got more Kiwis onto solar, with solar connections up 47 per cent since National came to office and more New Zealanders than ever making their own power.

• Delivered the biggest renewables boom in a generation, with more new renewable generation, including new solar farms, built in the past three years than in the previous eight.

• Fast-tracked big energy projects, with one-year consent decisions replacing years of red tape and eight renewable energy projects already approved.

“This election is going to be tight, and the choice couldn’t be clearer. A National Government that has a plan for more affordable power, including plug-in solar, with no new taxes. Or a Labour-Greens-Te Pāti Māori-Opportunity Party coalition that would put affordable energy at risk, and leave Kiwis worse off with nine new taxes.”

# National sets out plan to double exports by 2034

Source: <https://www.national.org.nz/news/261016-toddmcclay> (New Zealand National Party (national.org.nz)). Main article/policy content only; site navigation, footer and 'More policies/Latest news' lists removed. Text is verbatim.

## Full text

## National sets out plan to double exports by 2034

16 October 2026

·

Todd McClay

## National sets out plan to double exports by 2034

“The Primary sector is $4 billion ahead of schedule to deliver on National’s ambitious 2023 goal to double the value of exports in 10 years, and today we are laying out our plan to ensure that target is met,” says National Party Agriculture spokesman, Todd McClay.

“Food and Fibre exports have just hit a record $65.2 billion, and which shows our transformative work in the primary sector is paying real dividends.

“Our famers and growers generate around four in every five dollars of our goods exports and support about 360,000 jobs, most of them in our regions.

“That export income pays for the hospitals, schools and roads in every New Zealand community. When farming grows, it delivers more jobs, wages lift and the regions across the country thrive,” Mr McClay says.

“In 2023, National campaigned on getting Wellington out of farming. We have delivered. Dairy production has risen for the first time in a decade, with profitability at its highest level since the measure began.

“To get this done we replaced the RMA, scrapped the Ute Tax, removed farming from the ETS, banned full farm-to-forestry conversions, introduced Investment Boost, announced plans for water and fertiliser security, signed trade deals and slashed red tape.

“Our plan is working – and today, we go further,” Mr McClay says.

“National is announcing 19 new standards to slash red tape around the work farmers and growers do every day.

“In many cases, these standards will remove the need for consents entirely. Even where consents may still be required, they will be easier, faster, and cheaper. This means more time and money spent on growing their businesses, rather than paying for needless bureaucracy.

“National wants farmers to produce more, invest with confidence and help us double the value of our exports. It's how we fix the basics and build the future.

“If rural New Zealand wants the primary sector to continue growing, they should stick with the plan and party vote National.

“The choice is clear - a Labour Government propped up by the Greens, Te Pati Māori and Opportunity with nine new taxes, or National with no new taxes and a plan to keep our rural sector flourishing.”

# National to extend and improve paid parental leave

Source: <https://www.national.org.nz/news/paid-parental-leave> (New Zealand National Party (national.org.nz)). Main article/policy content only; site navigation, footer and 'More policies/Latest news' lists removed. Text is verbatim.

## Full text

## National to extend and improve paid parental leave

26 July 2026

·

Nicola Grigg

·

Nicola Willis

## National to extend and improve paid parental leave

Working mums and dads will benefit from National’s plan to give parents more time with their babies and more choice over how they take paid parental leave.

A re-elected National Government will gradually extend paid parental leave from 26 to 30 weeks by 2029, starting with an increase to 27 weeks in next year’s Budget and followed by further increases in the next two Budgets.

National will also give parents the option of taking some or all of their paid parental leave at the same time, in any order or combination up to the full entitlement.

“This is about better supporting working mums and dads as they do the vital work of raising children,” National’s spokesperson for Finance Nicola Willis says.

“National wants strong families, supported to give their kids the best start in life. Our modernisation of paid parental leave will support families by giving them more financial breathing space when they take on caregiving responsibilities.

“The birth of a child is an expensive time, as families juggle the costs that come with a new baby while their household income is less than when both parents are in paid work.

“Extending paid parental leave to 30 weeks will ease that pressure and give more parents the option to stay home with their baby for longer.

“This is part of National’s longer-term vision to eventually extend paid parental leave to 40 weeks, equivalent to around nine months.

“Gradually increasing paid parental leave over three Budgets means this policy can be funded responsibly, consistent with National’s plan to return the books to surplus and reduce government debt,” Nicola Willis says.

National will modernise paid parental leave by giving parents flexibility to divide their paid leave in the way that best suits them and their family.

“Under the current law, parents are prevented from taking paid leave at the same time or in overlapping instalments,” Nicola Willis says.

“These outdated restrictions are getting in the way of families doing what they think is best for their babies. National will let parents and caregivers share their paid leave entitlement and make choices that suit their family.

“For example, instead of one parent taking 30 weeks’ leave, both parents could take 15 weeks together. Or they could take four weeks together, one parent could then take 10 weeks, and then the other parent could take 12 weeks after that.

“Whether a dad wants to support mum in the first few weeks after birth, or two caregivers want to share paid leave in overlapping instalments, the choice should sit with families and not restricted by outdated government rules.

“This change recognises that every family's circumstances are different and gives parents the flexibility to make the choices that suit them best,” Nicola Willis says.

National’s spokesperson for Women Nicola Grigg says extending paid parental leave to 30 weeks and modernising the rules will better support mums through the often demanding postpartum period.

“Extending paid parental leave to 30 weeks gives more mums the option to stay home longer, giving them more time to recover and return to work with confidence.

“Some mums might need extra help from their partner after a difficult birth and allowing parents to take paid parental leave together means their partner can be home while they recover,” Nicola Grigg says.

National will also protect changes in the new Employment Leave Act so parents receive full holiday pay when taking annual leave after returning to work.

Annual leave is currently paid based on average weekly earnings over the previous 12 months, meaning a parent who takes a holiday soon after returning to work from paid parental leave can receive reduced holiday pay.

“Working mums and dads should not be penalised for caring for their baby. This change removes that unfair penalty, which has fallen overwhelmingly on working mums,” Nicola Grigg says.

This change complements National’s proposed KiwiSaver changes.

“Many parents stop contributing to KiwiSaver while household income is lower and costs are higher. As a result, these parents, overwhelmingly mums, miss out on the Government’s matching contribution,” Nicola Willis says.

“National will fix this by making a Government contribution to a parent’s KiwiSaver while they’re on paid parental leave, even if the parent is not contributing,” Nicola Willis says.

The contribution will be made at the default rate, applied to the paid parental leave a person receives, from 1 July 2027.

“A modern economy depends on parents being able to take the time they need with a new baby and then return to work with confidence,” Nicola Willis says.

“Supporting families and backing skilled people to stay in the workforce by improving paid parental leave settings is part of National’s wider plan to fix the basics and build the future for all New Zealanders,” Nicola Willis says.

In December 2025, the Government announced a 12-month maximum repayment period, interest after six months
and a hardship pathway. These decisions have not yet been enacted.
Cabinet has shortened the maximum period to nine months and replaced interest with an automatic 10 per cent
payment within four weeks.
The Bill will be introduced in the next Parliamentary term. A one-year transition will follow Royal assent before
these requirements apply to new occupation right agreements.
The new requirements will not alter existing occupation right agreements. Applying them immediately to all existing
agreements would bring the full financial impact forward, potentially affecting village affordability, services and
viability.
The payment will be 10 per cent of the resident’s net termination proceeds. The indicative $60,000 is based on a
projected average unit value in 2028/2029 of approximately $800,000 minus a 25 percent deferred management
fee. Actual payments will vary.
The initial payment applies when a former resident leaves to live elsewhere. It will not apply to a resident’s estate
following their death.
Residents needing to enter aged residential care, experiencing financial hardship or requiring more suitable
accommodation will be able to apply for early access for an amount up to their full net termination proceeds.
Weekly fees will stop and fixed deductions will stop accruing after an occupation right agreement ends. Operators
will also be required to provide monthly updates on the progress of relicensing a unit.
Operators will still be required to take all reasonable steps to enter into a new occupation right agreement for the
unit of a former resident in a timely manner and for the best price reasonably obtainable, keep the former resident
updated regularly, and get the unit valued after six months (if not relicensed by then).
A more efficient and effective dispute resolution system will be introduced to resolve disputes where operators are
not meeting their obligations.
Villages with fewer than 50 units will be exempt. Exemptions will also apply where the resident controls the sale
and price, at least half the capital gain is shared with the outgoing resident or their estate, or the village is in
receivership.
Extensions of up to six months to the maximum repayment timeframe may be available for village operators on
specified grounds.
Failure of an operator to make the initial or final payment within the required timeframe will be subject to civil
penalties of up to $25,000 for an individual and $50,000 in any other case. The Registrar or a statutory supervisor
can bring civil liability proceedings.
The estimated $3.2 billion to $4.1 billion is the capital the sector would need to hold or access for a three-month
maximum repayment timeframe. The potential increase in entry costs assumes operators pass all estimated costs
on to residents.

Retirement village exit repayment reforms

# A firm, fair and affordable welfare system

Published by the New Zealand National Party as a PDF policy document. Source: <https://assets.national.org.nz/web/prod/A%20firm,%20fair%20and%20affordable%20welfare%20system.pdf?v=1791407915>.
The text below is the verbatim text layer of the PDF extracted with `pdftotext` (reading order). Line breaks follow the
PDF; tables and multi-column layouts may read out of order in this section, so a second rendering that preserves the
page layout (`pdftotext -layout`) follows it. Nothing has been added, removed or paraphrased.

## Full text (reading order)

Fixing the Basics:

A firm, fair and affordable
welfare system
Introduction
New Zealand needs a welfare system that is firm,
fair and affordable. It should provide a safety net
when people need it, support Kiwis to move back
into employment, and remain affordable for taxpayers.
The longer someone remains on welfare, the harder
it can become to return to work, with consequences
for individuals, families and taxpayers.
However, under Labour, the number of people receiving
a Jobseeker unemployment benefit for more than two
years surged by 60 per cent – from 49,000 to 78,000 –
between 2017 and 2023, despite unemployment falling
over that period. Too many New Zealanders became
stuck on welfare for years, rather than getting the
support and facing the clear expectations needed
to move back into work.
Since coming into Government, National has put
employment back at the centre of the welfare system,
restoring the principle of rights and responsibilities
through clearer expectations and consequences under
the Traffic Light System.
But there is more to do.
A re-elected National Government will build on
the progress already made by investing earlier to
help people move into work, while strengthening
expectations for those who remain on Jobseeker long
term. With Treasury forecasting 220,000 more people
in employment over the next four years, we want to
ensure Kiwis are ready to take up those opportunities,
particularly in growth areas such as primary industries,
construction and infrastructure, tourism and hospitality.
Our plan is centred on five initiatives:
•

Investing earlier to help long-term Jobseekers into
work. National will provide more intensive, workfocused support for 30,000 work-ready jobseekers
who have been on a benefit for more than a year,
supporting them move into employment before
long-term dependency becomes entrenched, with
greater funding for employment programmes that
support young people into work.

•

Stronger expectations after two years. From 1 April
2028, jobseekers who have received Jobseeker
for two of the previous three years will move to a
lower rate of payment, with a smaller reduction for
households with dependent children.

Authorised by J de Joux, ps@national.org.nz

•

Introduce random drug testing for Jobseekers.
National will introduce random drug testing as part
of MSD’s work-readiness and employment planning,
starting with 10,000 tests in the first year and
expanding the programme once established.
Those who fail a second test will be required to
undertake an alcohol and drug assessment, with
continued non-compliance resulting in sanctions.

•

Double the stand-down for repeated voluntary
unemployment. People who repeatedly leave
employment without good and sufficient reason
will face a 26-week non-entitlement period, up
from 13 weeks.

•

Extending the benefit residency requirement
to five years. From 1 April 2028, the minimum
residence period for main benefits will increase
from two years to five years.

Together, these will provide more support to help people
into work, while making clear that those who can work
are expected to.

Welfare support should always be
temporary
National believes the Jobseeker unemployment benefit
should be a temporary safety net for New Zealanders
who find themselves out of work. However, historically
around 40 per cent of people receiving a Jobseeker
unemployment benefit have remained on a benefit
continuously for more than two years, irrespective of
underlying economic conditions.
This is not what the system was intended to do, and
the consequences of long-term dependency can be
significant. The longer someone remains on a benefit,
the harder it can become to return to work. Those
consequences can also carry across generations.
Children who grow up in benefit-dependent households
are more likely to receive a benefit themselves later
in life, increasing the risk that disadvantage becomes
entrenched from one generation to the next.
Reducing long-term dependency is therefore not just
about helping people into work today. It is also about
improving opportunities for their children and breaking
the cycle of intergenerational poverty.

However, there is strong evidence that targeted
employment support, backed by clear expectations,
can help more people move off welfare and into work.
Under the previous National Government, a series of
reforms introduced in 2012 and 2013 strengthened
work obligations and encouraged labour force
participation and formal education. Where work
and work-preparedness obligations were not met,
financial sanctions were introduced and applied to
encourage compliance.
In the period immediately following these reforms,
13,000 individuals moved off a main benefit, including
8,000 fewer jobseekers and nearly 5,000 fewer
people on sole parent support. This was estimated to
contribute to a $4.4 billion decline in the Government’s
long-term welfare liability, driven by higher rates of exit
from welfare and into work, and a lower rate of return
onto a benefit for those who had exited into work.
Getting the balance between support and responsibility
right is critical to reducing long-term welfare
dependency and ensuring the welfare system remains
sustainable for those who need it. A re-elected National
Government will invest earlier to help people into work,
while strengthening expectations and consequences
for those who remain on welfare long term.

National’s plan to rebalance welfare
towards work
Jobseeker Employment Support: Investing to
help long-term Jobseekers back into work
The best time to intervene is before long-term
dependency becomes entrenched and people
become increasingly detached from the labour
market. That is why National will establish a new
Jobseeker Employment Support initiative, providing
targeted, work-focused support to 30,000 work-ready
Jobseekers who have received a benefit for at least
12 months. At least 5,000 of these places will be
specifically targeted at young Jobseekers, aged 18-24.
Modelled on the “Invest to Save” initiative funded
through this year’s Budget, Jobseeker Employment
Support will fund intensive, work-focused case
management and greater access to employment
programmes. Recipients will receive a needs
assessment, an individual employment plan and
practical support to address the barriers keeping
them out of work, including targeted training,
employment assistance and support connecting
with employers.

1

Targeted case management works. By identifying what
is keeping someone out of work and providing practical
support to address those barriers, this initiative will help
more long-term jobseekers make sustained moves into
employment, lift household incomes and reduce the
number of New Zealanders reliant on welfare, including
children growing up in benefit-dependent households.
As part of Jobseeker Employment Support, National will
also invest an additional $12 million per annum in He
Poutama Rangatahi, on top of existing baseline funding,
to provide more employment support for young
New Zealanders at risk of long-term unemployment.
He Poutama Rangatahi has demonstrated strong
results in helping young people overcome barriers
and move towards work. The Ministry of Social
Development has evaluated the programme and
found it was effective at achieving its short-term
goals, delivering employment, education and training
outcomes for young people. This additional investment
will build on what is working and help more young
New Zealanders get the support they need to move
towards employment and independence1.

Reduce Jobseeker payments after two years
To rebalance Jobseeker Support towards its original
intent and strengthen the incentive to move into work,
National will introduce a lower rate of Jobseeker
Support for people who have been on the benefit
for two of the previous three years.
From 1 April 2028:
•

Single Jobseeker recipients without children
would now receive the rate paid to 20–24 year
olds and 18–19 year olds living independently. If
introduced today, this would be a reduction of
$48.05 per week.

•

If introduced today, couples without children would
receive $552.18 a week, an effective reduction of
$81.76 per week.

•

Jobseeker recipients with dependent children
would see a smaller reduction, equivalent to $24.02
per week if introduced today, half the reduction
applying to a single recipient without children.

Actual reductions will reflect Jobseeker rates in 2028,
which will have increased on 1 April 2027 and 1 April
2028 to reflect inflation. The Supported Living Payment
is unchanged.

Ministry of Social Development, He Poutama Rangatahi Evaluation, 2024.

To prevent people avoiding the lower rate through
short breaks from the benefit, eligibility will be based on
cumulative time receiving Jobseeker Support. Anyone
who has received Jobseeker Support for at least two
of the previous three years will move to the lower rate.
This change reinforces the principle that Jobseeker
Support is there to help people back into work, not to
keep them on a benefit indefinitely. It sends a clear
signal that support comes with an expectation of work,
strengthens the incentive to take up available jobs,
and helps keep the welfare system affordable for the
New Zealanders who need it most.

Introduce random drug testing for
Jobseekers
Being ready for work means being able to take up
the jobs that are available. For many New Zealanders,
drug testing is a normal condition of employment. It is
reasonable to expect work-ready Jobseekers to meet
the same basic expectation.
National will introduce random drug testing for
Jobseekers, integrated into MSD’s work-readiness and
employment planning. We will undertake 10,000 random
drug tests in the first year, with the programme expanding
once it is established and operating effectively.
Those who fail a random drug test will be required
to undertake a second test. A second failed test will
trigger a mandatory alcohol and drug assessment to
identify whether drug use is a barrier to employment
and what steps are needed to address it. Where
appropriate, those steps will become part of the
person’s work-readiness plan.
Jobseekers will be expected to comply with testing,
assessment and any resulting work-readiness
requirements. Continued non-compliance without
good and sufficient reason will result in sanctions.
New Zealanders are regularly required to pass drug
tests to get or keep a job. It is not too much to ask that
people receiving Jobseeker Support who are required
to be available for work take reasonable steps to
remain work-ready. Drug use should not be allowed to
become an unaddressed barrier to moving off welfare
and into employment. We expect this policy to cost
approximately $1.5 million per annum, which will be
funded from MSD baselines.

Double the stand-down for repeated
voluntary unemployment
The welfare system is there to support people
who need it, but it should not remove personal
responsibility. Where someone repeatedly chooses
to leave employment without good and sufficient
reason, taxpayers should not be expected to
immediately pick up the cost.
The current rules allow a 13-week non-entitlement
period for repeated voluntary unemployment, but
there should be stronger consequences where this
behaviour continues.
A re-elected National Government will extend the
current 13-week non-entitlement period for people
who repeatedly choose to leave their job to 26 weeks.
This is consistent with the approach taken in the
United Kingdom, where repeated failures relating
to employment can attract substantially longer
benefit sanctions.
This change reinforces the principle that Kiwis who
can work and repeatedly choose to leave employment
without good reason should be accountable for that
decision – not taxpayers. The welfare system should
provide support when people genuinely need it,
alongside clear responsibilities for those who are
able to work.

Extend the benefit residency requirement
to five years
New Zealand’s welfare system is funded by taxpayers
to provide a safety net for people who need it. But
under the current rules, a new resident can become
eligible for a main benefit after only two years in
New Zealand. That does not reflect the reasonable
expectation that people settling in New Zealand should
support themselves and their families through work
or their own resources before becoming eligible for
long-term taxpayer-funded income support.
A re-elected National Government will extend the
minimum residency requirement for main benefits from
two years to five years, from 1 April 2028. Starting on
that date gives time to pass any necessary legislation.
The new requirement will apply to everyone who has
not yet completed five years of residence at that date,
but anyone already receiving a main benefit will keep
it. Refugees and protected persons will continue to
be exempt, and MSD will retain its existing ability to
provide hardship assistance in genuine emergencies.

This is consistent with the approach in other countries.
In Australia, most new permanent residents must wait
four years before they can receive JobSeeker Payment.
In the United Kingdom, most migrants cannot claim

benefits until they are granted settlement, usually after
five years. This change will support the affordability of
the welfare system while maintaining a fair safety net
for those who need it.

Fiscal Impact
National’s welfare reforms will support more people into work while keeping the welfare system affordable
over time.

Jobseeker Employment Support will target 30,000

remaining on welfare long term. The cost and annual
funding profile for the initiative is based on the Budget
2026 Invest to Save initiative, adjusted pro rata from
25,000 to 30,000 places, with savings scaled for the
relative weekly cost of Jobseeker, and a modestly
lower rate of success, reflecting the reality that this
programme is targeted at individuals who have been
on jobseeker for longer than one year.

Lower Jobseeker Rate for Long-term
Recipients
The lower rate of Jobseeker for long-term recipients
is estimated to save around $572 million over the
forecast period.
This estimate starts from the number of people who
have been receiving Jobseeker Support for more than
two years and projects the affected cohort forward
using the PREFU 2026 forecast for Jobseeker numbers.
The fiscal costing is therefore based on the official
forecast rather than assuming National’s Jobseeker
reduction target is achieved.

Savings are net of tax and allow for one-fifth of the
reduction being offset by increases in other assistance.
Rates are indexed to inflation each year. Estimated
savings do not assume any further fiscal benefits from
more people moving off a benefit and into work.

Residency Requirement
The five-year residency requirement is estimated to
save around $50 million over the forecast period.
The change will take effect on 1 April 2028, which
allows time to legislate, and applies to all residents
who have not yet completed five years of residence
at that date.
Because the change stops new benefit grants rather
than removing existing ones, savings build over time.
These estimates allow for people already receiving a
benefit to keep it. The longer stand-down for voluntary
unemployment and mandatory clinical assessment will
generate further savings, although these are expected
to be modest and are not reflected here.

# Auckland Transport Police Teams

Published by the New Zealand National Party as a PDF policy document. Source: <https://assets.national.org.nz/web/prod/Auckland%20Transport%20Police%20Teams-1.pdf?v=1789952338>.
The text below is the verbatim text layer of the PDF extracted with `pdftotext` (reading order). Line breaks follow the
PDF; tables and multi-column layouts may read out of order in this section, so a second rendering that preserves the
page layout (`pdftotext -layout`) follows it. Nothing has been added, removed or paraphrased.

## Full text (reading order)

Building the Future:

More Police on Auckland’s
buses and trains
Auckland’s public transport network has just got a
lot bigger. The City Rail Link adds three underground
stations and lifts peak capacity through the city centre by
around half. That is a big win for Auckland, and it means
more passengers, later services, and enclosed platforms
below ground where help needs to be close at hand.
Most journeys on Auckland’s public transport network
pass without incident. But too many Aucklanders now
think twice before taking the train after dark, or before

National will establish a dedicated
Auckland Transport Police Team to
improve safety across Auckland’s public
transport network.
New Zealand Police will be funded to provide
a visible presence on buses, trains, ferries,
stations and interchanges.

letting their teenager catch the bus home from a late
shift. Drivers have been assaulted at the wheel and
passengers have watched anti-social behaviour unfold
in a carriage knowing help was a long way away.
Every Aucklander should be able to catch a bus, train
or ferry and feel safe doing it.
As Auckland’s public transport network grows,
National will ensure that safety measures grow with it.

over 3000 constables, is responsible for the
whole British rail network, with a significant
presence on London’s transport system. In
Australia, New South Wales and Victoria each
also have dedicated police presences on their
transport networks.

The team will focus on preventing anti-social
behaviour, protecting passengers and transport
staff, responding quickly to incidents, and bolstering
confidence in safety on public transport. The
purpose will be to deter crime before it happens,
and make sure that when a serious incident does
occur, it gets an immediate police response.

Auckland Transport’s transport officers already
play an important role in managing incidents and
supporting passengers, but they do not have the
powers of a sworn police officer. They cannot make
an arrest, they can only observe an incident and
report it. And while New Zealand Police regularly
support transport operations, there is no dedicated
transport policing capability focused on Auckland’s
growing network.

These types of units are commonplace in other
cities offshore with large, sophisticated transport
networks. The British Transport Police, comprising

The team will be established in Auckland in the first
instance, with expansion to other centres considered
if it succeeds.

Authorised by J de Joux, ps@national.org.nz

Building on National’s work to
restore law and order

How will the Auckland Transport
Police Team be established?

Since coming into Government, National has worked
hard to restore law and order after the previous Labour
Government oversaw increased levels of crime.

Following the election, the Minister of Police will refresh
the letter of expectations to the Commissioner of Police
to highlight the importance of police visibility on the
public transport network as a critical part of keeping
Auckland safe.

The National-led Government has sent a clear
message that we are tough on crime and we have
pursued policies that crack down on gangs and
criminals, including:
•

Banning gang patches in public.

•

Giving Police stronger powers and put more
officers on the beat.

•

Capping sentence discounts so judges can no
longer slash penalties for offenders.

•

Restoring Three Strikes for the worst repeat
offenders.

•

Introducing tougher tools, like move-on orders,
to reclaim our town centres.

We have also increased police visibility in our
communities. In 2025 alone, Police carried out nearly
double as many foot patrols as they did during Labour’s
final year in government.
The results show that when a Government is tough
on crime and prioritises increased police visibility in
our communities, there is less crime and fewer victims.
Compared to when Labour was in Government:
•

Ram raids are down 85 per cent.

•

Youth offending is down 26 per cent.

•

There are 37,000 fewer victims of serious violent
crime.

A visible police presence helps deter offending before
it occurs. Boosting the visible police presence on trains,
buses and ferries, and at stations and transport hubs,
reassures passengers and transport staff, and ensures
rapid intervention when something does go wrong.

Police will be explicitly resourced to establish this
team, with funding to recruit an additional 50 officers
to fulfil this function. Consistent with their independent
operational role, Police will retain full decision-making
powers on the size, location, and timing of any police
presence on Auckland’s public transport network,
including which stations and routes have more
visible policing.

Fiscal impact
An additional $7 million per year will be made available
to Police to run this pilot, funded through Budget
2027. This cost is based on the “500 Police” initiative
in Budget 2024, updated slightly to reflect the recent
Police pay round.
That funding will support Police to recruit an additional
50 sworn officers to fulfil this function. The exact size of
these teams and their locations will be an operational
matter for New Zealand Police.

# Back Pocket Boost for Graduates

Published by the New Zealand National Party as a PDF policy document. Source: <https://assets.national.org.nz/web/prod/Back%20Pocket%20Boost%20for%20Graduates.pdf?v=1788119937>.
The text below is the verbatim text layer of the PDF extracted with `pdftotext` (reading order). Line breaks follow the
PDF; tables and multi-column layouts may read out of order in this section, so a second rendering that preserves the
page layout (`pdftotext -layout`) follows it. Nothing has been added, removed or paraphrased.

## Full text (reading order)

Building the Future:

Back Pocket Boost for Graduates
Introduction
Encouraging young people to stay in New Zealand to
build a career, start a business, raise a family and make
a contribution to the community and economy is critical
to National’s plan to fix the basics and build the future.
Central to that vision is a low-tax society, where hardworking Kiwis keep more of their own money so they
can get ahead and save more for their own future. That

National will:
•

Reduce the compulsory student loan
repayment rate for domestic borrowers from 12
per cent to 10 per cent from 1 April 2027.

•

Get tougher on overseas borrowers, with new
financial penalties and stronger enforcement
actions.

This complements the work National has done
to boost the take-home pay of hardworking New
Zealanders. During this term of Government, we
have prioritised lower taxes for households and
businesses as part of our long-term economic plan
through:
•

Personal income tax relief worth an average of
$60 per fortnight

•

Tax relief for businesses prepared to invest and
grow through Investment Boost

•

Abolishing the Auckland Regional Fuel Tax and
the Ute Tax

•

Cancelling Labour’s tenant taxes, which pushed
rents higher and worsened the cost of living.

A re-elected National Government will continue
that work, by spending carefully, reducing wasteful
spending, supporting people to save more, and
finding opportunities for working Kiwis to have more
in their take-home pay, so life in New Zealand is
more attractive.
The economic fundamentals are increasingly shifting
in favour of building a future here at home, showing
that National’s long-term economic plan is working.
•

The New Zealand economy is projected to grow
faster than Australia and the UK for each of the
next three years.

Authorised by J de Joux, ps@national.org.nz

is why a re-elected National Government will introduce
no new taxes.
To make New Zealand even more attractive for young
Kiwis to stay and build their future, National will let Kiwis
with student loans keep more of what they earn, while
toughening up on those who leave the country before
paying back their loan.

•

220,000 new jobs are forecast to be created in
the next four years.

•

Wages are expected to grow faster than inflation
over the next four years.

•

Stable house prices and lower interest rates
have made home ownership more affordable.

•

Significant decline in wholesale energy prices in
the last two years, supporting a more competitive
manufacturing sector.

•

Fast Track is enabling investment in energy,
mining, manufacturing, housing, and commercial
construction, with 32 projects approved so far.

Those factors are helping to reverse the brain drain,
with a 14 per cent increase in Kiwis moving back
to New Zealand from Australia in the last year. But
there’s more to do.
Right now, the student loan regime is too soft on
people who leave New Zealand, and too hard on
people who stay, work and raise families here.
That can make leaving New Zealand and deferring
(or evading) student loan repayments look more
attractive for many young people.
The wider economic impact can be significant.
Losing sharp young Kiwi graduates to Sydney
and London makes it harder for Kiwi companies in
Christchurch and Auckland to take on the world and
win.
National is committed to making New Zealand even
more compelling for young Kiwis to build their future.
Improving the student loan system for those who
choose to stay in New Zealand is a key part of that
vision.

Back pocket boost for graduates

This means that:

Right now, student loan repayments are structured as
a tax, paid at 12 cents on every dollar earned above
$24,128 until the loan is fully repaid.
For a young graduate, like a nurse or an engineer,
compulsory student loan repayments can be one
of their biggest weekly costs. A young professional
earning $80,000 per year pays around $260 a fortnight
on their student loan, deducted automatically from their
pay.

•

An early career accountant earning $75,000 per
year will keep an additional $39 each fortnight, or
around $1,000 a year.

•

An early career engineer earning $80,000 per
year will keep an additional $43 each fortnight, or
around $1,100 a year.

•

A junior doctor earning $100,000 per year will keep
an additional $58 each fortnight, or around $1,500
a year.

These repayments materially increase a graduate’s
effective marginal tax rate. A borrower earning $80,000
faces a 33 per cent income tax rate plus 12 per cent
in loan repayments, or 45 cents lost from every extra
dollar earned. In practice, this often means a nurse
working an extra shift, or an engineer taking a risk on a
new role at a start-up, will only keep around half of any
additional pay.

Of course, it’s important that student loans are repaid.
Many graduates go on to successful careers, with good
salaries, so it would not be fair to make other taxpayers
heavily subsidise their education, which was the case
with Labour’s Fees Free scheme.

At the heart of National’s campaign at this year’s
election is a belief that Kiwis who work hard deserve to
keep more of what they earn.

However, National’s changes will mean that people
with student loans who choose to stay in New Zealand
will have more money in their take-home pay, often
at a time when they are just starting their careers and
are earning at the lower end of the scale for their
profession.

That is why a re-elected National Government will
reduce the compulsory student loan repayment rate
from 12 cents to 10 cents in the dollar, allowing interestfree loans to be repaid over a longer period of time.

Borrowers will also remain free to make additional,
voluntary repayments on top of their compulsory
repayments, as is the case today.

Worked example: what the change means for a new graduate

Take the example of a 24-year-old engineer with a
$65,000 student loan, starting work on $70,000 a
year, with their pay rising 3 per cent each year as
their career progresses.
Under the current 12 per cent rate, this engineer
clears their loan at age 34. Under National’s 10 per

cent rate, the loan is cleared around two years later,
at 36. Since their loan is interest-free, their slower
repayments come at no additional cost. Instead, they
have around an additional $10,000 available over
their first nine years, as they save for a deposit on a
house or start a family.

Fiscal impact
The fiscal impact of this change is summarised below.
Because a lower repayment rate delays repayments
rather than cancelling them, the cost to the operating
balance (OBEGALx) is limited to the fall in the present
value of the student loan book: the Crown gets the
same money back, but later, and because domestic
loans are interest-free, any money received later is
worth slightly less.
Most of that cost lands up front, as a one-off $283

million write-down of the existing loan book in 2026/27.
A smaller ongoing cost follows, as each year’s new
lending is written down slightly more than under current
settings.
There is also a near-term cash impact that slightly
increases net core Crown debt but does not affect
OBEGALx. This largely unwinds over time as delayed
repayments arrive.

The student loan landscape
New Zealand’s student loan scheme is one of the
Crown’s largest financial assets. The financial divide
between borrowers who stay in New Zealand and
those who move overseas is significant.
•

As at 31 March 2026, 631,310 New Zealanders had
a student loan, owing $16.8 billion in total. The
median balance is around $18,300.

•

516,586 borrowers (82 per cent) live in New
Zealand and 114,724 (18 per cent) live overseas.
Overseas borrowers hold $4.5 billion, or 26 per
cent of the total loan book.
At 31 March 2026

•

Total overdue repayments stand at $2.7 billion, of
which overseas-based borrowers owe $2.5 billion
(93 per cent).

•

84,272 overseas borrowers have overdue
repayments, averaging around $29,000 each. IRD
reports around 24,000 borrowers have debts more
than 15 years old with no repayment plan in place.

Getting tougher on borrowers in default
While National believes working New Zealanders
deserve to keep more of what they earn, it isn’t fair
for skilled graduates to move offshore and take their
skills with them, having received a heavily subsidised
education, with no penalty or bonding obligation.

That’s why, alongside more support for Kiwis who stay
in New Zealand, a re-elected National Government
will get tougher on overseas student loan borrowers,
with new financial penalties and stronger enforcement
actions.

Right now, the cost to a recipient of a tertiary degree
is only around 30 per cent of the full cost of that
qualification. A taxpayer-funded investment in those
skills can be justified when New Zealand sees a real
return from that training through a higher-skilled
workforce and stronger economic growth.

The focus of this policy is to recover more of the
cost of tertiary education from individuals who have
received significant state support while studying, and
then chosen to move overseas and make an economic
contribution in another country.

Tougher enforcement of overseas
borrowers
As at 31 March 2026, 114,724 borrowers (18 per cent
of all borrowers) were overseas-based, and 84,272 of
them (around three in four) had overdue repayments.
Overseas-based borrowers account for 93 per cent of
all overdue student loan debt, and fewer than three in
10 meet their repayment obligations in a given year,
compared to around 95 per cent of New Zealandbased borrowers.

•

•

The evidence shows action against overdue borrowing
works, but the problem is still significant, which is why a
re-elected National government will go further, with:
New financial penalties: an additional 1 per cent
annual interest on overseas-based borrower
balances, with tiered penalties for sustained
default, on top of existing late payment interest.

•

Restricted KiwiSaver withdrawals for overseas
borrowers, with any withdrawals or transfers under
the “permanent migration” test used to clear
outstanding student loan balances before they are
released.

•

Tighter arrest settings: lowering the threshold for
an arrest warrant, so warrants can be sought for
serious sustained default without needing to prove
a borrower knowingly refused to pay, and using
Customs border alerts to position warrants for
execution before departure.

•

Border monitoring: IRD is alerted when defaulters
cross the border through an information match with
Customs, and receives updated contact details
when borrowers renew their passports.

A statutory charge over New Zealand assets:
allowing IRD to register a charge or caveat over
New Zealand property owned by overseas
defaulters, without first obtaining a court judgment.

•

Offshore recovery: IRD exchanges borrower
information with the Australian Tax Office, has
registered civil proceedings against defaulters
in Australian and UK courts, and engages debt
collection agencies in both countries.

Broader information sharing: prioritising a new
data-exchange arrangement with the United
Kingdom, building on the existing arrangement with
Australia.

•

More enforcement funding: $10 million per year
of additional funding for IRD’s overseas collection
programme, with net recoveries of $15 million
per year expected after the cost of additional IRD
enforcement activity.

New enforcement measures will build on the powers
and funding already in place, which include:

•

What National will add

•

The tools IRD already has

•

Collections in the nine months to March 2026 reached
a further $233 million, up 29 per cent on the same
period a year earlier.

Interest and penalties: overseas-based borrowers
are charged interest on their balances (5.6 per cent
in 2026/27), and late payment interest of 9.6 per
cent applies to overdue amounts.
Arrest at the border: since 2014, it has been
an offence for an overseas-based borrower to
knowingly default after formal notification from IRD,
and the District Court can issue a warrant to arrest
a defaulter who is about to leave New Zealand.
In practice, the threshold is high and the power is
used only a handful of times each year.

•

Deduction notices: IRD can require New Zealand
employers and banks to deduct overdue amounts
from wages or accounts held here.

•

Compliance funding: Budget 2024 and Budget
2025 invested $29 million and a further $35 million
per year in compliance and collection.

•

Active monitoring: IRD actively monitors around
150 of the worst defaulters (owing a combined
$15 million, or roughly $100,000 each) for arrest if
they cross the border. Earlier this year, a medical
specialist who had built a 30-year career in
Australia was arrested at the airport over $180,000
in student loan arrears, spending three nights in
custody before arrangements were made.

The recent focus on enforcement is working. IRD
collected $243 million from overseas borrowers in
2024/25, beating its $189 million target by 28 per cent.

A conservative investment case
The $15 million per year of net recoveries assumes
gross returns of around $2.50 for every dollar invested.
That is conservative relative to IRD’s recent record.
IRD’s overall compliance programme returned $11.81
for every dollar invested in 2024/25, up from $9.50
the year before. Overseas student loan collections
exceeded IRD’s target by 28 per cent in the same year.
The lower assumed return reflects that this funding is
targeted specifically at overseas student loan debt,
where much of the outstanding amount is old and hard
to recover. It is also collected from individuals offshore
rather than businesses onshore. However, based
on recent performance, actual returns could exceed
budgeted savings.

# Backing First Home Buyers

Published by the New Zealand National Party as a PDF policy document. Source: <https://assets.national.org.nz/web/prod/Backing%20First%20Home%20Buyers.pdf?v=1788652154>.
The text below is the verbatim text layer of the PDF extracted with `pdftotext` (reading order). Line breaks follow the
PDF; tables and multi-column layouts may read out of order in this section, so a second rendering that preserves the
page layout (`pdftotext -layout`) follows it. Nothing has been added, removed or paraphrased.

## Full text (reading order)

Building the Future:

Backing First Home Buyers
Introduction
Owning a home is a central part of the Kiwi dream.
Home ownership provides families with stability,
financial security and a stronger stake in their
communities. It is also part of what makes
New Zealand an attractive place for ambitious
young people to build a career, raise a family and
invest in their future.
National believes that New Zealand should be a
country where if you work hard, you should be able
to get ahead.

National will:
•

Widen access to 5 per cent deposit home loans
by extending the First Home Loan income cap
to $300,000.

•

Apply the $300,000 income cap to all
applicants – a change from the current criteria of
the First Home Loan scheme where the income
cap for individual buyers with no dependents
is $95,000 and multiple buyers combined or
individual buyers with dependents is $150,000.

National wants more Kiwis to own their own home
because that is part of how people build their
financial security. Our long-term objective is to
restore New Zealand to peak homeownership rates
of around 74 per cent, up from 66 per cent currently.
Evidence increasingly suggests conditions are
improving for prospective home buyers:
•

First home buyers reached a record market
share of 29 per cent in July 2026.

•

Deposit affordability has improved by 11 per cent
since December 2023.

•

Mortgage serviceability has improved by 61 per
cent over the same period as interest rates have
come down, with the Official Cash Rate falling
from 5.5 per cent in December 2023 to 2.75
per cent today.

•

Housing supply continues to expand across
major urban centres.

•

Rents have remained broadly flat, after they went
up an average of $180 per week under Labour.

These improvements demonstrate that increasing
housing supply remains the most effective long-term
solution to improving affordability.
However, affordability challenges remain, particularly
for younger New Zealanders attempting to save
a deposit while managing everyday living costs.
For many households, the largest obstacle to
purchasing a first home is not servicing a mortgage
but accumulating an adequate deposit.

Authorised by J de Joux, ps@national.org.nz

That’s why a re-elected National Government will
introduce no new taxes, boost KiwiSaver savings,
extend paid parental leave, implement a rates cap
and lower the repayment rate for student loans.
It’s all part of our plan to make it easier for Kiwis
to get ahead and build their future in New Zealand.
The next part of that plan is to support more
New Zealanders to achieve the Kiwi dream of owning
their own home by making it easier to get a deposit
for a house through the First Home Loan scheme.

Most lenders require borrowers to contribute a
minimum deposit of 20 per cent. On a $750,000
home, that requires savings of $150,000 before
a purchase can proceed.
The First Home Loan scheme helps overcome this
barrier by allowing eligible buyers to purchase a
home with a deposit of as little as 5 per cent. First
Home Loans are issued by selected banks and other
lenders, and underwritten by Kāinga Ora. This allows
the lender to provide loans that would otherwise sit
outside their lending standards.
The scheme was originally established in 2003
as the ‘In Reach’ pilot programme and was
rebranded as the First Home Loan in 2019. It is
administered through Kāinga Ora in partnership
with participating lenders and has already helped
over 33,000 households into home ownership.
Between 1 July 2025 and 30 April 2026, more than
7,700 First Home Loan applications were approved.
The scheme has proven effective, but the income
thresholds that determine eligibility have not
kept pace with wage growth and current housing
market conditions.
To be eligible for a 5 per cent deposit under
the current scheme, individual buyers with no
dependents must earn $95,000 or less. Multiple
buyers combined or individual buyers with
dependents must earn $150,000 or less
The average gross income of first home buyers is
now approximately $146,000. This means around
half of ordinary working households buying their first
home exceed the current eligibility cap despite still
facing significant deposit constraints.
To address this, a re-elected National Government
will increase the income cap to $300,000, which
means more Kiwis will be able to access a 5 per cent
deposit rather than the standard 20 per cent. We
will apply the $300,000 threshold to all applicants,
including individuals without dependants.

Backing First Home Buyers
The current income limits under the First Home
Loan scheme increasingly exclude many working
New Zealanders who are capable of servicing a
mortgage but still struggle to save a 20 per cent
deposit as they juggle everyday costs like rent,
food and childcare.

Current income limits under the First Home
Loan scheme are:
Current
Income Cap

Applicant Type

$95,000

Multiple buyers or individual buyers
with dependants

combined

Examples of people excluded from the
current First Home Loan scheme:
•

A junior doctor earning around $100,000.

•

A young couple comprising an electrician earning
$85,000 and a secondary school teacher earning
$78,000.

•

A couple comprising a civil engineer project
manager on $130,000 and a nurse practitioner
on $150,000.

Nobody will get a bigger mortgage than their bank
says they can afford. The First Home Loan lowers the
deposit hurdle, not the income servicing test. Lenders
will still assess every applicant against stress-tested
interest rates and their responsible lending obligations,
and the lender ultimately makes the final decision.
This policy complements National’s wider housing
programme focused on increasing housing supply,
improving affordability and lifting home ownership
rates over time.
For three decades, a jungle of red tape constrained the
supply of new homes, pushing rents higher and putting
the dream of home ownership out of reach for tens of
thousands of New Zealanders.
For the first time in a generation, that’s changing. In July
this year, first home buyers made up 29 per cent of all
purchases – the highest monthly share in more than
20 years.
This Government’s reforms have accelerated that
success, by enabling greater housing supply in our city
centres, close to rapid transit, and on greenfield sites
on our urban fringe. That is because of work advanced
by National including:
•

The Going for Housing Growth programme

•

Fast Track

•

Permissive granny flat rules

•

Earthquake-prone-building reform

•

Improvements to the Building Act

•

Tackling joint and several liability

•

What National’s changes means
for first home buyers

Major changes to the Credit Contracts and
Consumer Finance Act

•

Self-certification for trusted builders

The First Home Loan scheme reduces the size of the
deposit required to purchase a home. For example:

•

Unlocking safe overseas building products

•

Upzoning Auckland through Plan Change 120

•

Resource Management Act reform.

•

Two or three mates who have recently graduated
from police college earning more than $77,000
each.

Difference

National’s changes mean that all first home buyers
earning up to $300,000 will be able to access the
scheme, no matter whether they are single without
dependents or a couple.

Fiscal Impact
The First Home Loan scheme cost approximately
$14.5 million to administer during FY2024/25 while
supporting 3,085 loan underwrites. This included the
cost of Government subsidising the cost of Lenders
Mortgage Insurance. The decision in Budget 2025
requiring borrowers to meet the full cost of Lenders
Mortgage Insurance then substantially reduced the
ongoing fiscal cost of the scheme.
Allowing for a doubling in the size of the First Home
Loan scheme, the fiscal impact of this policy would
be $4-6 million, which is expected to be funded from
existing baselines.

documents/pdf-backing-our-firefighters.m.text:
# Backing our firefighters

Published by the New Zealand National Party as a PDF policy document. Source: <https://assets.national.org.nz/web/prod/Backing%20our%20firefighters.pdf?v=1790120300>.
The text below is the verbatim text layer of the PDF extracted with `pdftotext` (reading order). Line breaks follow the
PDF; tables and multi-column layouts may read out of order in this section, so a second rendering that preserves the
page layout (`pdftotext -layout`) follows it. Nothing has been added, removed or paraphrased.

## Full text (reading order)

Backing our firefighters:

National’s three-point plan to fix
Fire and Emergency New Zealand
More than 14,000 firefighters, including volunteers, paid
staff, and frontline enablers, work hard every day to
keep our communities safe, often leaving paid jobs or
loved ones to respond when the public calls for help.
The service of our firefighters is one of the strongest
expressions of community in New Zealand. They
deserve more than our thanks; they deserve an
organisation that is as reliable and prepared as they
are. Nine years after Fire and Emergency New Zealand
was created, frontline firefighters still face equipment
and training shortages, and an organisation that has
shown itself to be unable to respond to the demands
and pressures of the front line.

National backs our firefighters, and we know that things
can be much better. Fire and Emergency New Zealand
can, and should, do better to support their volunteers.
National initiated an inquiry into Fire and Emergency
New Zealand’s fleet following confusing and
contradictory evidence, years of delays, and regular
reports from firefighters about trucks breaking
down or being unavailable. There is widespread
acknowledgement that the situation is not acceptable.
National will reset Fire and Emergency New Zealand
by backing firefighters and restoring accountability.

A re-elected National Government will:
1.

Restore accountability and reset Fire and Emergency New Zealand;

2. Support volunteer firefighters by requiring Fire and Emergency New Zealand to provide additional mental
and physical health support;
3.

Back the front line with the tools they need to do their job.

Authorised by J de Joux, ps@national.org.nz

1.	 Restoring accountability and
resetting the organisation.
Fire and Emergency New Zealand is a Crown agent
governed by a board and accountable through the
Internal Affairs portfolio. There are too many layers of
bureaucracy and accountability separating the front line
from Government.
The Board model has not given Ministers, Parliament
or the public the clear line of sight and accountability
they need over our national fire service. Firefighters
need confidence that decisions about stations, training,
staffing, health and safety, rural capability and major
capital projects are being made for the right reasons
and delivering tangible outcomes.
Similarly, the public need confidence that the money
collected through their insurance levies is reaching
the frontline.
Fire and Emergency New Zealand responds to
structure and vegetation fires, floods, storms, motor
vehicle accidents, hazardous substances, rescues,
medical events and national emergencies. It is a core
part of New Zealand’s emergency response system and
should be governed as one. A departmental agency
model, similar to the National Emergency Management
Agency, would retain professional operational
leadership while creating a direct and visible line
of accountability to the Minister for Emergency
Management and Recovery.

National will:
•

Clear unnecessary bureaucracy by removing
the Fire and Emergency New Zealand Board,
reorganising it as a departmental agency
accountable to a Minister, similar to the
National Emergency Management Agency;

•

Make Fire and Emergency New Zealand
directly accountable to the Minister for
Emergency Management and Recovery,
leaving operationally independent decisionmaking with fire and emergency professionals;

•

Direct Fire and Emergency New Zealand to
develop and implement a turnaround plan;
and

•

Meet all costs of this package of reforms
within baselines.

2. Supporting volunteer firefighters.
More than 11,000 volunteers serve communities from
over 600 stations. They step forward when their
communities need them most. Many volunteers serve
alongside paid firefighters at fires, crashes, floods
and traumatic incidents, wear the same protective
equipment and face the same risks.
Volunteer firefighters put themselves in harm’s way for
their communities; they deserve to be looked after if
they are injured or harmed as a result of their service.
That is why National will require Fire and Emergency
New Zealand to provide better mental health and injury
support for its frontline volunteers.
Volunteer firefighters can already access treatment
and rehabilitation through the public health system and
ACC. ACC provides a range of support, including cover
for qualifying physical injuries, mental injuries caused
by a covered physical injury, and treatment injuries.
It can also provide weekly compensation to eligible
volunteers where a covered injury prevents them from
doing their usual paid work.
These protections are important, but National believes
the support should not stop there.
National will require Fire and Emergency New Zealand
to provide an additional safety net for operational
volunteers affected by event-based mental injury and
gradual process injuries arising from their service. This
will help them access treatment, rehabilitation and
financial support when their service affects their health
or ability to work, through private insurance funded
by Fire and Emergency New Zealand. Mental injury
support is particularly important in rural communities,
where volunteers may respond to incidents involving
family or friends.

National will:
•

Require Fire and Emergency New Zealand
to provide private insurance covering eventbased mental injury and gradual process
injuries for operational volunteers, giving
volunteers and their families greater support
and financial security.

3.	 Backing the frontline with the tools they need to do the job.
Firefighters should have confidence that they have
the tools for the job. They need to know that the
truck in the bay will be available when the alarm
sounds and that their equipment is safe and fit
for purpose.
Fire and Emergency New Zealand has bought
hundreds of Type 1 and 2 appliances since 2017.
Additionally, they have ordered over 100 Type
3s and five aerial appliances. Serious failures in
both acquisition and introduction to service have
meant that less than half of Type 3s, and no aerial
appliances, have entered regular operational service.
The most recent Type 3s were ordered in 2019 but
none of the 30 appliances are currently operational.
The answer is not simply to place another order.
Appliances already purchased need to be accepted
and put into use. Future purchases need to be
transparent, follow due process, and not be delayed
by constant design changes. More consideration
should be given to off-the-shelf products.
Fleet renewal must also become continuous. A fire
appliance should last 20-25 years, but that relies
on Fire and Emergency New Zealand continually
renewing fleet each year so there are no spikes of
over-age appliances in use.
Additionally, the current state of live fire training is
unacceptable. Too often, new recruits are seeing
their first fire when responding to a real callout. Live
fire training must be a priority for Fire and Emergency
New Zealand.

National will:
•

Ensure Fire and Emergency New Zealand
get all currently ordered Type 3, 5 and 6
appliances delivered, accepted, and into
operational use;

•

Direct Fire and Emergency New Zealand
to develop a long-term fleet management
plan, with a 10-year procurement programme
that makes better use of existing funding
and brings average fleet age within
expected limits;

•

Use that plan to secure production slots
in advance and establish a predictable
replacement cycle, maintaining fleet age
limits and avoiding costly, ad hoc purchasing;

•

Direct Fire and Emergency New Zealand
to prioritise a plan to restore full live fire
training (not just gas prop) for all recruit
training courses;

•

Work with emergency services to modernise
axle mass rules, cutting red tape to allow fire
appliances to operate with the equipment and
water firefighters need to save lives; and

•

Allow Fire and Emergency New Zealand to
prioritise operational capability over emissions
profiles for frontline operational vehicles.
