# Building the Future - Backing Auckland to succeed

Published by the New Zealand National Party as a PDF policy document. Source: <https://assets.national.org.nz/web/prod/Building%20the%20Future%20-%20Backing%20Auckland%20to%20succeed.pdf?v=1791921113>.
The text below is the verbatim text layer of the PDF extracted with `pdftotext` (reading order). Line breaks follow the
PDF; tables and multi-column layouts may read out of order in this section, so a second rendering that preserves the
page layout (`pdftotext -layout`) follows it. Nothing has been added, removed or paraphrased.

## Full text (reading order)

Building the Future:

Backing Auckland
to succeed

Building the Future:

Backing Auckland to succeed
National is excited for Auckland’s future and, if
re-elected, will spend the next three years continuing
to back our largest city to grow and prosper.

Crime is also falling in Auckland. Between 2023 and
2025, burglaries fell 16 per cent, theft fell 11 per cent,
and Police foot patrols have increased significantly.

We share Aucklanders’ vision for a city where
families can get ahead, businesses can succeed,
and communities can be proud of where they live.

Fewer Auckland families are living in emergency
housing too, with the number of households falling
from 885 in November 2023 to 81 in August 2026.

Auckland is New Zealand’s largest economic
centre and home to more than 1.8 million Kiwis,
and contributes nearly 40% to our national GDP.

And household pressures are easing. Lower mortgage
rates mean an Auckland household with an average
sized mortgage could be paying more than $9000
less a year than under mid-2023 rates, while rents are
increasing at their slowest rate in around 25 years.

When Auckland succeeds, New Zealand succeeds.
Under National the economy is growing faster than
the US, the UK, Canada, and Australia. Exports are up
$20 billion, inflation is down from a 32-year high, and
220,000 new jobs are expected with wages growing
faster than prices.
We want to help Auckland capitalise on that opportunity.
National has a strong record of backing Auckland, from
the Waterview Tunnel and City Rail Link to the new
infrastructure and services being delivered today.
This term, we have opened the City Rail Link, funded
727 new classrooms, expanded cancer treatment in
West Auckland, restored 24/7 urgent care in Counties
Manukau, secured land in Drury for a future South
Auckland hospital, signed the Auckland Regional Deal,
and funded two Roads of National Significance that will
benefit Aucklanders.
And the results are starting to show.
In Auckland, regular school attendance has risen to
66.7 per cent, while 85.3 per cent of school leavers
now achieve at least NCEA Level 2 or above.
More patients are being seen sooner. The proportion
of Auckland emergency department patients being
dealt with within six hours has risen from 67.1 per cent
in 2023/24 to 77.3 per cent in 2025/26.

Authorised by J de Joux, ps@national.org.nz

There is more to do. Auckland is still growing, and
National’s focus is on building the infrastructure,
services and opportunities the city needs for the future.

A re-elected National Government will:
• Plan ahead for Auckland’s future, working
with Auckland Council through the Auckland
Deal to align housing, infrastructure and
economic growth.
• Build the infrastructure Auckland needs to
grow, with better transport, more classrooms
and health services that keep pace with
new communities.
• Back Auckland families with the cost of
living, by growing the economy, supporting
more housing and keeping pressure off
household costs.
• Keep driving crime down, with more visible
Police, tougher consequences for serious and
repeat offenders, and safer neighbourhoods
and public spaces.
• Keep lifting health and education
performance, so patients are seen and treated
sooner, more children are in school, and more
young Aucklanders leave with the skills and
qualifications they need.

Growth and opportunity: unlocking Auckland’s potential
Auckland’s future is not just about building more roads,
classrooms and hospitals. It is also about making better
use of the infrastructure we already have, removing
rules that hold the city back, supporting more homes
and jobs, and backing the places and institutions that
make Auckland attractive to live in, work in and visit.
National is making it easier for Auckland to grow in
the right places and take advantage of the investment
already going into the city.

Already delivering
• Unlocking more homes around key City Rail Link
stations, enabling greater density in the places that
make sense.
• Unlocked Auckland’s City Centre, progressing the
removal of planning restrictions that are holding the
CBD back, potentially allowing for 17,000 additional
dwellings and 37,200 more jobs.
• Opening Eden Park up to more major events, with
planning restrictions eased for more concerts, sport
and cultural events.
• Keeping water infrastructure affordable, saving
Auckland households an estimated $899 million
over four years while enabling record Watercare
investment.

• Delivering more social housing, with more than
3,000 net new social homes added across Auckland
since November 2023.
• Bringing more major events and visitors to Auckland,
with the New Zealand International Convention Centre
now open. Next year’s State of Origin match, alone, is
expected to bring in more than 50,000 international
visitor nights and $17.4 million in economic activity.
• Backing Auckland as a technology and innovation
hub, with the New Zealand Institute for Advanced
Technology launched at GridAKL.
• Scrapped the Auckland Regional Fuel Tax, taking
11.5 cents a litre off the price of petrol and diesel for
Auckland motorists.
• Reformed the planning system, ensuring that
Aucklanders can do more with their property without
having to battle red tape, which could remove the
need for 45% of resource consents.
• 13 Fast-track projects approved, including the
Auckland Port Expansion – creating thousands of
jobs and billions in investment.
• Invested $400m nationwide to support councils
with the costs of housing growth.

• Saving Auckland building owners around $4.5 billion
through earthquake-prone building reforms, removing
more than 1,300 Auckland buildings from costly
strengthening requirements that were disproportionate
to the city’s relatively low seismic risk.
• Securing the future of the ASB classic, contributing
$5 million towards a new centre court roof that will
protect play from the weather and open the venue to
more major events year-round.

Aucklanders know all about the access and safety
issues this policy has created. Some people are having
to walk 10 minutes or more to get home from where
they’ve parked. We’re committing to fixed it.

A re-elected National Government will:
• Abolish the blanket ban on minimum car
parking requirements.

• Brought the Michelin Guide to New Zealand for
the first time, putting Auckland’s food scene on
the global stage, with 46 Auckland restaurants
recognised, including five awarded a Michelin star.

• Allow councils to use minimum car parking
requirements in suburban areas outside those
identified for intensification (e.g. in city centres
or around rapid transit stops).

Next, National will…

This means councils will be able to set minimum
car parking requirements in many suburban
neighbourhoods, greenfield subdivisions, and
business and industrial parks.

National backs growth and wants Auckland to grow
further. But we know that some Kiwis are concerned
about what growth means for them and their streets,
especially in suburban Auckland.
The blanket ban on minimum car parking requirements
has not worked and does not account for the reality
of New Zealand’s suburban streets. Many streets,
especially in Auckland, are clogged and hard to
get through, and people are now parking on berms
and footpaths.

New homes should come with the parking
residents need – in the right places. National
will unclog our streets and make them safer and
more manageable, enabling our suburbs to be
more liveable.

Transport: connecting a growing Auckland
Getting around Auckland should not be one of the
hardest parts of the day. But too many Aucklanders
are still spending too much time sitting in traffic. For
families, that is time lost at home. For tradies and small
businesses, it means fewer jobs in a day. For exporters
and freight operators, congestion adds cost every time
goods have to move across the city.
Under this National-led Government, Auckland has
started moving again. But there is more work to do.
We have to keep investing in the state highway network
that our growing city depends on.
A re-elected National government will allocate $1.75
billion in Budget 2028 to start building Mill Road
Stage One, connecting Manukau and Alfriston, with
construction beginning in late 2028.
We will also invest $100 million to protect the route
for Stages Two and Three towards Drury, making sure
future governments can continue the connection south
as demand grows.

Already delivering
National has already made good progress on some
of Auckland’s biggest transport priorities, with major
projects completed, funded or now underway.
• City Rail Link is open, giving Aucklanders a faster
and more connected rail network.
• The Eastern Busway is underway, with funding
approved and construction progressing on the final
connection to Botany.
• Auckland is receiving a record $8.4 billion in
transport investment through the 2024–27 National
Land Transport Programme.
• The Auckland Deal has been signed, creating a
long-term framework for Government and Auckland
Council to plan infrastructure, housing and transport
growth together.
• Transport decision-making has been reformed,
restoring democracy and accountability to transport
in Auckland and laying the foundations for a joint
Crown/Council 30-year transport plan.

• Invested in critical new Roads of National
Significance in Northland and Waikato, to improve
regional connectivity for people and freight heading
to and from Auckland.
• Improved the rail network, with the Third Main Line,
electrification to Pukekohe, and new stations at
Drury and Paerātā now open, with a third to open
at Ngākōroa next year.
• Accelerated level crossing removals in Takanini
and Glen Innes, improving safety for pedestrians and
efficiency for motorists in South and East Auckland.

Next, National will
• Fund $1.75 billion to construct Mill Road Stage
One and $100 million to route protect Stages Two
and Three, progressing this critical new transport
connection for South Auckland.
• Take the next steps on Auckland’s future harbour
crossing, progressing the Detailed Business Case
and the work needed to determine how this project
can be funded and delivered.
• Complete the Eastern Busway through to Botany,
giving East Auckland a faster and more reliable
public transport connection.
• Progress North-West Rapid Transit, improving
public transport along one of Auckland’s busiest and
fastest-growing corridors.
• Progress CRL level-crossing removals, improving
connections and safety across South and East
Auckland and making the rail network safer and
more reliable.
• Deliver the Auckland Deal, including a coordinated
30-year transport strategy so Auckland can plan
ahead rather than constantly play catch-up.
• Explore options to speed up rapid transit projects
like the Botany to Airport Busway, through rescoping
and cost saving measures.

Law and order: keeping crime
coming down

What we’re doing next

Aucklanders should feel safe in their homes, walking
through their neighbourhoods, running a business,
heading into the city, or catching public transport.

The focus has been on getting Police back into
communities, strengthening consequences for
serious and repeat offending, and targeting the
places Aucklanders should be able to use without
fear of crime or intimidation.

For too long, too many Aucklanders saw crime
becoming more common and more brazen. National
has been focused on restoring consequences for
offenders, putting Police back into communities and
making public spaces safer.

National has also announced a dedicated Auckland
Transport Police Team within New Zealand Police,
adding a visible Police presence across buses, trains,
ferries, stations and interchanges and supporting
Auckland Transport’s existing transport officers.

The early results are encouraging, but there is much
more to do.

National will

Between 2023 and 2025, burglaries across Auckland
fell by 16 per cent, theft fell by 11.0 per cent, and
robbery, blackmail and extortion fell by 5 per cent.
At the same time, there have been an increase in
police foot patrols across Auckland, with a 203%
increase in Waitemata, 156% in Counties Manukau,
and 11% in Auckland City.
Ram raids have also collapsed from their 2022 peak.
Across Auckland’s three Police districts, recorded ram
raids fell from 348 in 2022 to just 14 in 2025, a 96 per
cent reduction.

• Deliver the Auckland Transport Police Team and
make public transport safer, putting dedicated
officers across buses, trains, ferries, stations and
interchanges to protect passengers and staff.
• Keep Police visible and focused on the places and
offenders causing the most harm, with a strong
presence in neighbourhoods, town centres and other
public spaces.
• Keep driving down burglary, theft and violent
offending, with tougher consequences for serious
and repeat offenders and a continued focus on
reducing the number of victims.

Frontline services: healthcare closer
to home
When you are sick, you should be able to get the care
you need quickly and close to home.
That means knowing urgent care is available when
your child gets sick at night. It means cancer patients
spending less time travelling across the city for regular
treatment. And it means making sure Auckland has
the hospital capacity, specialist services and health
workforce it will need as the city grows.
National inherited a health system from Labour where
too many Aucklanders were waiting too long.
In Auckland district, the proportion of emergency
department patients dealt with within six hours fell from
89.9 per cent in 2017/18 to 67.1 per cent in 2023/24,
elective treatment within four months fell from 92.5 per
cent to 65.6 per cent, and immunisation coverage for
two-year-olds fell from 94.0% to 76.3%.
But under National, that decline is starting to turn around.
By 2025/26, 77.3 per cent of Auckland emergency
department patients were dealt with within six hours,
elective treatment to 69.3 per cent, and immunisation
coverage for two-year-olds reached 88.2 per cent.
But there is still more to do.

National is already delivering
Improving the numbers matters, but so does what
patients can see and experience on the ground.
National is investing in more services, more capacity
and better access to care across Auckland.
• Cancer patients in West Auckland can now receive
more treatment closer to home, with infusion
services opened at Waitākere Hospital and Te
Whānau o Waipareira’s Whānau Centre in Henderson.
• Families in South and East Auckland once again have
access to urgent care 24 hours a day, after round-theclock services were restored in Counties Manukau.
• Land has been secured for a future South Auckland
hospital, with the purchase of a 13-hectare site in Drury.
• A new 30-bed spinal rehabilitation centre is being
built at Manukau Health Park, backed by $128.5
million of investment.
• Auckland City Hospital is getting upgraded stroke
and interventional radiology services, with new
investment increasing capacity and replacing ageing
equipment used in some of the most complex
procedures.
• Cardiac services are being upgraded across the
region, with catheter laboratory improvements
planned or underway at Auckland City, Counties
Manukau, North Shore and Starship.
• More care is being shifted closer to patients
through primary care, with a new Auckland and
Northland workforce hub supporting more than 400
GP clinics and training clinicians to provide more
procedures outside hospital.

Next, National will
The next step is to keep lifting performance while
building the health services Auckland will need for the
decades ahead.
• Reduce waits and improve outcomes for Aucklanders,
continuing to deliver National’s elective boost with
more hip, knee and cataract surgeries, alongside
a continued focus on emergency care, specialist
assessments and childhood immunisation.
• Catch cancer earlier and get more medicines
to Aucklanders, with a further $604 million for
Pharmac, free bowel screening from age 50, free
breast screening extended to 74, free cervical
screening for women aged 25 to 69, and new
prostate and lung cancer screening pilots.

• Build more care closer to home across Auckland,
through local hospitals, primary care, community
providers and 24/7 urgent care in South and East
Auckland, while continuing to invest in Auckland’s
specialist services and hospital capacity.
• Progress the future South Auckland hospital at
Drury, now that the 13 hectare Karaka Road site
has been secured, so planning can continue for the
services Auckland’s growing south will need.

Education: classrooms for growing
communities
When families move into a growing community, they
need to know there will be a place for their children
at a good local school.
That means making sure new housing is matched by
new classrooms, and that schools have the space and
facilities they need as rolls grow. It also means investing
in specialist education, so children with high and
complex needs can learn in an environment designed
for them.

Already delivering

• Secure land now for the schools growing
communities will need next, with land acquired for
a future secondary school in Kumeū and planning
underway, alongside funding to secure a 3.2-hectare
site for a future primary school in Drury East.

better educational outcomes. Auckland is making
progress on both attendance and achievement.

National is building more classrooms across Auckland,
with 727 new classrooms funded. Of these, 228 have
already been delivered, 203 are under construction,
and a further 296 are fully funded and ready to
get underway.

Next, National will

That investment is creating more space in schools now,
while preparing for the families who will move into
Auckland’s growing communities in the years ahead.

The next step is to keep building the classrooms
Auckland needs while lifting attendance and
achievement across the city.

• Deliver more classrooms across Auckland, with
228 already completed and another 499 funded and
in the pipeline, including expansions at Ahutoetoe
School, Scott Point School and Ormiston Senior
College.

• Deliver the remaining 499 funded classrooms,
completing the 203 already under construction and
getting the next 296 underway.

• Build new schools in fast-growing communities,
with the new Flat Bush primary school already open,
Massey Redhills Primary opening in early 2027, a
new 30-classroom junior college under construction
at Chapel Downs, and a new 14-classroom primary
school planned for Pōkeno West.
• Expand specialist education in South Auckland,
with Drury Specialist School under construction,
providing six purpose-built classrooms for up to 54
students with high and complex needs and planned
to open in Term 1, 2028.

• Progress Drury Specialist School towards opening
in Term 1, 2028, delivering six classrooms for up to
54 students with high and complex needs.
• Secure the Drury East primary-school site, protecting
the land needed for future school capacity as
southern Auckland grows.
• Keep lifting attendance, so more Auckland children
are in the classroom regularly and getting the benefit
of every school day.
• Keep improving achievement, with a focus on
making sure more students leave school with
the qualifications they need for work, training or
further study.

# Building the Future - Belfast to Pegasus and Woodend Bypass

Published by the New Zealand National Party as a PDF policy document. Source: <https://assets.national.org.nz/web/prod/Building%20the%20Future%20-%20Belfast%20to%20Pegasus%20and%20Woodend%20Bypass.pdf?v=1791173966>.
The text below is the verbatim text layer of the PDF extracted with `pdftotext` (reading order). Line breaks follow the
PDF; tables and multi-column layouts may read out of order in this section, so a second rendering that preserves the
page layout (`pdftotext -layout`) follows it. Nothing has been added, removed or paraphrased.

## Full text (reading order)

Building the Future:

SH1 Belfast to Pegasus Motorway
and Woodend Bypass
More New Zealanders are choosing to make
Canterbury home, drawn by affordable housing,
good jobs and a great lifestyle. National is committed
to supporting Christchurch and the wider region
to grow.

•

Began construction of the Second Ashburton
Bridge, keeping our promise to start it in our first
term. This is a key route for ensuring our people
and goods can get up and down the South Island
and needs to be future proofed.

Canterbury is the engine room of the South Island.
It is home to around 695,000 people, roughly one
in eight New Zealanders, and is our second-largest
regional economy, generating $55.5 billion of GDP
in the year to March 2025.

•

Invested $38.5 million towards the replacement
of Christchurch’s nearly 100-year-old Pages Road
Bridge, the lifeline and evacuation route for New
Brighton and Southshore, carrying more than
13,000 vehicles a day.

North Canterbury is at the forefront of that growth.
The Waimakariri District has more than doubled in size
since the early 1990s to around 70,000 people, making
it one of the fastest-growing districts in the country.

•

Began work on the SH1 Rolleston Access
Improvements project, making it safer and
easier to enter or exit Rolleston and providing
a less congested connection for freight into the
industrial area.

•

Successfully launched the National Ticketing
Solution in Canterbury, the first city in the country
to benefit from this $1.36 billion investment to
provide an easier and more convenient way for
passengers to pay for public transport.

•

Completed major roading improvements for
State Highway 75/Halswell Road in Christchurch
competed months ahead of schedule, increasing
resilience and supporting housing growth in the
southwest of Christchurch.

But the roads haven’t kept up. They face long queues
at peak times, a main street clogged with trucks,
and a poor safety record. Under this National-led
Government, the Belfast to Pegasus Motorway and
Woodend Bypass is finally moving after two decades
of talk, and if re-elected, the next National government
will fund it and get it built.

Building on National’s investments in
Canterbury
National has a proud history of delivering for
Canterbury.
•

Increased transport investment in Canterbury
to $1.8 billion, around 50 per cent more than
under Labour.

•

Funded upgrades to SH76 Brougham Street, one
of Christchurch’s busiest roads and the main freight
route to Lyttelton Port, carrying more than 45,000
vehicles a day. Construction began in July 2025.

•

Progressed Belfast to Pegasus and the
Woodend Bypass, allocating $127 million to preimplementation, property purchase and early
works. Early physical works are already under
way, and the project secured fast-track approval
in July 2026.

Authorised by J de Joux, ps@national.org.nz

National’s Canterbury Transport Plan
A re-elected National Government will:
•

Fully fund construction of the Belfast to
Pegasus Motorway and Woodend Bypass,
so NZTA begin to deliver this important project
for Canterbury.

•

Commit $800 million in our first Budget to
deliver the project, with construction starting
next year.

Belfast to Pegasus Motorway and
Woodend Bypass
The Belfast to Pegasus Motorway and Woodend Bypass
will extend the Christchurch Northern Motorway around
11 kilometres north, from just south of the Waimakariri
River to beyond Pegasus and Ravenswood.
This much needed road will boost economic growth,
reduce congestion, and improve safety. SH1 approaching
Woodend currently carries around 21,500 vehicles per
day, of which nine percent is freight. The traffic volume
is expected to reach 28,000 vehicles per day by 2048.
There were 280 crashes on SH1 through Woodend
between 2014 and 2023, with three fatalities and 25
serious injuries.
During peak times it can take up to 20 minutes to travel
through Woodend, and it’s difficult for people to access
the shops, or drop off and pick up children from the local
primary school.
This project will improve travel times, reduce congestion,
and improve safety. It includes:

Delivering this project has substantial benefits, including
up to 10 minutes time saving at peak. It is expected to
reduce traffic through Woodend from 21,500 vehicles
per day to 8,000, and a reduction in deaths and serious
injuries by 78%.
This project demonstrates strong value for money,
returning up to $2.30 in benefits for every dollar
invested.
Critically, it will also make the corridor more reliable for
people and freight travelling to and from Christchurch,
Christchurch Airport and Lyttelton Port.
For locals, the bypass means getting their town centre
back. With through-traffic and heavy trucks moved from
Woodend onto the new motorway, enabling a safer and
more vibrant main street.
Because of National’s work in Government, the project
is ready to go and is the next investment-ready project
on the Major Transport Projects Pipeline. We will fund
the Belfast to Pegasus Motorway and Woodend Bypass
directly in our first budget, allowing construction to
commence in 2027.

•

Widening the southern section of the existing SH1
from two to four lanes.

Fiscal impact

•

A new four-lane motorway bypass in the northern
section.

•

A grade separated interchange at the Williams
Street intersection with SH1.

National’s Canterbury Transport Plan commits
$800 million of Crown capital, held in tagged
contingency and released once the project is ready
to proceed.

•

Replace the Pegasus roundabout with an
overbridge and signalised intersection.

•

Kaiapoi Bridge seismic strengthening and widening.

•

Construction of new bridges over the Cam River
and overbridges at Woodend Beach Road and
Gladstone Road.

$800 million will be provided to deliver construction
of the Belfast to Pegasus Motorway and Woodend
Bypass, based on the 2025 NZTA Investment
Case. Any additional costs to be met from the State
Highway Improvements Activity class of National Land
Transport Fund.

Building the Future:

Mill Road

National knows that when Auckland succeeds,
New Zealand succeeds.
Auckland is New Zealand’s capital city of growth. It is
home to one third of New Zealand’s population and
contributes nearly 40% to our national GDP. It has
higher labour productivity than the rest of New Zealand,
and is home to some of New Zealand’s most exciting
growth-industries, with 116 of our country’s top 200 tech
firms calling Auckland home.
We are not going to be successful in growing our
economy if we don’t think carefully about how we
enable Auckland, as our largest and most important
city, to thrive. If it is congested and hard to get around,
the whole country pays for it through increased prices
being passed on to consumers.
Under this National-led Government, Auckland has
started moving again. But there is more work to do.
We have to keep investing in the state highway network
that our growing city depends on.

Building on National’s investments in
Auckland
National has already put the foundations in place to
support Auckland’s growth.
•

We scrapped Auckland’s Regional Fuel Tax on
30 June 2024, taking 11.5 cents a litre off the price
of petrol and diesel for Auckland motorists.

•

Invested in critical new Roads of National
Significance in Northland and Waikato, to improve
regional connectivity for people and freight heading
to and from Auckland.

•

The City Rail Link is open - National funded it,
and National has seen it completed. The CRL
will fundamentally change the way Auckland’s
rail network operates, with faster journeys, more
frequent services, and better connections across
the city.

Authorised by J de Joux, ps@national.org.nz

•

We have delivered the reforms to Auckland
transport governance restoring democracy and
accountability to transport in our largest city and
laying the foundations for a joint Crown/Council
30-year transport plan.

•

The Third Main Line, electrification to Pukekohe,
and new stations at Drury and Paerātā are now
open, with a third to open at Ngākōroa next year.
That means more reliable train journeys, and rail
access for the fastest-growing communities in
the south.

•

We are also investing in the wider rapid transit
network, so Aucklanders can get to where they
need to go faster and more reliably, with the $1.4
billion Eastern Busway under construction, and
the Northwestern Busway has been progressed
through fast-track.

•

Funded the acceleration of level crossing removals
in Takanini and Glen Innes, improving safety
for pedestrians and efficiency for motorists by
unlocking the full benefits of City Rail Link.

A re-elected National Government will:
•

Fund construction of Mill Road Stage One,
between Manukau and Alfriston.

•

Progress route protection work on Mill Road
Stages Two and Three, between Alfriston
and Drury.

Mill Road Stage One (Manukau to
Alfriston)

Mill Road Stages Two and Three
(Alfriston to Drury)

South Auckland is one of the fastest-growing parts of the
country, and Drury is at the centre of it. But the roading
network hasn’t kept up. People travelling between
Drury, Papakura and Manukau are funnelled onto an
already congested Southern Motorway, and roads like
Redoubt Road and Mill Road were built for a semi-rural
community, not tens of thousands of new households.

National is committed to completing Mill Road all the way
to Drury. Stages Two and Three will connect the corridor
directly into the heart of the Drury growth area.

Mill Road will change that. Once complete, it will be a
new four-lane, 21.5-kilometre corridor running alongside
State Highway 1 from Manukau to Drury, crushing
congestion, improving safety, and unlocking land for the
homes and jobs the region needs.
Mill Road Stage One is one of the highest ranked
projects on the Government’s Major Transport Project
Pipeline. Published by this government, the pipeline sets
the order for major transport projects based on value for
money, and how quickly they can be delivered. Funding
this project, which has already been identified as ready
to build, is the responsible next step.
This project is also identified as a priority project in the
Auckland Regional Deal, as well as identified in the NZTA
Auckland Motorway Strategic Plan.
Stage One is expected to deliver:
•

a four-lane corridor, with a westbound bus lane at
the northern end.

•

two new and six upgraded intersections between
the SH1 interchange and Murphys Road, plus three
new roundabouts.

•

new bridges across Puhinui Creek and Cheesman’s
Bush.

•

a 30 percent reduction in congestion on the
corridor, 25 percent faster journey times, and a
more than 60 percent reduction in deaths and
serious injuries.

For too long, landowners along the route have lived with
uncertainty about where the road will go and how their
properties will be impacted. That isn’t fair on them, and it
holds back development in the area.
A National Government will allocate $100 million to NZTA
to progress route protection for Stages Two and Three
as soon as possible, giving landowners, developers
and Auckland Council the certainty they need to
plan properly.
Progressing route protection for Stages Two and
Three was a key commitment in the Auckland Regional
Deal. We will also continue to work with Auckland
Council, through the new Auckland Regional Transport
Committee, to confirm the timing of Stages Two and
Three in Auckland’s 30-year transport plan.

Fiscal impact
National will commit $1.75 billion of Crown capital
in Budget 2028, held in tagged contingency for the
construction of Mill Road Stage One (Manukau to
Alfriston).
$1.75 billion will be provided based on the 2025
NZTA Investment Case. Any additional costs will
be met from the State Highway Improvements Activity
class of National Land Transport Fund. This is the same
approach taken in Budget 2026 to fund Cambridge
to Piarere.
$100 million of Crown capital is being allocated to
progress route protection on Mill Road Stages Two
and Three (Alfriston to Drury). This cost is consistent
with recent NZTA funding approvals for comparable
Roads of National Significance.

It also demonstrates strong value for money, returning
up to $3.10 in benefits (untolled) or $2.20 in benefits for
every dollar invested (tolled).
National will fund Mill Road Stage One through a Crown
Capital contribution in Budget 2028.

# Building the Future - New Zealand’s Next Billion Customers

Published by the New Zealand National Party as a PDF policy document. Source: <https://assets.national.org.nz/web/prod/Building%20the%20Future%20-%20New%20Zealand%E2%80%99s%20Next%20Billion%20Customers.pdf?v=1783393242>.
The text below is the verbatim text layer of the PDF extracted with `pdftotext` (reading order). Line breaks follow the
PDF; tables and multi-column layouts may read out of order in this section, so a second rendering that preserves the
page layout (`pdftotext -layout`) follows it. Nothing has been added, removed or paraphrased.

## Full text (reading order)

2026

Building the Future:
New Zealand’s Next
Billion Customers

Authorised by J de Joux, 41 Pipitea St, Wgtn.

Building the Future:

New Zealand’s Next Billion Customers

Building the Future:
New Zealand’s Next Billion Customers
Introduction
National believes New Zealand is a trading nation. We create jobs and lift incomes by supporting great Kiwi
companies to compete on the world stage for a rising share of global trade and investment.
That can sound abstract, but the impact of trade is deeply local.
When a Hawke’s Bay apple grower wins preferential access to a market of 1.4 billion people, or a kiwifruit grower
in Te Puke gets tariff-free access to India ahead of every other country in the world, that means better returns at
the orchard gate and more jobs in the packhouse. When a Marlborough winery sees tariffs fall from 150 per cent
to 25 per cent, the vineyard hires more staff and invests in expansion. When a Southland sheep farmer sells lamb
duty-free into new markets, that’s more money flowing into rural towns, local schools and main-street businesses.
Ultimately, more trade means higher wages, more jobs and more money in people’s pockets. Trade supports one
in four New Zealand jobs. Our goal of doubling export value by 2034 is not just a number – it’s a plan for stronger
communities right across New Zealand, from the orchard to the factory floor to the main street.
That’s why in our first term, National has been relentlessly focused on making New Zealand exporters more
competitive offshore. In the last three years, National has:
•

Completed an FTA with India, which eliminates or reduces tariffs on 95% of our exports.

•

  rought the NZ–EU Free Trade Agreement into force ahead of schedule, supporting an additional $3 billion in
B
exports to the European Union.

•

  ompleted New Zealand’s first FTA in the Middle East with the UAE, which eliminates duties on 98.5% of
C
exports, supporting a 37.9% growth in exports since the deal was signed.

•

  ompleted negotiations with the six-nation Gulf Cooperation Council, an economic bloc worth $4 trillion in
C
GDP, which eliminates duties for 99% of our exports over 10 years.

•

Completed 23 trade missions to 18 countries, generating $2 billion of deals and commitments.

•

Eliminated $733 million of non-tariff barriers.

National’s trade agenda has supported rapid growth in exports, which have risen from $94.4 billion to $114.1 billion,
on track to exceed our objective of doubling New Zealand’s exports by 2034.
Major contributors to that success have included our food and fibre exports, projected to hit $64.3 billion this year,
and international tourism, now worth $13.7 billion.
Now, National is announcing how we secure New Zealand’s Next Billion Customers.
We will do this by:
•

Prioritising new trade deals with European, South American, African and Asian countries.

•

  egotiating new essential supplies agreements with like-minded partners, using the NZ–Singapore AOTES
N
agreement as the template.

•

Cutting red tape by expanding paperless trade and digital customs, eliminating $1 billion in non-tariff barriers.
2

Building the Future:

New Zealand’s Next Billion Customers

•

Creating new tools for businesses to help streamline their export experience.

•

  iving New Zealand Trade and Enterprise a sharper mandate – leading Kiwi businesses to new opportunities
G
and backing the next generation of exporters.

•

  ompleting at least 23 trade missions over the next term, with a sharper focus on sector-specific missions and
C
measurable commercial outcomes.

•

Re-affirm our commitment to doubling the value of exports by 2034.

Prioritising new trade deals
In the last three years, National has worked hard to conclude new trade arrangements, bring existing trade
agreements into force sooner, and bolster traditional trade arrangements, with new agreements that protect New
Zealand from the risks of a more volatile world, like the Agreement on Trade in Essential Supplies with Singapore.
With the India Free Trade Agreement signed and now progressing through Parliament, National is focused
on securing the next phase of New Zealand’s trade agenda. That starts with an intention to commence trade
negotiations with seven new economies in the next five years.

In the next five years, National will commence negotiations with:

These seven markets combined represent almost 700 million people and a GDP of more than US$5 trillion, similar
to the size of the German and Japanese economies today, and growing rapidly.
Meanwhile, the total value of New Zealand’s exports to those countries is just $1.8 billion, demonstrating the scale
of the opportunity. These are large, fast-growing economies with rising demand for the high-quality food, fibre,
services, technology, and expertise New Zealand can offer, fitting into three broad categories:
•

High value, high-income European economies

•

Large, high-growth South American economies

•

Emerging high growth, high potential Asian/African economies

3

Building the Future:

New Zealand’s Next Billion Customers

Each category offers a distinct opportunity for New Zealand.
•
Switzerland and the EFTA states are home to some of the wealthiest consumers in the world, paying
premium prices for high-quality food and offering deep markets for New Zealand services and technology.
•
Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay anchor a South American continent of more than 400 million people, where
New Zealand’s agritech, services and specialised food and beverage exports are well placed to grow.
•
Bangladesh and Nigeria are among the fastest-growing large economies on earth, with young
populations, rapidly expanding middle classes and rising demand for the safe, high-quality food New Zealand
produces.
A re-elected National Government will prioritise commencement of negotiations with each of these economies in
the next five years, focusing on better access for Kiwi companies to boost exports, create jobs and lift incomes.
This is an ambitious programme, but National has already shown it can be done. In the last two and a half years,
National has signed three high-quality free trade agreements, with India, the United Arab Emirates and the Gulf
Cooperation Council, while also bringing the NZ–EU FTA into force ahead of schedule.
A re-elected National Government will apply the same disciplined approach that delivered those agreements:
clear negotiating mandates set early, sustained ministerial engagement, and a relentless focus on high-quality,
commercially meaningful outcomes for exporters. New Zealand’s reputation as a serious, reliable negotiating
partner – reinforced by the India, UAE and Gulf agreements, means partners come to the table knowing that a
deal with New Zealand can be done quickly, and done well.
Following that next tranche of immediate trade priorities, National has identified six other economies for trade
negotiation, with negotiations to commence over the next decade, between now and 2036:
•

South Africa

•

Turkey

•

Colombia (via Pacific Alliance)

•

Morocco

•

Sri Lanka

•

Mauritius

Together, these two tranches span thirteen economies and almost one billion people – New Zealand’s next billion
customers.
In addition to opening new doors, National will focus on getting more value from the trade agreements New
Zealand already has. That means:
•
Growing services exports, which have already increased from around 23% to 27% of total exports under
National, and driving them towards 35% of total export value by 2030.
•
Modernising our existing FTAs, starting with China, by shifting to a negative list approach so services
markets are treated as open unless specific restrictions are listed.
•

Growing the Digital Economy Partnership Agreement.

•

Pursuing a digital trade agreement between the CPTPP and the European Union.

•
Continuing to expand the membership of CPTPP and RCEP so New Zealand exporters have better access
into some of the world’s most dynamic economies.
4

Building the Future:

New Zealand’s Next Billion Customers

The AOTES Agreement: a new model for trade security
On 4 May 2026, New Zealand and Singapore signed the Agreement on Trade in Essential Supplies (AOTES) – a
landmark agreement that ensures both countries maintain the flow of essential goods to each other during times
of disruption, shortage or crisis.
AOTES is a direct response to the supply chain shocks of recent years – from COVID-19 to the Suez Canal
disruptions and the war in Iran – that exposed how quickly global trade in critical goods can seize up. For a small,
open trading nation like New Zealand, reliable access to essential supplies is a matter of national security as much
as economic policy.
What AOTES delivers:
•
Guarantees that essential goods – including food, medicines, medical supplies and critical inputs –
continue to flow between New Zealand and Singapore, even during emergencies or global supply disruptions.
•
Commits both countries to avoid imposing export restrictions on essential supplies to each other,
providing New Zealand businesses and consumers with greater certainty.
•
Creates a framework for rapid information sharing and coordination when supply chains come under
pressure, so governments can act quickly to protect access to critical goods.
•
Positions New Zealand as a trusted, reliable supplier of food and agricultural products to Singapore and
the broader region – reinforcing our reputation as a safe, stable source of premium exports.
Singapore is one of New Zealand’s most important trade and investment partners, and a gateway to Southeast
Asian markets. AOTES deepens that relationship and sets a new standard for how like-minded trading nations can
work together to build supply chain resilience.
A re-elected National Government will:
•
Use AOTES as a template, negotiating essential supplies agreements with other like-minded partners to
protect New Zealand’s access to critical goods and cement our position as a trusted trade partner.
•
Extend the AOTES model across the FIT Partnership, developing shared early-warning systems and supply
chain resilience frameworks with our closest trading partners.

Expanding paperless trade and digital customs
Making trade easier for our exporters is also a priority.
A re-elected National Government will drive the next phase of the Future of Investment and Trade Partnership, a
fast-growing network of 16 like-minded economies that New Zealand helped convene with Singapore, Switzerland,
and the UAE. The FIT Partnership is expected to expand to more than 20 members in the near future – making it
an increasingly significant force for trade facilitation among small and mid-sized open economies.
We will use this platform to cut the practical costs of trade, expand paperless documentation, reduce non-tariff
barriers, strengthen supply chains, and make it easier for exporters to move goods and services across borders
faster and at lower cost.
Through the FIT Partnership, a re-elected National Government will pursue four practical workstreams:

5

Building the Future:

New Zealand’s Next Billion Customers

•
Paperless trade and digital standards: extending real-time digital trade documentation across the FIT
network, building on the NZ–Singapore electronic certification arrangement.
•
Non-tariff barrier elimination: using the FIT Partnership as a coordinating platform to identify and
systematically remove non-tariff barriers across member markets.
•
Supply chain resilience: extending the AOTES model of shared frameworks and early-warning systems
across the FIT network.
•
Mutual recognition agreements: aligning standards and regulatory requirements to lower compliance
costs for exporters operating across multiple markets.
A re-elected National Government will also modernise the border systems exporters rely on. Building on New
Zealand and Singapore’s electronic certification arrangement, we will expand real-time digital certification to the
UK and more of our closest trading partners, while investing in automated customs and origin systems so New
Zealand products clear borders faster, with fewer delays and lower compliance costs.
Together, these measures will help remove more of the practical barriers exporters face, building on the $733
million in non-tariff barriers eliminated since 2023 and supporting our objective of eliminating a further $1 billion in
non-tariff barriers by 2030.
A re-elected National Government will:
•
Drive the next phase of the FIT Partnership to reduce trade frictions among small and medium-sized
trading nations.
•
Modernise red tape at the border for exporters, with a focus on expanding paperless trade and digitalised
systems.

New AI tools to streamline businesses’ export experience
New Zealand’s FTA network reaches more than 60 countries, but the benefits are not always immediately
apparent. Exporters often have to navigate thousands of tariff lines, certification requirements, customs
procedures, and regulatory conditions. For many businesses, this means paying for specialist advice before they
even know whether a market is worth pursuing.
As a result, too many New Zealand businesses, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises, are leaving
money on the table because they don’t understand the tariff advantages, market access rules and regulatory
requirements that our agreements have secured for them.
A re-elected National Government will help exporters make better use of New Zealand’s trade agreements by
creating three AI-powered digital tools:
•

an FTA tariff adviser,

•

a rules of origin navigator, and

•

a market access requirements tool.

These will be natural language AI tools rather than conventional databases, where exporters describe their
product and destination market in plain English, and the tools provide the tariff preference they qualify for, the
rules of origin they must meet to claim it, and the requirements that apply before their goods ship. For exporters,
that means they will not need to know tariff classifications, or read the legal text of the agreements themselves.

6

Building the Future:

New Zealand’s Next Billion Customers

New Zealand Trade and Enterprise: a sharper focus on growth
New Zealand Trade and Enterprise is the engine room of our export growth strategy. NZTE currently works with
around 1,000 companies to grow and expand their exports to important markets around the world – providing
in-market intelligence, buyer connections and capability building that help businesses take the next step in their
export journey. Under a re-elected National Government, NZTE will be given a sharper mandate, more resources
in key markets and a clearer mission: helping more New Zealand businesses sell more to the world.
From follow to lead
Historically, NZTE has largely responded to the interests and requests of companies seeking export support – a
responsive model that has served many exporters well. A re-elected National Government will ask NZTE to do
more: to actively lead companies to new opportunities and markets, not just follow where they point.
This means NZTE will shift from a ‘follow’ to a ‘lead and follow’ model – proactively identifying high-value market
opportunities created by our new FTAs, targeting the New Zealand companies best placed to capitalise on them,
and bringing those opportunities directly to businesses rather than waiting to be asked.
•
Where a new FTA opens a tariff window, in India, the Gulf, or future markets, NZTE will identify which
New Zealand exporters stand to benefit most and proactively engage them with market intelligence, buyer
introductions and entry support.
•
NZTE will develop forward-looking sector opportunity maps – identifying where global demand is growing
fastest and matching New Zealand’s export strengths to those opportunities before competitors move.
Sector-wide growth initiatives
Alongside its work with individual companies, NZTE will drive sector-wide initiatives that lift the entire export
economy:
•
Food and beverage: deepening market access and premiumisation strategies across Asia, the Middle East
and Europe, building on record export highs in horticulture, seafood and dairy.
•
Technology and fintech: growing New Zealand’s reputation as a source of high-value tech exports,
particularly in markets where our new FTAs have reduced barriers.
•
Mānuka honey: capitalising on growing demand in India, China and the Gulf, where our new agreements
have dramatically reduced tariffs.
•
Wood, forestry and building products: driving value-added exports rather than raw logs, with a focus on
markets opened by CPTPP, RCEP and the India FTA.
•
Education: working alongside Education New Zealand to convert growing student interest – boosted by
expanded air connectivity – into enrolments that benefit institutions across the country.
Export development: the Next 200
Too many New Zealand businesses have the products, the quality and the ambition to export – but lack the
connections, the market knowledge or the first step. National will direct NZTE to establish a dedicated Export
Development function, with a specific focus on identifying the next generation of New Zealand exporters –
companies that are not yet exporting but have the potential to do so.
The centrepiece of this function will be the ‘Next 200’ programme: an intensive, targeted initiative focused on 200
high-potential businesses ready to begin or significantly scale their export activity:

7

Building the Future:

New Zealand’s Next Billion Customers

•
NZTE will identify 200 small and medium-sized businesses across goods and services sectors with
genuine export-ready products and the capacity to grow.
•
Each business will receive a dedicated NZTE relationship manager, tailored market intelligence,
introductions to in-market networks, and support navigating regulatory and customs requirements.
•
The programme will be designed around results, with clear targets for export revenue, new markets and
jobs, and progress publicly reported annually.
•
Sectors will be prioritised based on the opportunities created by our new FTAs. India, the Gulf and the
UAE will be key focus markets in the first year.
Aligning all export agencies
NZTE does not operate alone. A re-elected National Government will ensure that NZTE, Investment New Zealand
and Education New Zealand operate under a single coordinated strategy – sharing in-market presence, aligning
campaigns and maximising the return on every dollar invested in promoting New Zealand offshore.
•
Coordinated in-market teams will mean New Zealand presents as one country, not separate agencies
competing for attention and resources.
•
Investment New Zealand will use the same networks and relationships built by NZTE to attract high-quality
foreign direct investment that creates jobs and strengthens our export base.

Trade missions: taking New Zealand to the world
Trade missions are one of the most effective and direct tools a government has to grow exports. When the Prime
Minister and Minister of Trade lead a delegation of New Zealand businesses into a new or growing market, doors
open that would otherwise take years to unlock. Relationships are built, deals are done and New Zealand’s
reputation as a premium, reliable trading partner is reinforced.
National is committed to trade missions – not as photo opportunities, but as serious commercial exercises with
clear targets, rigorous follow-up and measurable outcomes.
A record of delivery
Under National’s previous term in government, we completed 18 trade missions to open opportunities to the
world. In 2023 we committed to doing more trade missions in this term than any previous government – and
we’ve delivered, completing 23 trade missions to 18 countries and generating more than $2 billion in deals,

Our commitment for the next term
A re-elected National Government commits to matching and building on that record. We will complete at least 23
trade missions over the next parliamentary term, with a sharper focus on sector-specific missions and a stronger
results framework.

Sector-specific missions
The next term will see a greater emphasis on missions built around specific sectors rather than only broad country
visits – bringing together the right companies, with the right buyers, in the right markets.
•
Technology and fintech: showcasing New Zealand’s growing tech sector to investors and buyers in
Singapore, Japan, the UK, EU and the United States.
8

Building the Future:

New Zealand’s Next Billion Customers

•
Food, beverage and seafood: premium food missions into India, the Gulf, Southeast Asia and China –
capitalising on our new FTAs, record seafood export highs and the growing demand for trusted, high-quality food.
•
Services: dedicated services sector missions into markets where our new FTAs have opened services
commitments – including financial services, professional services, digital services and education.
•
Mānuka honey: targeted missions into China, India and the Middle East, where tariff reductions under
new agreements have made New Zealand honey significantly more price-competitive.
•
Wood, forestry and building products: value-added forestry missions into Asia and the Gulf, promoting

•

•

Building the Future:
New Zealand’s Next Billion Customers
Introduction
National believes New Zealand is a trading nation. We create jobs and lift incomes by supporting great Kiwi
companies to compete on the world stage for a rising share of global trade and investment.

That can sound abstract, but the impact of trade is deeply local.

When a Hawke’s Bay apple grower wins preferential access to a market of 1.4 billion people, or a kiwifruit grower
in Te Puke gets tariff-free access to India ahead of every other country in the world, that means better returns at
the orchard gate and more jobs in the packhouse. When a Marlborough winery sees tariffs fall from 150 per cent
to 25 per cent, the vineyard hires more staff and invests in expansion. When a Southland sheep farmer sells lamb
duty-free into new markets, that’s more money flowing into rural towns, local schools and main-street businesses.

Ultimately, more trade means higher wages, more jobs and more money in people’s pockets. Trade supports one
in four New Zealand jobs. Our goal of doubling export value by 2034 is not just a number – it’s a plan for stronger
communities right across New Zealand, from the orchard to the factory floor to the main street.

That’s why in our first term, National has been relentlessly focused on making New Zealand exporters more
competitive offshore. In the last three years, National has:

•   Completed an FTA with India, which eliminates or reduces tariffs on 95% of our exports.
•     rought the NZ–EU Free Trade Agreement into force ahead of schedule, supporting an additional $3 billion in
    B
    exports to the European Union.
•     ompleted New Zealand’s first FTA in the Middle East with the UAE, which eliminates duties on 98.5% of
    C
    exports, supporting a 37.9% growth in exports since the deal was signed.
•     ompleted negotiations with the six-nation Gulf Cooperation Council, an economic bloc worth $4 trillion in
    C
    GDP, which eliminates duties for 99% of our exports over 10 years.
•   Completed 23 trade missions to 18 countries, generating $2 billion of deals and commitments.
•   Eliminated $733 million of non-tariff barriers.

National’s trade agenda has supported rapid growth in exports, which have risen from $94.4 billion to $114.1 billion,
on track to exceed our objective of doubling New Zealand’s exports by 2034.

Major contributors to that success have included our food and fibre exports, projected to hit $64.3 billion this year,
and international tourism, now worth $13.7 billion.

Now, National is announcing how we secure New Zealand’s Next Billion Customers.

We will do this by:

•   Prioritising new trade deals with European, South American, African and Asian countries.
•     egotiating new essential supplies agreements with like-minded partners, using the NZ–Singapore AOTES
    N
    agreement as the template.
•   Cutting red tape by expanding paperless trade and digital customs, eliminating $1 billion in non-tariff barriers.

                                                                                                                          2

Building the Future:                                                                   New Zealand’s Next Billion Customers

•     Creating new tools for businesses to help streamline their export experience.
•       iving New Zealand Trade and Enterprise a sharper mandate – leading Kiwi businesses to new opportunities
      G
      and backing the next generation of exporters.

      measurable commercial outcomes.

In the last three years, National has worked hard to conclude new trade arrangements, bring existing trade
agreements into force sooner, and bolster traditional trade arrangements, with new agreements that protect New
Zealand from the risks of a more volatile world, like the Agreement on Trade in Essential Supplies with Singapore.

With the India Free Trade Agreement signed and now progressing through Parliament, National is focused
on securing the next phase of New Zealand’s trade agenda. That starts with an intention to commence trade
negotiations with seven new economies in the next five years.

These seven markets combined represent almost 700 million people and a GDP of more than US$5 trillion, similar
to the size of the German and Japanese economies today, and growing rapidly.

Meanwhile, the total value of New Zealand’s exports to those countries is just $1.8 billion, demonstrating the scale

services, technology, and expertise New Zealand can offer, fitting into three broad categories:

premium prices for high-quality food and offering deep markets for New Zealand services and technology.

•     Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay anchor a South American continent of more than 400 million people, where
New Zealand’s agritech, services and specialised food and beverage exports are well placed to grow.

•       Bangladesh and Nigeria are among the fastest-growing large economies on earth, with young
populations, rapidly expanding middle classes and rising demand for the safe, high-quality food New Zealand
produces.

A re-elected National Government will prioritise commencement of negotiations with each of these economies in
the next five years, focusing on better access for Kiwi companies to boost exports, create jobs and lift incomes.

This is an ambitious programme, but National has already shown it can be done. In the last two and a half years,
National has signed three high-quality free trade agreements, with India, the United Arab Emirates and the Gulf
Cooperation Council, while also bringing the NZ–EU FTA into force ahead of schedule.

clear negotiating mandates set early, sustained ministerial engagement, and a relentless focus on high-quality,

markets are treated as open unless specific restrictions are listed.

•       Growing the Digital Economy Partnership Agreement.

•       Pursuing a digital trade agreement between the CPTPP and the European Union.

The AOTES Agreement: a new model for trade security
On 4 May 2026, New Zealand and Singapore signed the Agreement on Trade in Essential Supplies (AOTES) – a
landmark agreement that ensures both countries maintain the flow of essential goods to each other during times
of disruption, shortage or crisis.

AOTES is a direct response to the supply chain shocks of recent years – from COVID-19 to the Suez Canal
disruptions and the war in Iran – that exposed how quickly global trade in critical goods can seize up. For a small,
open trading nation like New Zealand, reliable access to essential supplies is a matter of national security as much
as economic policy.

What AOTES delivers:

•       Guarantees that essential goods – including food, medicines, medical supplies and critical inputs –
continue to flow between New Zealand and Singapore, even during emergencies or global supply disruptions.

•       Commits both countries to avoid imposing export restrictions on essential supplies to each other,
providing New Zealand businesses and consumers with greater certainty.

•       Creates a framework for rapid information sharing and coordination when supply chains come under
pressure, so governments can act quickly to protect access to critical goods.

•       Positions New Zealand as a trusted, reliable supplier of food and agricultural products to Singapore and
the broader region – reinforcing our reputation as a safe, stable source of premium exports.

Asian markets. AOTES deepens that relationship and sets a new standard for how like-minded trading nations can
work together to build supply chain resilience.

an increasingly significant force for trade facilitation among small and mid-sized open economies.

barriers, strengthen supply chains, and make it easier for exporters to move goods and services across borders
faster and at lower cost.

systematically remove non-tariff barriers across member markets.

across the FIT network.

•       Mutual recognition agreements: aligning standards and regulatory requirements to lower compliance
costs for exporters operating across multiple markets.

A re-elected National Government will also modernise the border systems exporters rely on. Building on New
Zealand and Singapore’s electronic certification arrangement, we will expand real-time digital certification to the
UK and more of our closest trading partners, while investing in automated customs and origin systems so New
Zealand products clear borders faster, with fewer delays and lower compliance costs.

Together, these measures will help remove more of the practical barriers exporters face, building on the $733
million in non-tariff barriers eliminated since 2023 and supporting our objective of eliminating a further $1 billion in
non-tariff barriers by 2030.

A re-elected National Government will:

•       Drive the next phase of the FIT Partnership to reduce trade frictions among small and medium-sized
trading nations.

•      Modernise red tape at the border for exporters, with a focus on expanding paperless trade and digitalised

New AI tools to streamline businesses’ export experience
New Zealand’s FTA network reaches more than 60 countries, but the benefits are not always immediately
apparent. Exporters often have to navigate thousands of tariff lines, certification requirements, customs
procedures, and regulatory conditions. For many businesses, this means paying for specialist advice before they
even know whether a market is worth pursuing.

As a result, too many New Zealand businesses, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises, are leaving
money on the table because they don’t understand the tariff advantages, market access rules and regulatory
requirements that our agreements have secured for them.

A re-elected National Government will help exporters make better use of New Zealand’s trade agreements by
creating three AI-powered digital tools:

•       an FTA tariff adviser,

•       a rules of origin navigator, and

•       a market access requirements tool.

These will be natural language AI tools rather than conventional databases, where exporters describe their
product and destination market in plain English, and the tools provide the tariff preference they qualify for, the
rules of origin they must meet to claim it, and the requirements that apply before their goods ship. For exporters,

Building the Future:                                                               New Zealand’s Next Billion Customers

New Zealand Trade and Enterprise: a sharper focus on growth
New Zealand Trade and Enterprise is the engine room of our export growth strategy. NZTE currently works with

Delivering on our 2023 Hunting and Fishing
commitments
National supports the right of New Zealanders to hunt and ﬁsh. Tens of thousands
of Kiwis grow up ﬁshing in our lakes and rivers or in the sea. Many learn to hunt
with their friends and family.
Hunters help to control animal numbers, protect
biodiversity by eradicating pests, and provide food for
their families. Hunting and ﬁshing also foster tourism
and are pillars of New Zealand’s culture and heritage.

National believes conservation and recreation can
work in harmony, and our plan supports the rights of
New Zealanders to continue to hunt and ﬁsh while
protecting and enhancing our natural environment.

1.

Establish a Minister for Hunting
and Fishing

Complete.

2.

Strengthen the Game Animal
Council and designate ‘herds
of special interest’

Complete. The Game Animal Council (Herds of Special Interest)
Amendment Act 2026 clariﬁed the ability to designate a herd of special
interest in national parks will be passed by July. Two herds of special
interest (wapiti and sika) were designated in July, with the Game
Animal Council responsible for implementing the Sika Herd of Special
Interest, the ﬁrst time the GAC has been designated this responsibility.

3.

Change the law so game
animals are not pests

Complete as not strictly required. Game animals are not classiﬁed as
pests under the law, however a bill to provide express recognition of
game animals as valued introduced species to be managed in line
with their recreational value has been drafted as a member’s bill.

4.

Guarantee access to public
land for hunting and ﬁshing

Complete. The Access Charter for Recreational Hunting and Fishing
on Public Conservation Land and Waters was announced on
2 November 2024.

5.

Establish the ‘Huts of
Recreational Importance’
Partnership to maintain huts in
the DOC estate

Complete. Through the Community Hut Programme, the Backcountry
Trust received $4.2m in partnership with DOC to maintain and enhance
30 recreational hut projects in January 2025.

6.

Support Fish & Game New
Zealand and protect trout and
salmon ﬁshing

Partially complete. Cabinet agreed on policy decisions to modernise
and strengthen Fish and Game, and enacting legislation awaits ﬁrst
reading before the election.

7.

Not introduce recreational
licences for game animal
hunting or sea ﬁshing

Complete.

Authorised by J de Joux, ps@national.org.nz

## Full text (reading order)

Building the Future: Early Childhood Education

Set up for Success

National wants to ensure children are Set Up for
Success when they start school through consistent,
high-quality experiences in Early Childhood Education.
The early years of a child’s life lay the foundations for
everything that follows. Early Childhood Education
should help every child develop the language, social,
physical and early learning foundations they need to
thrive when they start school.
Today, we do not have a clear shared picture of what
being “school ready” looks like in New Zealand.
Teachers tell us children are arriving at school with
a wide range of skills and levels of readiness. That
can include differences in oral language, listening and
following instructions, holding and controlling a pencil,
recognising their own name, interacting with other
children and managing age-appropriate self-care.
There are some important foundations that help
children make a strong start at school. National wants
to make those expectations much clearer, give parents
better information about how their child is progressing,
and make sure extra support is put in place early where
it is needed.
Set Up for Success will establish clearer developmental
milestones throughout ECE, drawn directly from
Te Whāriki, the New Zealand Early Childhood
Curriculum, so parents and teachers have a shared
understanding of what children should be developing
and when.
Parents will receive clearer and more regular
information about how their child is progressing
against those milestones, making it easier for families
and ECEs to work together and for additional support
to be provided early where a child needs it.

Authorised by J de Joux, ps@national.org.nz

Before children transition to primary school, a new
School Start Check will bring that information together
and provide a clear picture of the foundations a
child has developed and where they may need
further support.
National also wants children spending significantly less
time learning through screens.
Screens and individual devices have become
increasingly common in children’s lives and in
education. For our youngest children, we want greater
emphasis on books, handwriting, conversation, handson activities and direct interaction with teachers and
other children.
We have already seen through the cellphone ban
in schools what clear limits around technology
can achieve by reducing unnecessary distraction
and allowing students to focus more closely on
their learning.
We will now take that approach further.
National will end screen and individual-device
use in ECE and place tight limits around their use in
primary schools.
Technology still has a place in education, but it
should enhance learning, not become the default way
children learn.
We will also place a renewed emphasis on handwriting.
Writing by hand is an important part of learning to
read and write, and the writing components of twiceyearly primary school assessments will be completed
on paper.
Every child should arrive at school as ready as possible
to learn, participate and make a strong start to their
primary school journey.

A re-elected National Government will:
End screen use in ECE and tightly limit it in
primary schools
•

End screen and individual-device use in ECE.

•

Tightly limit screen and individual-device use in
Years 1 to 3, with age-appropriate limits for older
primary students.

•

Ensure technology is used where it enhances
learning rather than becoming the default way
children learn.

•

Prioritise handwriting, including requiring the
writing component of twice-yearly primary school
assessments to be completed on paper.

Introduce a School Start Check
National will introduce a School Start Check for every
child before they transition to primary school.
There are some important foundations that help
children make a strong start at school. These
include being able to communicate, listen and follow
instructions, hold and control a pencil, interact with
other children, recognise their own name and manage
age-appropriate self-care.
The School Start Check will:
•

set clear expectations about the foundations
children should be developing before they
start school

•

draw those expectations directly from Te Whāriki

Require ECEs to report on children’s
progress against developmental milestones

•

bring together information about how the child has
progressed throughout ECE

•

Introduce clear and measurable developmental
milestones throughout ECE, drawn directly from
Te Whāriki.

•

give parents and schools a clear picture of how
ready the child is to start school

•

Give parents clearer and more regular information
about how their child is progressing against
those milestones.

•

identify where a child may need additional support
so it can be provided early.

•

Ensure families and ECEs can work together and,
where a child needs extra help, support can be put
in place early.

•

Continue the rollout of the strengthened Early
Intervention Service to provide targeted support
where children have additional needs.

The milestones will cover areas such as oral language
and communication, listening and following instructions,
fine motor skills, early literacy and numeracy, social
development and age-appropriate independence.

The School Start Check will not be a pass-or-fail test
and will not prevent a child from starting school.
The aim is simple: to give every child the strongest
possible foundations for learning before they walk
through the school gate.

Fiscal impacts
A significant part of the support infrastructure is already
funded through the $266 million Early Intervention
Service expansion. The screen rules themselves
are primarily regulatory, and the milestone reporting
and School Start Check will be designed to build on
information ECEs already collect.

Set Up for Success

The evidence behind the policy
Children develop quickly in their first five years. When
a child needs help with language, behaviour or other
foundations, it is better to identify that need early than
wait until they arrive at school.
Set Up for Success will introduce clearer milestones
throughout ECE, regular progress information for
parents, earlier support and a School Start Check.
It will also remove screen use from ECE and place
tight, age-appropriate limits on screen use in primary
schools, with exemptions for disability and specific
learning needs.

What ERO found
ERO reported that a large New Zealand study found 20
per cent of five-year-olds struggling with oral language.
Only one-third of new entrant teachers surveyed by
ERO said most children began school at the expected
oral-language level. Fifty-three per cent of parents said
their ECE service had not provided information about
their child’s oral-language progress. [1]
ERO recommended: [1]
•

clear and consistent oral-language progress
indicators across Te Whāriki and the school
curriculum

•

better tools for ECE teachers to track progress and
identify difficulties

•

an oral-language assessment when children start
school so support can be tailored

•

regular progress updates for parents and whānau,
with targeted support where it is needed

These recommendations are central to Set Up for
Success. Parents will get clearer information, teachers
will be better able to identify concerns, and children
who need extra help can receive it earlier.

What being ready for school means
ERO’s work on the transition to school found that
teachers and ECE staff saw readiness as broader
than early reading and maths. They pointed to oral
language and listening, following instructions, holding
a pencil, managing classroom routines, self-regulation
and age-appropriate independence with lunch, bags
and toileting. [2]
The School Start Check will bring this information
together before a child moves into primary school. It
will not be a pass or fail test. Its purpose is to show
parents and schools where a child is doing well and
where further support may be needed.

Building on Te Whāriki and Kōwhiti
Whakapae
The Ministry of Education’s Kōwhiti Whakapae resource
already covers social and emotional learning, oral
language and literacy, and maths. It describes progress
through four overlapping phases linked to Te Whāriki,
but those phases are deliberately not age-based. [3]
The policy will build on Te Whāriki and Kōwhiti
Whakapae. Education and child-development
experts will help turn the key foundations into clear,
age-appropriate milestones that can be reported
consistently to parents.

Why reduce screen use
Two GUSTO studies followed children over time.
One linked screen exposure at 12 months with
differences in brain activity at 18 months and poorer
attention and executive function at age nine. A later
study linked higher screen use in early childhood with
poorer academic performance and working memory. The
studies involved 437 and 502 children respectively. [4][5]
Both studies mainly measured viewing at home and
cannot prove that screens caused the outcomes. They
add to the case for caution about prolonged screen use
among very young children.

What the wider research shows
A 2024 review covered 100 studies and 176,742
children under six. Programme viewing and background
television were associated with poorer cognitive
outcomes, while adult co-use was associated with
better outcomes. [6]
An analysis of 42 studies and 18,905 children linked
greater screen use with lower language skills.
Educational content and watching with a caregiver
were associated with better skills. The amount,
content and context of screen use all matter. [7]
The World Health Organization recommends no
sedentary screen time for infants and one-year-olds,
and no more than one hour a day for ages two to four.
These are whole-day health guidelines, not classroom
rules. [8]

Screen use at school
PISA 2025 found that New Zealand 15-year-olds
used devices at school for learning for 2.5 hours a day,
compared with an OECD average of 1.7 hours. Thirtyeight per cent reported distraction by other students’
devices in most or every science lesson, compared
with 28 per cent across the OECD. [9]
Across OECD countries, students reporting distraction
tended to perform worse, although the difference
within New Zealand was not statistically significant.
Moderate device use for learning was associated
with better results than either no use or very high use.
This supports clear limits and purposeful use. [9]

Why handwriting matters
Writing by hand helps build the brain pathways children
use to recognise letters and learn to read. Research
found these pathways became active after children
wrote letters by hand, but not when they typed or
traced them. [10][12]

Handwriting can also improve memory and
understanding. A review of 24 studies found students
who took and reviewed handwritten notes did better
in later assessments than those who typed. Writing by
hand may help because students must process the
main points rather than simply copy them. Research
with school-age children also found they wrote faster
and produced longer pieces by pen than by keyboard.
[11][13][14]

Governments overseas are also acting
New South Wales will introduce no individual device
use in public preschools and daily limits of 15 to 45
minutes in primary school. Victoria will require minimal
use in Foundation to Year 2 and a 90-minute daily cap
in Years 3 to 6 from 2027. [15][16]

What Set Up for Success will do
•

Introduce age-appropriate ECE milestones drawn
from Te Whāriki and Kowhiti Whakapae

•

Give parents regular, plain-language progress
information against a progression framework.

•

Identify needs earlier and connect children with
support.

•

Introduce a School Start Check before primary
school.

•

Remove screens from ECE and introduce tight limits
in lower primary schools with age appropriate limits
for upper primary.

•

Add a paper-based writing component to twiceyearly primary progress checks.
