# Electrify NZ 2.0

Published by the New Zealand National Party as a PDF policy document. Source: <https://assets.national.org.nz/web/prod/Electrify%20NZ%202.0.pdf?v=1790887430>.
The text below is the verbatim text layer of the PDF extracted with `pdftotext` (reading order). Line breaks follow the
PDF; tables and multi-column layouts may read out of order in this section, so a second rendering that preserves the
page layout (`pdftotext -layout`) follows it. Nothing has been added, removed or paraphrased.

## Full text (reading order)

Building the Future:

Electrify NZ 2.0
Delivering secure, affordable energy is critical to
National’s plan to grow the economy and support
New Zealanders with the cost of living. That’s why
over this term National has undertaken a series of
significant actions designed to enable new renewable
generation, supported by more backup supply, and
pro-competition rules that ensure the market works
for everyone.
As a result, wholesale electricity prices have fallen
significantly, and the country now has the strongest,
most secure pipeline of new renewable generation

in a generation – with new wind farms, solar farms,
geothermal and battery projects. According to the
Electricity Authority, more renewable generation
has now been built in the last three years than the
previous eight.
For households, that means there now exists a credible
path to more affordable electricity prices over time.
For businesses, lower wholesale electricity prices
also mean manufacturers and exporters can remain
internationally competitive, supporting economic
growth, job creation, and higher wages.

So far this term, a National-led Government has:
•

Repealed Labour’s reckless ban on oil and gas exploration: Reopening New Zealand’s oil and gas fields
to bring gas back into the system to firm our renewables, protect manufacturing jobs, and keep power
prices down for households and businesses.

•

The biggest boom in renewables in a generation: New Zealand has been generating up to 96 per cent
of its electricity from renewables, with more new renewable generation built in the past three years than in
the previous eight, and the first ever permits for offshore wind about to open.

•

Putting power in the hands of households: More New Zealanders than ever are generating their own
affordable electricity, with solar connections up 47 per cent since National came to office.

•

Fast-track consenting: One-year consent decisions and 35-year consents mean nationally significant
infrastructure now has a single, time-bound pathway rather than years of litigation, driving new investment.
Eight renewable energy projects have already been approved by Fast-track panels.

•

Restored confidence in energy investment: National scrapped Labour’s Lake Onslow scheme and
unrealistic 100 per cent renewables target, both of which were chilling investment in new generation.

•

Stronger competition: The Energy Competition Task Force was established between the Electricity
Authority and the Commerce Commission, delivering eight initiatives to strengthen competition in the
electricity market.

•

A level playing field: Since 1 July, the four big gentailers have had to supply hedge contracts to
independent retailers and generators on a non-discriminatory basis, rather than favouring their own retail
arms, giving consumers more genuine choice.

•

A strategic coal stockpile: New Zealand now holds strategic fuel reserves at Huntly, so that a dry year is
managed rather than a national crisis that puts jobs and industry at risk.

•

LNG procurement: New Zealand households and businesses are a step closer to relief on their power
bills and greater energy security with National starting a procurement process to deliver an LNG facility
that will keep the lights on and protect jobs.

•

EV charging: National is co-funding a nationwide public charging network so New Zealanders can
travel the length of the country with confidence, using the cheapest transport fuel available to us –
our own electricity.

Authorised by J de Joux, ps@national.org.nz

However, there is more work to do to put downward
pressure on the total cost New Zealanders pay.
While wholesale electricity prices have now fallen
considerably over the last two years, network charges,
the extent of retail competition, and the cost of

keeping the lights on in a dry winter all still determine
the price and security of supply that households and
businesses get, and the jobs that depend on secure,
affordable energy.

That’s why, to deliver secure, affordable energy for more households and businesses, a
re-elected National Government will introduce our nine-point energy plan, Electrify NZ 2.0:
• Unlock new energy development zones by letting developers, major energy users, and investors build
and own new transmission, and recover their costs from the parties who use the lines.
• Make connections faster and cheaper by giving every household, builder, and business the right to
choose an accredited contractor for the connection work they’re paying for, not the one their network
hands them.
• Let Kiwis sell their power to the best buyer, giving every household and business with solar or a battery
the right to sell the power they export to any power company, not just the one they buy from.
• Addressing the dry year problem by levelling the playing field for backup power. National will use
transparency, a standardised backup power contract, and regular auctions to open the closed backup
market and draw in the competition and investment that keeps the lights on through dry periods.
• Tackle lines charges through a targeted review of Part 4 of the Commerce Act and put an end to slow
solar approvals by requiring distribution businesses to sign off residential and small business
connections within two working days.
• Make affordability a core objective for the Electricity Authority by writing it into law, so the cost of
power for households and businesses carries equal weight with competition, reliability, and efficiency in
every decision the regulator makes.
• Cut more red tape holding back renewables at every scale, from national rules letting Kiwis install solar,
micro-hydro, and batteries on their own property without a consent, to implementing the RMA
replacement so wind, solar, and hydro get built fast as standard, not the exception.
• Launch the Home Energy Fund, giving Kiwis low-interest, long-term loans to invest in their own power
and cut their own bills.
• Require AI data centres to bring new, firmed power, so new digital investment adds to the grid and
creates jobs instead of pushing up prices for families and businesses.

Unlocking new energy development
zones
Some of New Zealand’s best wind, solar, and
geothermal resources are in parts of the country where
limited transmission capacity restricts how much new
generation can connect and how much power can reach
major centres of demand. That makes it harder to build
generation where it is needed and stops cheaper power
in one region from reaching consumers in another.
Cost allocation is a further barrier. When new
transmission is treated as a connection asset, the

first party to trigger the investment can be left paying
for infrastructure that will ultimately benefit multiple
generators, electricity users, and regions. This firstmover risk discourages the coordinated investment in
generation and transmission that New Zealand needs.
The Electricity Authority’s transmission pricing
methodology already allocates the costs of
Transpower’s interconnection investments according to
who benefits. The same principle should apply where
a private investor is prepared to finance, build, and
own high-voltage infrastructure that serves a wider
interconnection function.

A re-elected National Government will:

A re-elected National Government will:

•

•

Establish a single accreditation scheme for
connection contractors, with standards set
by the Electricity Authority and assessed
by independent certification bodies rather
than by the networks contractors will be
competing against.

•

Make it so a contractor accredited once will
be able to work on any network in the country.

•

Allow anyone paying for a new connection,
or an upgrade to an existing one, to seek
quotes from accredited providers and choose
the best price and timeline.

•

Require networks, which will still set their
own safety and technical rules, approve
designs, inspect finished work and connect
it, to complete their part within set timeframes
so competition cannot be frustrated by delay.

•

•

Allow private businesses to help build
the transmission New Zealand needs,
by amending the Electricity Industry Act
and working with the Electricity Authority
on changes to the Electricity Industry
Participation Code, so the transmission
pricing methodology can recover the costs
of qualifying interconnection investments
made by parties other than Transpower.
Require privately funded interconnection
investments to use the same benefit-based
charging methodology as Transpower’s,
so costs fall on the parties who benefit from
the extra capacity rather than entirely on the
first mover.
Provide a clear regulatory pathway for
privately owned transmission assets
to connect to and operate alongside
Transpower’s grid, subject to the same
fundamental technical, reliability and systemoperation requirements as comparable
transmission infrastructure.

Faster, cheaper connections
Solar is not the only connection that takes too long.
Connecting a new home, subdivision, farm, factory
or business to the network can be one of the slowest
and most expensive steps in any development, and
every week of delay adds to the cost of building
homes and electrifying businesses, holding back
investment and the jobs that come with it. In most
cases the customer pays for the work but has little
say over who does it, since the network company
sets the requirements, prices the job, and either
builds it or picks who will.
This term, the Electricity Authority has set new
rules for how connections are priced and processed,
and the Commerce Commission has told every
distribution business and Transpower that it expects
them to let approved independent providers compete
for connection work wherever it is safe to do so.
National will turn that expectation into a right.

Selling your power to the best buyer
More Kiwi households and businesses are putting in
solar panels and batteries, but the rules still assume
power flows one way, from a big power station to a
customer. Today each home can have only one retailer,
so a family exporting surplus solar has to sell it to the
same company it buys from. The only way to get a
better price for what they sell is to move everything
they buy as well. That hurts competition for Kiwis.
This term, the Electricity Authority has consulted on
letting households use one company for the power
they buy and another for the power they sell. National
will turn that proposal into a right, so families who invest
in their own power, including through the Home Energy
Fund, get the best price for the power they don’t use.

A re-elected National Government will:
•

Give every household and business the right
to sell the power they export to any retailer or
buyer they choose, and direct the Electricity
Authority, through the Government Policy
Statement and legislation if needed, to have
this in place within two years.

•

Require lines companies to base export limits
on the real capacity of their local network, so
households can export more wherever there
is room, and make any lines company that
restricts exports demonstrate the genuine
network constraint that justifies it.

Addressing the dry year problem

Tackle lines charges

New Zealand runs on renewable power, some of the
cheapest and cleanest in the world. But when the lakes
are low for weeks on end, we need backup that can
run for weeks or months. Gas used to do that job, but
domestic gas is running down, and wind and solar can’t
store energy for months at a time.

Network charges now make up a substantial and
rapidly growing share of household power bills. Unlike
generation and retail, they are set by regulation rather
than competition. Part 4 of the Commerce Act, passed
in 2008 and applying to lines companies since 2009,
determines how much revenue most lines companies
may recover from consumers and what standards they
must meet. It was designed for a stable, one-directional
system, not one in which households generate, store
and export their own power.

Part of the problem is that the market for backup power
is thin and concentrated. The four big gentailers own
more than 95 per cent of the flexible generation that
backs these contracts, much of it used to cover their own
customers. There is now a standard product for covering
daily peaks, but still no standard, tradable contract for
the weeks or months of cover a dry year needs.
National has already levelled the playing field in the retail
and hedge markets this term, with the level playing field
reforms, the non-discrimination rules, and the Energy
Competition Task Force. Now it’s time to do the same for
backup power, the next step in the same job.

A re-elected National Government will:
•

Require the Electricity Authority to publish a
single, regular, independent assessment of
the backup gap’s size and timing, covering dry
periods when the sun’s not shining, the wind’s
not blowing, and the lakes are low.

•

Promote greater transparency of the backup
market, with the Authority publishing data on
contract volumes, lengths, and price ranges,
so buyers, sellers, and investors know what
cover is worth.

•

Require the creation of a backup power
contract, so any retailer, business, or new
investor can buy guaranteed backup cover
from any supplier, on standardised terms,
with large generators required to participate
in regular auctions of these contracts.

For most lines companies, the Commerce Commission
sets a five-year revenue cap that includes a return
linked to interest rates. The current cap was set in
November 2024, when interest rates were high after
the highest inflation in more than 30 years, and it locks
in a higher allowed return until March 2030. Over the
past year, lines charges accounted for around twothirds of the rise in the average power bill.

A re-elected National Government will:
•

Undertake a targeted review of Part 4 of
the Commerce Act on electricity distribution
businesses, examining whether the regime
delivers value for money for consumers,
balances investment with affordability,
and gives distribution businesses the right
incentives to make efficient use of the networks
New Zealanders have already paid for.

•

Require distribution businesses to approve
residential and small business solar connection
applications within two working days, backed
by automatic compensation for the customer
for every day a network runs over.

Putting affordability at the heart of
electricity regulation
Every household and business in New Zealand
depends on affordable power, whether it’s a family
heating their home through winter, a small business
keeping its doors open, or a manufacturer competing
on the world stage. However, the main objective of the
Electricity Authority, New Zealand’s electricity market
regulator, does not require it to consider what its
decisions mean for the power bills Kiwis pay.
Competition, reliable supply, and an efficient
market will continue to guide the Electricity
Authority’s work. National will give affordability
for households and businesses the same standing
in law, so the regulator considers the cost to families
and businesses in every decision it makes.

A re-elected National Government will:
•

Implement the replacement of the RMA,
with more enabling rules for new renewable
generation built in as standard, so wind, solar,
and hydro projects are developed quickly and
power prices are kept down, without every
project needing to compete for a place on
Fast-track.

•

Set clear, national rules so that small-scale
renewables are largely permitted as of
right on people’s own property, including
letting property owners install rooftop solar
without a consent, even where height limits
or landscape overlays would otherwise get
in the way.

•

Make small-scale on-farm ground-mounted
solar a permitted activity, with standard rules
to manage genuine effects.

•

Allow small-scale battery storage not enclosed
by an existing building as of right, subject only
to standard rules.

•

Permit small run-of-river micro-hydro for
on-site use, within a set size and standard
conditions to protect rivers, fish passage and
other water users.

A re-elected National Government will:
•

Amend the Electricity Industry Act to make
affordability for households and businesses a
core objective of the Electricity Authority, with
equal weight alongside competition, reliability,
and efficiency.

Cutting red tape for renewables, big
and small
RMA reform this term has already made a measurable
difference. The Southland Wind Farm was declined
under the old Act after years of process, then approved
in around five months once it moved to Fast-track. That
shows what a properly designed planning system can
do, and it should not take a special process to get that
result, or that investment and those jobs, delivered.
The same problem shows up at the other end of the scale.
Kiwis putting solar, micro-hydro, or a battery on their own
land still face costly, confusing rules that vary from council
to council. Environment Canterbury has required groundmounted solar installations to get a water discharge
consent, because rain running off the panels could
carry bird droppings. Hurunui District Council requires
consent for any free-standing installation larger than
25 square metres, barely enough to power an average
home. Micro-hydro and battery storage face the same
fragmented, region-by-region treatment.
New Zealanders should be able to draw on the
resources on their own land, and the country’s best
renewable resources at scale, with as little red tape
as possible.

The Home Energy Fund
Kiwi families are under pressure from rising power bills.
Rooftop solar, batteries, insulation and modern electric
appliances can ease that pressure and make homes
more resilient, but high upfront cost put them out of
reach for many households, and existing green loans
from commercial banks are limited.
The Ratepayer Assistance Scheme, long advocated for
by Local Government New Zealand (LGNZ) and
Rewiring Aotearoa, offers a practical, market-based
answer by providing a low-interest loan secured against
a homeowner's property and repaid over time on their
rates bill.
At the same time, National is enabling plug-in solar so
renters, who often cannot install rooftop systems, can
also generate their own cheaper power.

A re-elected National Government will:
•

•

•

•

•
•

Implement a narrower version of the
Ratepayer Assistance Scheme, called the
Home Energy Fund, a national financing
platform jointly owned by central government
and participating councils that offers
ratepayers low-interest, long-term loans
secured against their property.
Have the Fund pay the approved installer
upfront, with the homeowner repaying the
low-interest loan over ten years, either
through a charge on their rates bill or on sale
of their property.
Make eligible for support: residential solar
and battery storage; and insulation, heat
pumps, and other investments in residential
electrification.
Amend the Local Government Act and make
a one-off Crown equity investment of $7
million for a 20% shareholding in the new
entity, with the balance funded by
participating councils and the LGFA.
Make loans available to ratepayers with at
least 20% equity in their property.
Enable plug-in solar so renters can easily
generate their own cheaper power.

Data centres that bring their own
power
Large-scale data centres represent a significant
economic opportunity for New Zealand, offering
high-value investment, skilled employment and export
revenue, particularly in regions like the South Island that
combine abundant renewable energy with a cool climate
well suited to the technology. That opportunity must not
come at the expense of household power bills.

A re-elected National Government will:
•

Require new large-scale data centres to bring
their own new, firmed power, applying an
additionality test so that data centre load is
always matched by new generation sufficient
to cover it.

Don’t put it all at risk
New Zealand’s energy security has been hard won this
term. Chris Hipkins and Labour would throw it away,
again, if given the chance.
•

Labour banned new oil and gas exploration once
already, and has pledged to do it again. A second
ban would tell investors New Zealand can’t be
trusted, choke off the gas that firms our renewables,
and push power prices up.

•

Labour let inflation rip out of control, and
construction and network costs went with it. If given
the chance again, every dollar lands straight back
on the lines charges in power bills.

•

Labour would leave New Zealand exposed
to every dry winter, again. No firming, no fuel
reserves, no new generation. Just rationing,
outages, and Wellington ideology deciding whether
the lights stay on, instead of a plan.

New Zealand is on the right track. A re-elected National
Government will keep delivering the secure, affordable
energy, and the jobs, that New Zealanders need.

# Growing More to Feed the World

Published by the New Zealand National Party as a PDF policy document. Source: <https://assets.national.org.nz/web/prod/Growing%20More%20to%20Feed%20the%20World.pdf?v=1792108210>.
The text below is the verbatim text layer of the PDF extracted with `pdftotext` (reading order). Line breaks follow the
PDF; tables and multi-column layouts may read out of order in this section, so a second rendering that preserves the
page layout (`pdftotext -layout`) follows it. Nothing has been added, removed or paraphrased.

## Full text (reading order)

Building the Future:

Growing More
to Feed the World

Building the Future:

Growing More to Feed the World
New Zealand’s farmers and growers are the best in the
world. When they do well, the whole country does well.

National is focused on the key drivers that make a
difference to growth:

Food and fibre earns around four in every five dollars
of our goods exports and supports about 360,000
jobs, most of them in our regions. That export income
pays for the hospitals, schools and roads in every
New Zealand community. When farming grows,
it delivers more jobs, wages lift and the regions
across the country thrive.

• More markets, less risk for farmers. We have
concluded free trade agreements with India, the
UAE and the Gulf states, and brought our EU
agreement into force early. Seven in ten of our
exports are now covered by free trade agreements.
National is focused on securing the next phase of
New Zealand’s trade agenda by commencing trade
negotiations with seven new economies in the next
five years.

The Plan is Working
In 2023 National set an ambitious goal to double
the value of New Zealand’s exports in ten years.
For food and fibre, that means growing from $53.3
billion in the year to June 2024 to around $106 billion
by 2034. It needs growth of 7.2 per cent a year, every
year, well above the 4.7 per cent average of the past.
To get this done we embarked on a transformational
work programme. We replaced the RMA, revoked the
agricultural intensification rules, slashed the growthstunting red tape, introduced investment boost and gave
long life consents to critical primary sector infrastructure
to support a lift in capital outlay. Our plan is working.
Food and fibre exports reached a record $65.2 billion
in the year to June 2026, up almost $12 billion, or
22 per cent, in two years. That puts us about $4 billion
ahead of the path to doubling. We are ahead of
schedule, but the job is not done.

Authorised by J de Joux, ps@national.org.nz

• Get more from our land and more value from every
kilo. We will slash red tape even further by delivering
19 national standards for everyday farm jobs, $300
million in concessional loans for water storage, and
land use flexibility so farmers can put their land to
its best use. In combination with the New Zealand
Grass-Fed standard, faster approvals for new farm
products, and stronger plant variety rights leading to
premium prices for growers.
• Secure and enabling foundations. Reliable access
to water, fertiliser and energy generation, stable
regulatory settings, more rural vets for healthy
animals, a stronger biosecurity system and farmerled conservation.

National got Wellington out of farming
In 2023, National campaigned on getting Wellington
out of farming. We have delivered. Dairy production
has risen for the first time in a decade, and Federated
Farmers’ latest Farm Confidence Survey shows
farmers are in their strongest position in a decade, with
profitability at its highest level since the measure began.
National’s ambition is clear: to make New Zealand the
world’s leading producer of high-value, premium and
sustainable food and fibre.

It’s been three years of delivery for
rural New Zealand
Cutting red tape and restoring common sense

• Opened the Primary Sector Growth Fund to water
storage feasibility studies.
• Passed the Fast-track Approvals Act.
• Backed 51 farmer-led catchment groups and
17 regional collectives.
• Tackled wilding pines with a $80 million funding boost.
• Increased grazing on DOC land to manage weeds,
pests and fire risk.
• Supported our rural communities with increased
funding for Rural Support Trusts, a $4 million Rural
Wellbeing Fund, and $250,000 for Rural Women.
• Backed A&P shows with direct grants.
• Rolled out six rural urgent and after-hours care pilots.

• Replaced the RMA.

• Started building the Waikato Medical School to train
rural doctors.

• Simplified freshwater farm plans.

• Backed new rural scholarships and NZ Young Farmers.

• Introduced practical rules for winter grazing, stock
exclusion and on-farm water storage.

• Signed and ratified a Free Trade Agreement
with India.

• Removed requirements for new Significant Natural
Areas.

• Brought the NZ–EU Free Trade Agreement into
force early.

• Scrapped the Ute Tax.

• Brought New Zealand’s first Middle East FTA,
with the UAE, into force.

• Modernised the ACVM Act to speed up approvals
for new farm products.
• Introduced Investment Boost for new machinery
and equipment.
• Disbanded He Waka Eke Noa.
• Removed Agriculture from the ETS.
• Committed to investigate a split-gas target.

• Concluded a Free Trade Agreement with the
Gulf Cooperation Council.
• Launched the New Zealand Grass-Fed standard.
• Backed Taste Pure Nature with $8 million to market
red meat in China.
• Backed wool in construction of government buildings.

• Stopped full-farm conversions to forestry in the ETS.

• Expanded the Regional Seasonal Employer Scheme.

• Gave water storage 35-year permits.

There is more to do. That is why a re-elected National
Government will secure the future of New Zealand
farming for the generations to come.

• Cut compliance costs for smaller dams.

National’s 10 commitments to farmers
National has a plan to secure the future of New Zealand
farming for the next generation. A re-elected National
Government will deliver 10 commitments to farmers:
1.

No new taxes

2. No price on agricultural emissions
3.

Boost farm productivity through land use
flexibility

4.

Practical and sensible rules that make everyday
farm jobs easier

5. Greater water security for our regions
6. Secure access to energy generation and soil
nutrients that farmers need
7.

Strong biosecurity at the border and on the farm

8. Better access to vets and rural health services
9.

More markets and better returns at the farm gate

10. Back farmers to lead local environmental and
conservation solutions

No new taxes and no price on
agricultural emissions
National is the party of low tax. We delivered income
tax relief for working New Zealanders for the first time
in 14 years and we have committed to no new taxes if
re-elected.
New Zealand’s farmers are among the most emissionsefficient food producers in the world. It makes no sense
to shut down efficient production here and send it
offshore to countries with a larger emissions footprint.
National’s climate policy is based on practical solutions.
We kept agriculture out of the ETS and invested more
than $400 million with industry to get real emissionsreduction tools into farmers’ hands.
We’ve also reset the methane target to a more realistic,
science-based level. Our focus is lower emissions, not
lower production.
Some believe New Zealand should step back from
international climate commitments altogether. Others
think the answer is more pricing, more regulation
and more cost. We don’t agree with either approach.
There will be no tax on agricultural emissions under
a National government.
We will meet our commitments, keep New Zealand in
Paris, back innovation over taxation, and make sure
farmers remain competitive.

Deliver 19 national standards to
make farming easier
Last election, National made a commitment to rural
New Zealand that we would reform our broken
planning system, and we have delivered.
We scrapped Labour’s failed RMA replacement, slashed
red tape for farmers, overhauled National Policy
Statements, passed the Fast-track Approvals Act, and
have passed the most transformational planning reform
in New Zealand’s history.
For more than 30 years, many everyday farm jobs have
needed expensive consents.
Unclear rules and red tape have led to uncertainty
around what farmers are allowed to do with their own
land. That stops in National’s new planning system.
Replacing the legislation is only half the job. A reelected National-led Government will finish it, by
delivering planning rules that work for farmers and
make a real difference on the ground.
Right now, rules are different and fragmented from
one council to the next, driving inefficiency, uncertainty
and leading to huge compliance costs for farmers.

Federated Farmers undertook a survey last year which
showed the average bill for gaining a new consent
under the RMA had hit nearly $45,000. Every dollar
a farmer spends on consenting is a dollar they aren’t
investing in their farms.
If re-elected, National will set 19 national standards
for the work farmers and growers do every day. We
will work with farmers, growers, and the wider sector
to ensure these standards are fit for purpose and
practical. We will prioritise the delivery of these based
on which will remove the highest number of consents,
balanced with the complexity of the standard.
In many cases, these 19 national standards will remove
the need for consents entirely. Even where consents
may still be required, they will be easier, faster, and
cheaper. This means more time and money spent
on growing their businesses, rather than paying for
needless bureaucracy.
National will slash red tape for farmers. We want to
get Wellington out of the way of farmers, so they can
produce more, invest with confidence, and help us
double the value of our exports. It’s how we fix the
basics and build the future.

A re-elected National Government will:
Deliver 19 national standards for farming…
Farm Plans: A national standard for farm
plans will give farmers one practical,
consistent, risk-based way to identify and
manage environmental risks on their land.
This will ensure approaches to farm plans
don’t differ wildly from council to council.

10. On-farm solar: We will make small-scale
on-farm ground-mounted solar, as well
as rooftop solar, permitted activities with
standard rules to manage genuine effects
and sensible safeguards to protect land that
is environmentally significant.

2. Vegetable growing: A national standard for
vegetable growing, including making it a
permitted activity when certain conditions
are met, will give growers certainty to keep
producing the fresh food that feeds our country.

11. Micro-hydro: A national standard for small
run-of-river micro-hydro will help farmers
generate the power they need to run their
businesses, using the water they already have
on their property.

3.

12. Energy storage: A national standard for energy
storage will let farmers install batteries and other
storage that support on-farm energy generation
and resilience.

1.

On-farm water storage: We value on-farm
storage and want more of it, built well. A national
standard will make it easier to build low-risk
water storage, like ponds and small dams, to help
farmers and growers get through dry periods.
Gravel extraction: Responsible gravel extraction
can reduce the flood risk and provide a local
source of aggregate. A national standard will
allow farmers to remove gravel from rivers
under clear, consistent conditions that protect
ecosystem health.

13. Irrigation: A national standard for Irrigation
will make consenting easier for farmers and
growers, providing them with a set of nationally
consistent rules so that irrigation systems are
designed and operated in accordance with
recognised best practice, improving efficiency
and environmental protection.

5. Drain maintenance: Consents can be required
for certain types of on-farm drain maintenance,
adding cost and complexity. A national standard
for drain maintenance will let farmers clear and
maintain their existing drains without navigating
confusing, fragmented rules.

14. Small-scale seasonal-worker accommodation:
A national standard for small-scale seasonalworker accommodation, modelled off our
successful granny-flats standards, will make it
easier for farmers and growers to house the
workers they need at peak times.

6. Effluent management: A national standard for
effluent management will set clear nationwide
requirements for the storage and application
of farm effluent. This will ensure there are
consistent best practice rules so farmers can
realise on-farm benefits while still protecting
the environment.

15. Farm tracks: A national standard for farm tracks
will let farmers build and maintain access tracks,
with sensible controls on erosion and sediment.

4.

7.

Fertiliser application: A national standard for
fertiliser application will set consistent rules for
using fertiliser in a way that supports productivity
while protecting waterways.

8. Farm quarries: Small-scale on-farm quarries
provide gravel, sand, and rock required to build
and maintain important infrastructure. A national
standard for farm quarries will let farmers extract
rock and aggregate from their own land without
consenting processes rendering this uneconomic.
9.

Wetlands: Wetland rules are confusing and
have led to significant amounts of uncertainty
and litigation in the past. A national standard for
wetlands will make it simpler for farmers, removing
the red tape in the way of doing the right thing.

16. Agricultural aviation: A national standard for
agricultural aviation will provide consistent rules
for airstrips, aerial topdressing and spraying,
which Kiwis rely on for both farming and
conservation efforts.
17. Culverts: A national standard for culverts will set
clear requirements for installing and replacing
basic culverts so stock and vehicles can cross
waterways safely, without the costly red-tape.
18. Offal holes: A national standard for offal
holes will give farmers clear, consistent rules
for disposing of dead stock and offal on farm
without the need for a consent.
19. Managing contaminated soils: A re-worked
national standard for managing contaminated
soils will give farmers a consistent, pragmatic
approach to dealing with legacy contamination
on their property while still ensuring the land is
safe to use.

Land use flexibility: producing more
to sell to the world
National knows New Zealand farmers have always
done better when they are empowered to solve
problems, innovate, and make decisions about what
happens behind their own farm gate.
We have worked hard over the last term of government
to axe the rules that were too rigid, systems that were
too slow, and the old approach that the primary sector
is something to constrain, rather than something
to champion.
The future of farming will not be about prescribing one
model from Wellington. It will be about giving farmers and
growers the flexibility to choose the best use of their land
as markets, technology and climate conditions change.
For some, that could mean shifting part of the farm into
a higher-value use. For others, it could mean combining
pastoral, cropping and horticultural systems in smarter
ways, while retaining the strengths of the existing
farm business.
It could mean investing in irrigation and water storage
to strengthen resilience, manage dry periods and make
new land use options commercially viable.
It could mean adopting precision tools, animal wearables,
automation, improved genetics and better data to lift
productivity and farm output.
The goal is not for every farm to look the same. It is for
every landowner to have the confidence, information and
freedom to adapt their business, respond to opportunity
and make the best long-term choices for their land.
Land use flexibility is how New Zealand farms will keep
lifting productivity and secure their future.

At Fieldays 2026, we announced $143 million of land
use flexibility projects across dairy, sheep and beef,
horticulture, forestry, whenua Māori and aquaculture.
These projects test new ideas on real farms, so farmers,
banks and investors can see what works before
they commit.

Water security for growth
Water is one of New Zealand’s greatest strategic
advantages. It underpins our food and fibre production,
supports regional jobs and earns the export income
that pays for hospitals, schools and roads.
We get more rainfall and renewable freshwater per
person than almost any other developed nation. Yet too
many regions still face water shortages. We have the
water. We just don’t store enough of it. New Zealand
captures and uses about two per cent of its available
water resources. We can and should do better.
National believes we should plan for water security the
same way we plan for fuel and energy. That means storing
water when it is plentiful and using it well when it is scarce.
It means knowing where water will be needed and giving
regions a clear path to build the storage they need.

Get schemes built
A re-elected National Government will commit $300
million in concessional loans to get water storage projects
built. The Primary Sector Growth Fund will continue to
provide support for pre-construction studies for productive
water storage projects. Water projects can spend years
moving between hydrology, engineering, environmental
assessment, land access, user commitments, consenting
and finance. National wants water storage projects
approved and built faster. Our promise of concessional
loan support will help bridge the gap.

Deliver New Zealand’s first long-term water
infrastructure pipeline

A proportionate approach to on-farm water
storage and irrigation

New Zealand has many promising water infrastructure
proposals, but there is no single national view of
existing storage, future demand, climate risk or
project readiness. Work is often commissioned one
project at a time; information is gathered to different
standards and specialist capability is lost between
projects. A national water infrastructure pipeline
will allow connected storage, distribution, managed
aquifer recharge, renewal and on-farm options to be
considered together.

We value on-farm storage and want more of it, built
well. National will make it easier for farmers and
growers to build water storage on their own land,
by developing a National Standard for on-farm water
storage under the new planning system. This will allow
on-farm water storage infrastructure to be built without
the need for costly resource consents.

We will start by prioritising five key regions
• Northland
• Tairāwhiti
• Hawke’s Bay
• Wairarapa
• Canterbury
Behind those five, the register will build a longer,
nationally prioritised pipeline. Further priority areas
identified include:
• Bay of Plenty orchards
• Central Otago and Waitaki fruit growing
• Upper South Island: Marlborough and Nelson
• Southern dryland areas, where stored water
is the difference between a normal season
and destocking.

National will also make it easier to get consents
by introducing a National Standard for Irrigation to
ensure irrigation systems are designed and operated
to recognised best practice, improving water-use
efficiency, reducing environmental risk and providing
farmers with a simpler, nationally consistent set of rules.

A re-elected National Government will:
• Commit $300 million in concessional loans to
get water storage projects built.
• The Primary Sector Growth Fund will continue
to provide grants for feasibility studies.
• Deliver New Zealand’s first long-term water
infrastructure pipeline, in partnership with
farmers, growers, councils and iwi.
• Publish the first National Rural and Provincial
Water Use Strategy in 2027, backed by a
national water storage register.
• Introduce a National Standard for on-farm and
other lower-risk off-stream water storage, and
• Introduce a National Standard for Irrigation to
make consenting easier for farmers and growers.

On-farm energy independence
Farms use a lot of power for milking, cooling,
pumping and irrigation, and lines charges are set
to keep rising through to 2030. Farms are also well
placed to generate their own.
Farmers and growers know what it costs when the lines
go down in a storm, or when global events push up fuel
and fertiliser prices. National trusts farmers to make the
right decisions for their land, and that includes energy.
But they still face costly, confusing rules to develop
small-scale renewables on their own property, making
the process slow and expensive.
For example, Rewiring Aotearoa found Environment
Canterbury has required ground-mounted solar
installations to apply for a water discharge consent,
because rain runs off the panels and could carry
bird droppings. Hurunui District Council, meanwhile,
requires consent for any free-standing installation
larger than 25m², barely enough to power an average
New Zealand home.
It’s not just consenting that’s hard. Energy network
regulations get in the way of farmers making the most
of the energy they produce as well.
National is committed to supporting on-farm energy
independence. Farmers and growers should be able
to harness the resources available on their own land,
easier, faster, and cheaper. If re-elected, we will clear
the way for them to generate, store and sell their own
power. This will cut costs, build resilience and give
farmers and growers another way to earn from their
own land without unreasonable rules getting in the way.

A re-elected National Government will:
1.

Set a national standard for paddock-based
solar. Small-scale ground-mounted solar
on farms will be a permitted activity, with
standard rules to manage any real effects.
Farmers will know what is allowed and won’t
need a resource consent for a standard setup.

2. Make it easier to put in micro-hydro. Small
run-of-river micro-hydro for on-farm use will
be permitted within set limits that protect
rivers, fish and other water users.
3.

Allow small-scale battery storage as of
right, so farmers can make the most of their
investment in solar, micro-hydro and other
renewables.

4.

Let farmers sell their power to the best
buyer. Every farmer will have the right to sell
the power they export to any power company,
not just the one they buy from.

5. Make lines companies base export limits on
what the local network can handle. If they
want to restrict how much a farm exports, they
will have to show there is a genuine constraint.
6. Speed up connections. Farmers will be able
to choose their own accredited contractor for
connection work, cutting costs and delays.
7.

Allow rural developers, major energy
users, and investors to build and own new
transmission and recover their costs from the
parties who use the lines.

8. Let property owners install rooftop solar
without a consent, even where height limits
or landscape overlays would otherwise get in
the way.

Guaranteeing critical nutrients
Fertiliser is a critical nutrient input into New Zealand’s
food and fibre economy. Reliable access supports soil
fertility, farm productivity, export earnings and rural
communities. A serious supply disruption would
be felt well beyond the farm gate through lower
production, higher costs and weaker export returns.
New Zealand uses over two million tonnes of fertiliser
to grow food each year. Our fertiliser production relies
on imported phosphate, which is then processed
on shore. This leaves our primary sector exposed
to international supply shocks. National will reduce
New Zealand’s exposure by supporting domestic
production, strengthening supply relationships,
and attracting investment in strategic infrastructure.
This is about ensuring a continued, stable supply
of fertiliser in the country. We will back measures
to support farmers to responsibly manage their
nutrient use to better support productive farming
and the environment.

Strengthening supply partnerships
New Zealand imports around two-thirds of its
urea, with significant volumes sourced from the
Gulf, particularly Saudi Arabia. Recent conflict and
disruption in the Middle East have shown how quickly
shipping risks can flow through to global fertiliser
prices and availability. Other key nutrients, including
phosphate rock, potash and sulphur, are also exposed
to concentrated production, commodity cycles and
long transport routes.
National will treat fertiliser as a strategic priority
in trade, diplomatic and investment engagement.
Using the New Zealand–Singapore Agreement
on Trade in Essential Supplies as a blueprint,
National will pursue arrangements with key
supplier countries focused on reliable access,
market diversification, early warning and rapid
government-to-government coordination.

A re-elected National Government will:
• Negotiate fertiliser security agreements
with key supplier countries, using the
New Zealand–Singapore Agreement on
Trade in Essential Supplies as a model.
• Establish a $10 million Critical Agri Inputs
Fund to co-invest in fertiliser production,
processing, storage and distribution projects
from the Primary Sector Growth Fund.

Double baseline funding for the
QEII National Trust

thirds of farmers say pest numbers have increased
over the past five years, while average pest-control
spending has risen to $6.18 per hectare.

National backs farmer-led conservation. Most land in
New Zealand is privately owned, and much of it holds
native bush, wetlands and biodiversity. That makes the
QEII National Trust’s work with farmers and landowners,
through voluntary covenants, critical to protecting our
unique landscapes.

Wild deer, feral goats and pigs move across the
boundaries between conservation land, forestry, farms
and whenua Māori. They eat pasture and young trees,
damage fences, threaten lambs, prevent native forest
regeneration and undermine earlier conservation
investment. Fragmented responsibility leaves farmers
carrying costs created beyond their boundary.

National will provide the QEII National Trust with longterm funding certainty and support its work alongside
farmers and landowners protecting New Zealand’s
natural and cultural heritage.
Permanent funding certainty means QEII Trust
can plan ahead, respond to growing demand, and
continue providing practical support for fencing,
weed and pest control, revegetation, and covenant
enhancement. Covenants protect the bush remnants,
lookouts, landscapes and special places that give rural
districts their character and identity. They also build a
community’s resilience to natural disasters, protecting
hillsides from erosion, mitigating flooding impacts and
reducing fire/disease risk.

A re-elected National Government will:
• Double the baseline funding for the QEII
National Trust from approximately $4.2 million
to approximately $8.5 million per year. The
increase will be confirmed in Budget 2027 and
will be a permanent, not a time-limited top-up.

Backing farmers to beat the pest crisis
National will invest $16 million over four years from the
International Visitor Conservation and Tourism Levy to
reduce damaging populations of wild deer, feral goats
and other priority pests across public, Māori and private
land. This builds on previous IVL investment in wild
animal management, and the wider wild goat and deer
work DOC delivers.
Farmers are spending more time and money controlling
pests but feel like they are still going backwards.
Federated Farmers’ 2026 National Pests Survey
estimates pests cost farmers about $466 million each
year through control costs and lost production. Two-

National will back coordinated control at landscape
scale. We will target the source of pest pressure,
protect productive land and conservation gains, and
build local capability so pest numbers stay down.
This new investment will mean fewer pests moving
from public and forestry land onto farms, less damage
to pasture, fences, young trees and native vegetation,
stronger protection for conservation gains, and more
skilled rural jobs.

A re-elected National Government will:
• Invest a further $16 million over four years
from the International Visitor Conservation
and Tourism Levy to concentrate efforts to
reduce wild deer, feral goats and other priority
pests across public, Māori and private land.
• Fund coordinated control programmes
across land tenures. National will combine
aerial and ground control, surveillance,
monitoring by partnering with councils, iwi
and hapū, landowners, forestry, hunters and
community groups.
• Focus on the Central North Island and Southern
Westland regions first. Work will initially target
the Whanganui–East Cape corridor and protect
the gains made through Predator Free South
Westland and Zero Invasive Predators, with final
detailed plans agreed locally.
• Finalise the National Introduced Wild
Animal Management Framework to
improve the management of introduced wild
animals, and steer coordinated management
programmes and enable stakeholders to work
effectively together.

More vets for rural New Zealand
National will double the number of graduate vets
placed in rural New Zealand through the Voluntary
Bonding Scheme, from around 35 a year to 70 a year.
Animal health is the foundation of more than
$40 billion a year of dairy, meat and wool exports,
of our biosecurity defences, and of the rural
communities that depend on them. Yet rural practices
are struggling to recruit, too many of our young vets
are heading offshore, and New Zealand relies on
overseas-trained vets for two in every three new
registrations. The bottom line is that our farmers
can’t grow the economy if they can’t get a vet.
National is already strengthening the domestic training
pipeline. From 2027, the number of funded domestic
places in Massey University’s Bachelor of Veterinary
Science will increase from 125 to 140 each year,
allowing an additional 15 New Zealand students to
begin veterinary training annually.
The expansion of the bonding scheme is expected to cost
up to $3.4 million over the four year forecast period rising
to around $2 million a year once fully implemented, and
will be funded from within MPI baselines.

Training more vets matters, but we also need them
working where they are needed most. The Voluntary
Bonding Scheme gives new graduates a financial
incentive to start their careers in rural areas where
shortages are worst. The scheme helps attract and
retain veterinarians in hard-to-staff regions, easing
pressure on existing clinics and improving access
to animal care for farmers.

A re-elected National Government will:
• Double the scheme to up to 70 places a year
from the 2027 funding round, for new graduate
vets committed to five years of rural practice
with production animals and working dogs.
• Open the scheme to New Zealand citizens
and permanent residents who graduate from
accredited Australian vet schools and are
registered to practise here.
• Report on results each year, publishing where
bonded vets work and how many stay, with a
full review of the scheme in three years.

Common-sense rules and regulatory certainty
Farmers need rules they can plan around and that match how farming works today. A re-elected National
Government will finish the job on several important changes.

A re-elected National Government will:
• Introduce no new taxes on farmers
• Keep agriculture out of the ETS
• Pass the KiwiSaver (First Home or Farm)
Amendment Bill so farm workers can use
their KiwiSaver to buy their first home or
a farm, including those living in employerprovided housing.
• Progress the Gene Technology Bill to speed
up innovation while safely managing risks
to people and the environment.
• Review the Sharemilking Agreements Act
to reflect the growth of contract milking,
protect young entrants and reduce disputes.
• Update agricultural vehicle weight rules so
modern tractors and harvesters don’t need routine
overweight permits, while protecting vulnerable
roads and bridges. In the meantime, NZTA will
be directed to improve the permit system.
• Simplify wild meat rules so small processors
can handle both farmed livestock and certified
wild game, with strict food safety and traceability.

• Create regional wildfire readiness plans with
forest owners, farmers, Fire and Emergency
New Zealand and councils, so firefighters can
act fast with the right information. Wildfire risk
is rising and too often crews arrive not knowing
which tracks a fire engine can use or where
the nearest available water source is.
• Pass the Crown Land Legislation Amendment
Bill so high-country leaseholders can add
farm shops, hospitality, arable, horticulture and
renewable energy alongside pastoral farming.
• Keep the ban on full-farm conversions to exotic
forestry in the ETS, while still allowing farmers
to plant up to 25 per cent of their own land
if they choose. We must preserve our most
productive farmland.
• Extend the Plant Variety Rights (PVR) Act 2022
to secure the development of future high-value
varieties.
• Open seven new markets through Next Billion
Customers, so what farmers grow has buyers
ready to pay a premium.

Strong biosecurity at the border and on the farm
Farmers care deeply about biosecurity. It is our
first line of defence against pests and diseases
that could devastate our primary industries,
environment and economy. The arrival of Highly
Pathogenic Avian Influenza, H5N1, shows the value
of preparation and cooperation between industry
and government. Producing more for the world
depends on keeping our biosecurity status.
Growers want faster approvals for new crop protection
tools. The National-led Government opened a pathway
for growers to follow international Codex standards for
agrichemicals where New Zealand limits have not been
set. In September 2026 we passed the Agricultural
Compounds and Veterinary Medicines Amendment
Act, which will speed up approvals for new products.
As travel and trade grow, so does the risk at our border.
National will strengthen our biosecurity laws so our
border protections stay among the strongest in the
world, and those who put our biosecurity at risk face
real consequences.

A re-elected National Government will:
• Pass the Biosecurity Act Amendment Bill
to modernise our biosecurity system and
strengthen our ability to prevent, detect and
respond to threats.
• Pass the Hazardous Substances and
New Organisms (HSNO) Amendment Bill
to accelerate access to agricultural and
horticultural products and veterinary medicines.
• Increase penalties for serious biosecurity
breaches at the border so they are a genuine
deterrent and reflect the damage an incursion
can do by increasing conviction fines from
$1,000 to $2,000 and grant officers the
discretion to refuse entry or deport certain
temporary visa holders.

Improving Rural Diagnostic Access
National is focused on delivering timely, high-quality
healthcare for rural New Zealand. That means putting
rural communities at the centre of health planning,
shifting the focus towards prevention and earlier
diagnosis, bringing more services closer to home,
supporting people who still need to travel, and building
a stronger rural health workforce.
The message from the frontline is clear: access to
diagnostics remains one of the biggest unmet needs
in rural healthcare. A survey of 192 rural health
professionals identified diagnostic imaging and cardiac
testing as major unmet needs, with travel barriers the
single greatest obstacle to timely care.
For rural families, accessing a routine diagnostic test
can mean hours of travel, time away from work and
additional pressure on those juggling family and caring
responsibilities. These barriers can delay diagnosis and
treatment, adding unnecessary pressure to patients,
families and the wider health system.
A re-elected National Government will build on
progress in rural healthcare by maximising capacity in
our public and private hospitals and continue to roll out

mobile diagnostic scanners to deliver more services for
patients. By making better use of existing resources,
technology and partnerships with healthcare providers,
National will bring more essential diagnostic services
closer to rural communities.
Improving access to diagnostics will help patients
get answers sooner, reduce unnecessary travel and
hospital transfers, support earlier treatment and make
better use of the rural health workforce..

A re-elected National Government will:
• Maximise diagnostic capacity across public and
private hospitals, making better use of existing
equipment, facilities and clinical expertise to
deliver more timely testing for patients.
• Roll out mobile diagnostic scanners, prioritising
rural communities facing the greatest access
barriers and working with local health providers
to bring more services closer to home.
• Measure and report results, including
diagnostic wait times, avoided patient travel
and hospital transfers, service volumes and
improvements in access and patient outcomes.

Growing the next generation of farmers
New Zealand’s food and fibre workforce is ageing.
The average farmer is now 58, and over the next
decade more than 17,000 farm and orchard owners
will reach 65. For a sector that supports 360,000
jobs, makes up 15 per cent of GDP and earns a
record $65.2 billion in exports, we need more
young people coming through.
National refreshed the Agricultural and Horticultural
Science curriculum, rescued Apprenticeship Boost
from a funding cliff and targeted it to high-growth
areas including agriculture, horticulture, viticulture
and forestry. Apprentice completion rates have lifted
from 67 per cent in 2021 to 86 per cent.
We saved Telford, disestablished the centralised
Wellington bureaucracy of Te Pūkenga and restored
standalone regional polytechnics, so rural and
agricultural training is delivered locally and shaped
by local industry needs.
At Fieldays 2026 we launched the Future Leaders
Scholarship, giving emerging leaders in agriculture,
horticulture and forestry $10,000 towards study,
industry experience and governance skills.
We want to go further.

A re-elected National Government will:
• Introduce an industry-led secondary school
subject of Food and Fibre Systems for Years 12
and 13, starting in 2029.
• Double Trades Academy places to 20,000
by 2030 and expand Youth Guarantee places
by 1,000 a year, giving more young people
early, practical pathways into food and fibre.
• Work with Landcorp to expand the
Apprenticeship Scheme so more young
New Zealanders can gain recognised
agricultural qualifications and build a long-term
career in farming.
• Grow Landcorp’s dairy and livestock
equity partnership schemes, creating more
opportunities for young farmers to build
equity, progress into business ownership
and ultimately their own farm.
• Back the Future Leaders Scholarship to
encourage young people to develop the
necessary skills to lead the primary sector
in the years to come.

A plan for rural New Zealand
The plan is working but the job is not done. Farmers know National backs them. New Zealand’s farming families
are helping us fix the basics by growing the economy, and together we are building the future for a prosperous
New Zealand.

Lower costs. Simpler rules. Secure inputs. More markets.
Stronger rural communities.

# International Visitor Levy Reset

Published by the New Zealand National Party as a PDF policy document. Source: <https://assets.national.org.nz/web/prod/International%20Visitor%20Levy%20Reset.pdf?v=1788837206>.
The text below is the verbatim text layer of the PDF extracted with `pdftotext` (reading order). Line breaks follow the
PDF; tables and multi-column layouts may read out of order in this section, so a second rendering that preserves the
page layout (`pdftotext -layout`) follows it. Nothing has been added, removed or paraphrased.

## Full text (reading order)

Building the Future:

Resetting the International
Visitor Levy to keep taxes low
Growing New Zealand’s tourism industry is a critical
part of National’s plan to fix the basics and build the
future. Tourism is our second-largest export earner and
supports around one in nine jobs. A thriving tourism
industry means stronger exports, more jobs and higher
wages, in Auckland and Queenstown, and in the small
towns and regional centres that host our visitors.

The Government’s Tourism Growth Roadmap and
first national Tourism Policy Statement set the goal
of doubling the value of tourism exports by 2034.
National believes that growth should be managed
responsibly, so regions that experience the benefits
of New Zealand’s tourism industry aren’t also left to
carry all of the costs.

The tourism recovery is well under way. New Zealand
welcomed 3.67 million international visitors in the year
to June 2026, up 9 per cent on the previous year, with
monthly arrivals now back to 95 per cent of 2019 levels.
Total tourism expenditure for the year ending March
2025 was $46.6 billion, or 114 per cent of 2019 levels.

To support a vibrant tourism industry capable of
maintaining its social licence, a re-elected National
Government will reset funding from the International
Visitor Levy (IVL), so councils see a direct and growing
financial return from the visitors they host, without a
new bed tax.

Building on National’s plan for tourism growth
National has already put the foundations in place.
The IVL reset is the next step, by delivering on the
Tourism Policy Statement’s commitment to consider
future funding arrangements to enable management
of visitor pressures at place and delivery of
sustainable tourism growth.
•

•

•

A national direction. The Tourism Policy
Statement, released in June 2026, sets
eight objectives for the tourism system,
including “tourism that works for regions
and communities”, and clarifies the roles
of central government, councils, iwi
and industry.

•

Growing demand. Sustained investment in
international marketing, a visa-waiver trial, new
trans-Tasman and Chinese airline capacity, and
a cruise season of close to 200,000 passengers
are all lifting visitor numbers.

National’s IVL reset
From 1 July 2027, funding from the IVL will be split
three ways:

Backing regional tourism. Three rounds
of the Regional Tourism Boost, including
$5 million announced in June 2026, have
encouraged visitors to travel beyond the main
centres and outside peak season.
Events. A $70 million events and tourism package
is bringing world-class sport and concerts to
New Zealand cities and regions, with local
government expected to partner in hosting them.

•

$100 million per annum will be directed to the
Department of Conservation to keep investing
in the conservation estate that underpins
New Zealand’s visitor experience.

•

$50 million per annum will be ring-fenced for
a Tourism Priorities Fund, to keep supporting
tourism growth and resilience.

•

All remaining IVL revenue, starting at $86 million
in 2027/28 and rising to $106 million in 2030/31, will
be distributed directly to councils. As visitor numbers
grow, more of the levy flows to the regions, rather
than to central government activities, rather than to
central government activities.

At the same time, National will continue to back the industry to grow by committing that there will be no
increase in the IVL for at least the next three years.

Authorised by J de Joux, ps@national.org.nz

. What changes
There are three changes under National’s policy:
•

•

•

Certainty for conservation. The Department of
Conservation will receive all of the baseline funding
from the IVL. Right now, the levy offsets Crown
appropriations to both DOC and Tourism New
Zealand, and funding for conservation rises and
falls with visitor numbers. From 1 July 2027, annual
baseline funding will be fixed at $100 million to
support the Department of Conservation.
A sharper central government fund. Right now,
$90 million a year is available for discretionary
central government spending. National will replace
this pool with a $50 million Tourism Priorities
Fund, focused on international marketing, visitor
infrastructure in high-growth regions, event
attraction, and tourism system requirements
such as investment in tourism data and the
tourism workforce.
More support for the regions. All remaining IVL
revenue will be distributed to councils, based on
their share of international visitor guest nights as
measured by MBIE.

Backing the councils that host our
visitors
New Zealand doesn’t need a new tax. International
visitors already pay their way through GST, fuel taxes
and the international visitor levy. The problem is that
councils who meet many of the costs of tourism don’t
see enough of the direct financial benefit.
Roads, car parks, public toilets, waste collection,
freedom-camping enforcement and water infrastructure
all have to be delivered to manage peak visitor

demand, but the rates that fund them do not grow with
visitor numbers. In Queenstown Lakes, where around
three-quarters of visitors come from overseas, some
roads serving just a handful of ratepayers carry tens
of thousands of visitors a year. Rotorua, Mackenzie,
Westland, Kaikōura and many smaller districts face the
same imbalance.
National believes we don’t need a bed tax. Instead,
the regions that benefit from tourism just need to see
more of the direct financial benefit that comes to New
Zealand from having a thriving tourism industry. Under
National’s policy, every council that hosts international
visitors will receive a growing share of the IVL, without
justifying themselves to central government through
lengthy applications or complicated funding rounds.
Over the long term, sharing more of the proceeds from
tourism with communities will protect the industry’s
social license and ensure New Zealand remains on
track to double the value of tourism to the economy
by 2034.

Regional funding for councils
IVL revenue will be distributed to territorial authorities
in proportion to international guest nights, as measured
by the MBIE Accommodation Data Programme.
Councils that host the most international visitors receive
the most, and every council that hosts international
visitors receives something.
As required by section 399A of the Immigration Act
2009, councils will need to show that each dollar
is spent only on conservation or tourism purposes.
Eligible uses include freedom-camping enforcement,
public toilets and waste management, tourism
promotion, event attraction, visitor infrastructure,
and traffic and parking management.

Fiscal impact
Guaranteeing the Department of Conservation $100 million costs the Crown the difference between that fixed
amount and the larger sum the levy would otherwise have offset against Crown baselines. The estimated impact
on the Crown is set out below.

# Making Trans-Tasman travel seamless

Published by the New Zealand National Party as a PDF policy document. Source: <https://assets.national.org.nz/web/prod/Making%20Trans-Tasman%20travel%20seamless.pdf?v=1790833234>.
The text below is the verbatim text layer of the PDF extracted with `pdftotext` (reading order). Line breaks follow the
PDF; tables and multi-column layouts may read out of order in this section, so a second rendering that preserves the
page layout (`pdftotext -layout`) follows it. Nothing has been added, removed or paraphrased.

## Full text (reading order)

Building the Future:

Making Trans-Tasman travel
seamless to grow tourism
Introduction
Growing New Zealand’s tourism industry is a critical
part of National’s plan to fix the basics and build the
future. Tourism is our second-largest export earner and
supports around one in nine jobs.
Australia and New Zealand share two of the most
closely integrated economies in the world, including
each other’s largest tourism markets. New Zealand
recorded 1.52 million visitor arrivals from Australia in the
year ended December 2025, the highest annual result
since early 2020. In July 2026, New Zealand recorded
134,900 Australian visitor arrivals, the highest July
month on record. Australian visitors spent $4.2 billion
in New Zealand in the year ended March 2026, with
holiday visitors spending an average of $4,397 per trip.
To support our shared tourism industry to keep
growing, a re-elected National Government will work
with Australia to trial seamless travel for Australian
and New Zealand citizens travelling between the
two countries.

In practice, this means a fully digital trans-Tasman
travel experience, where eligible travellers can rely
on a smartphone, digital credentials and biometric
technology through more of the airport journey. This
would mean no paper passport required at the gate and
faster movement through airports, while maintaining
the security and integrity of New Zealand’s border and
preserving the ability of border agencies to intervene
where risk is identified.
With the ICC Men’s T20 World Cup 2028 to be jointly
hosted by Australia and New Zealand from 21 October
to 19 November 2028, we are expecting a surge in
cross-border travel from Kiwis and Australians. National’s
objective is to introduce a trial for seamless digital travel
prior to that tournament.

How it would work
Eligible travellers (Australian and New Zealand passportholders) will:
•

Provide their passport and travel details digitally
before departure, building on information already
provided to airlines and through the New Zealand
Traveller Declaration.

•

National’s policy

Complete their New Zealand Traveller Declaration
before flying, allowing immigration, customs and
biosecurity information to be assessed earlier.

•

National has already put the foundations in place for
seamless travel. In 2009, the National-led Government
officially launched SmartGate for trans-Tasman
passengers. This was the first step in streamlining
travel between the two countries.

Have their eligibility and identity checked digitally,
with travellers requiring further examination
removed from the streamlined pathway.

•

Use a dedicated trans-Tasman arrival pathway
at Auckland, Wellington, Christchurch and
Queenstown airports, which are supported by
existing eGate and facial-recognition technology.

•

Continue to meet all New Zealand biosecurity
and customs requirements, including baggage
inspection where required. Seamless immigration
processing does not mean bypassing biosecurity.
Travellers would still have to make the same
declarations and could still have baggage
inspected or be referred to an officer.

Making it easier for Australians to visit New Zealand
means more visitors exploring our cities and regions
which results in more incomes for local businesses,
more jobs opportunities for New Zealanders, and a
stronger economy.

In 2024, Prime Ministers Luxon and Albanese endorsed
the work of the Trans-Tasman Seamless Travel Group
and committed to exploring ways to move closer to
seamless travel between the two countries.
A re-elected National Government will deliver on that
commitment and work with Australia to trial seamless
travel for Australian and New Zealand citizens travelling
between the two countries.

Authorised by J de Joux, ps@national.org.nz

New Zealand already has much of the infrastructure
required. The New Zealand Traveller Declaration
is linked to a traveller’s passport, while eGates use
biometric technology to match a traveller’s face with
their ePassport.
To enable this policy, legislative changes to the
Immigration Act 2009 and Customs and Excise
Act 2018 will be required, as they currently impose
obligations to present a travel document and be
presented to a border official on arrival.

International comparisons
•

Singapore has implemented passport-less
clearance in Changi Airport. Arriving and departing
Singapore passport-holders can clear immigration
simply using facial and iris biometrics, without the
need to present their passport. All foreign visitors
can also enjoy the convenience of passport-less
clearance when they depart Singapore.
»

»

•

•

With the full roll-out of passport-less clearance
at Changi Airport, the average clearance time
for each traveller has been reduced by 60%,
from 25 seconds to 10 seconds.
International reporting identifies Singapore’s
passport-free biometric clearance as a leading
operational example.

Common Travel Area – Ireland and the UK – there
are no routine passport controls in operation for
Irish and British citizens traveling between the two
countries. However, you must show identification
to board a ferry or an airplane, and some airlines
and sea carriers only accept a passport as valid
identification. You may also be asked by an
immigration officer to prove that you are a citizen
of Ireland or the UK, so people are encouraged to
still carry a passport on them.
Indonesia is the first country in the world to
introduce an AI-powered biometric ‘seamless
corridor’ system. This system uses AI-enabled
biometrics to validate passenger identities “in
motion”. AI cameras scan and match your face in
real-time as you walk through a wide corridor, so
people do not need to stop, pull out their passport,
or talk to a border official. This is part of the “All
Indonesia” initiative, a major government-led
digital transformation aiming at streamlining the
entry process for international travellers. Testing
shows the system processes over 30 passengers
per minute, which is ten times faster than standard
e-gates. The initial phase focuses on serving
elderly and disabled travellers. The government
plans to expand the technology to all international
passengers across the country’s airport network.

Managing immigration risk
No immigration, customs, biosecurity or lawenforcement powers will be removed. Travellers who
trigger a border alert, do not meet the trial criteria,
cannot be reliably matched to their passport, make a
declaration requiring further examination, or otherwise
require additional checks will be diverted into normal
border processing.

Historical background
•

From 1973-1981, Australia and New Zealand
enjoyed a passport-free understanding where,
under the Trans-Tasman Agreement, Kiwis and
Aussies could live and work in either country with
relatively few restrictions.

•

In 1981, the Australian government announced that
all people entering Australia would be required
to carry a passport. It was prompted in part by
concerns that international terrorists and drug
traffickers could pose as New Zealanders and
enter Australia.

•

In 1987, New Zealand returned the favour and it
became official that Australians needed a passport
to visit New Zealand.

•

In 2009, Prime Minister John Key officially launched
SmartGate for trans-Tasman passengers. This was
the first step in streamlining travel between the
two countries.

•

In 2023, the Trans-Tasman Seamless Travel
Group was established between Albanese and
Hipkins to deliver on Australian and New Zealand’s
commitment to explore ways to move closer
to seamless travel between the two countries.
It is chaired by Australian Border Force (ABF)
Commissioner and New Zealand Customs Service
Chief Executive.

•

In August 2024, Prime Ministers Luxon and
Albanese endorsed the work of the Trans-Tasman
Seamless Travel Group and its vision for easier
travel between Australia and New Zealand while
ensuring the highest levels of security at our
borders. They announced that governments
and industry would implement this vision via
coordinated activities to enhance traveller
experience. This would include Australia trialling
a digital incoming passenger card for the first
time, and New Zealand upgrading eGates.
Prime Ministers noted these were steps towards
‘contactless travel’ when passengers would be
able to rely on digital credentials throughout the
airport journey.
