documents/pdf-more-grocery-competition.m.title: More Grocery Competition
documents/pdf-more-grocery-competition.m.text:
# More Grocery Competition

Published by the New Zealand National Party as a PDF policy document. Source: <https://assets.national.org.nz/web/prod/More%20Grocery%20Competition.pdf?v=1789522994>.
The text below is the verbatim text layer of the PDF extracted with `pdftotext` (reading order). Line breaks follow the
PDF; tables and multi-column layouts may read out of order in this section, so a second rendering that preserves the
page layout (`pdftotext -layout`) follows it. Nothing has been added, removed or paraphrased.

## Full text (reading order)

Building the Future:

More grocery competition
New Zealanders deserve a fair deal at the checkout and
a grocery market where supermarkets have to compete
hard for every customer.

If the Commerce Commission recommends separation,
National will act by legislating to require that separation
to occur.

Competition puts pressure on businesses to sharpen
their prices, improve service, innovate and give
consumers more choice. When competition is weak,
consumers pay higher prices.

How we got here

The Commerce Commission concluded in its 2022
grocery market study that competition was not working
well for consumers and competition between the major
retailers was muted.
National believes New Zealand needs at least three
strong grocery businesses competing at scale.

National’s proposal
National will pursue the structural separation of
Foodstuffs into two genuinely competing nationwide
grocery groups, subject to an independent Commerce
Commission assessment that it can be implemented
in a way that enhances competition for the benefit of
New Zealand consumers.
The proposed structure would be:
•

one nationwide PAK’nSAVE group

•

one separate nationwide New World and Four
Square group.

That would create three major nationwide grocery
competitors: PAK’nSAVE, New World/Four Square
and Woolworths.
National believes the work undertaken to date
provides a strong case for pursuing this option. The
Commerce Commission will be asked to take the
proposal to the next stage, develop and assess a
detailed implementation plan, and determine whether
the restructure can be delivered in a way that leaves
consumers better off.
To give the Commission that mandate, National
will amend the Grocery Industry Competition Act
2023 in our first 100 days and require it to make its
recommendation within six months.

Authorised by J de Joux, ps@national.org.nz

National did not start with structural separation.
Our first objective was to get more competitors into the
grocery market.
Following the Commerce Commission’s market study,
we went to the market with a Request for Information
(RFI) and asked potential entrants and expanding
retailers what was stopping them entering New Zealand
or growing here.
Two things became clear.
First, there were regulatory and practical barriers
to entry and expansion that Government could do
something about.
The Government has spent the past three years working
to remove and reduce those barriers. We have made it
easier to consent and build new supermarkets, improved
the pathway for overseas investment, strengthened
competition settings and backed the Commerce
Commission in its role as grocery regulator.
We will keep doing that work.
But the second message from the market was more
fundamental.
Even with those barriers reduced, the scale and market
power of the existing major retailers would continue to
make it very difficult for a new competitor to enter and
grow to national scale.
Foodstuffs and Woolworths still account for around 82
per cent of the grocery market. Smaller competitors have
entered and expanded, but they have not yet reached
the scale required to materially change competition
nationwide.
The existing major retailers also have substantial
advantages in sites, distribution networks, brand
recognition, customer data and bargaining power
with suppliers.

The ideal outcome remains a new competitor entering
New Zealand and growing to scale.
But the evidence suggests that could take a decade
or more.
So, the question became: if a third major competitor
is unlikely to get to scale quickly enough on its
own, is there another way to create three strong
competitors sooner?
One option is to restructure the existing market.

Testing structural options
Structural reform has been considered before.
The previous Government examined a ‘Pick’n Mix’ option
that would have forced Foodstuffs and Woolworths to
divest selected stores to create a new third retailer.

The analysis found that restructuring Woolworths as well
would involve significantly higher costs and deliver much
lower overall net economic benefits.
We then had the CBA independently peer reviewed and
further tested.
That work has given us what is, in effect, an indicative
business case for structural separation.
It tells us there is enough of a case to move to the next
stage. But it is modelling, not a guarantee.
Structural separation comes with costs. These include
the cost of establishing additional logistics and
distribution functions, changes to supply arrangements,
and transition costs. The results are sensitive to those
assumptions and that is why implementation matters.
The CBA proves this proposal is worth pursuing. The
next step is to develop a detailed implementation plan
and assess whether it leaves consumers better off.

That would have involved assembling a new
supermarket business from a mix of existing stores,
with significant implementation complexity. It could
have required a new brand, and head office, and very
significantly impinged on the property rights of individual
store owners.

Why split Foodstuffs?

This National-led Government took a different approach.
Rather than create a new supermarket business, we
commissioned an independent cost-benefit analysis
to test whether existing supermarket brands could be
reorganised into stronger nationwide competitors.

At present, Foodstuffs is divided geographically.

We commissioned Sense Partners to conduct an
independent cost-benefit analysis of two options:
•

restructuring Foodstuffs into two nationwide
grocery groups

•

restructuring both Foodstuffs and Woolworths.

The stronger case was for restructuring Foodstuffs alone.
Under its central assumptions, the independent CBA
estimates restructuring Foodstuffs could deliver:
•

household benefits of around $200 to $1,320 a
year by full rollout, depending on household type
and income

•

grocery prices around 3.5 per cent below the
baseline in the first year after retail separation,
increasing to around 5 per cent

•

$12.58 billion in net consumer benefits over
20 years

•

$2.92 billion in overall net economic benefits

The objective is not simply to create more supermarket
names. It is to benefit shoppers and create more
businesses with a genuine commercial incentive
to compete.
Foodstuffs North Island operates New World, PAK’nSAVE
and Four Square across the North Island. Foodstuffs
South Island operates the same banners across the
South Island.
Foodstuffs North Island and Foodstuffs South Island do
not compete against each other for customers in the
same local markets.
So the fundamental divide within Foodstuffs is currently
North Island versus South Island, rather than New World
and Four Square versus PAK’nSAVE.
In practice, that means each island is largely a contest
between Woolworths and the Foodstuffs cooperative
operating in that island.
National wants to change that competitive dynamic.
Under the proposal, PAK’nSAVE would become one
nationwide grocery business, competing directly against
a separate nationwide New World and Four Square
business, as well as Woolworths.

This is not about taking stores away from local owners.
The proposal is to reorganise the structure so that two
Foodstuffs groups compete against each other across
both islands.
Foodstuffs owner-operators are New Zealand
business owners who employ local people, invest
in their communities and, particularly through
Four Square, provide an essential service in many
smaller towns. National wants those businesses
to succeed.
Existing owner-operators would:
•

retain ownership of their businesses

•

continue operating under their existing
banners,

•

while remaining part of a larger group with the
scale and infrastructure needed to support
and supply its members.

Our view, based on the CBA, is that a restructure will
give businesses and banners within Foodstuffs the
strongest possible incentives to compete, invest,
and grow.

How separation would strengthen
competition
A separated structure increases the commercial
incentives New World, Four Square, and PAK’nSAVE
owners would have to compete against each other.
A customer won by PAK’nSAVE would be a customer
lost by New World and Four Square, and vice versa.
A supermarket site secured by one would be a site its
direct competitor could not use.
Each group would have stronger reasons to compete
for the same customers on price, location, format, range
and service.
There is evidence that this competition is not happening
as directly today as it might between genuinely
independent competitors.
The Commerce Commission’s 2022 market study
found evidence suggesting Foodstuffs positioned New
World and PAK’nSAVE to minimise direct competition
between the banners while competing more effectively
with Woolworths.
The location of stores illustrates that pattern.

The average distance from a PAK’nSAVE to the nearest
Woolworths is under 2.5 kilometres. The average
distance from a PAK’nSAVE to the nearest New World
is more than six kilometres.
There are also examples around the country. In Wānaka
and Mosgiel, shoppers have New World and Woolworths
stores but no PAK’nSAVE within 10 kilometres. In
Taupō and Gisborne, shoppers have PAK’nSAVE and
Woolworths but no New World within 10 kilometres.
The profitability data points in the same direction. In
2025, Foodstuffs North Island’s net profit after tax
margin was around 4 per cent, while Foodstuffs South
Island’s was around 3 per cent. By comparison, major
Australian supermarkets have net profit margins of
around 2 to 2.5 per cent.

Recent Commerce Commission
action
There is also public evidence raising questions about
how freely individual stores are able to compete within
the existing structure.
•

The Commerce Commission has commenced
civil proceedings against Foodstuffs South Island
alleging restrictions prevented independently
owned PAK’nSAVE stores from discounting some
products below centrally set promotional prices.

•

It has separately brought cartel proceedings against
Foodstuffs North Island and Gilmours alleging
market-allocation conduct involving a national
grocery supplier and a hospitality customer.

Those allegations remain before the Courts.
A restructure of this sort could also make New Zealand
a more attractive market for future entrants. The market
power of the existing incumbents can itself deter further
entry. A more competitive domestic market could make it
easier for another retailer to see an opportunity to enter
and compete.
National has always been aiming for three strong
competitors. If a third entrant cannot reach scale
organically in the near term, restructuring Foodstuffs
could be a faster way to create that competitive tension.
Any separation would also need to work for the local
businesses and communities that rely on Foodstuffs.
That is why the Commerce Commission will be required
to test commercial viability, continuity of supply,
distribution costs, rural and regional access, and impacts
on owner-operators and suppliers before recommending
that separation proceed.

The Commerce Commission
assessment
The Commerce Commission will not be asked to repeat
the CBA.
The work to date has narrowed the structural
options down to the one National believes has the
strongest case.
The Commission’s job will be to take that option, develop
an implementation plan and make an independent
assessment of whether it should proceed.
The statutory test will be: whether the restructure would
enhance competition to the benefit of consumers once
all of the practical implementation considerations are
taken into account?
In making that assessment, the Commission will be
required to have regard to factors including:

•

formally consult affected businesses, owneroperators, suppliers, competitors and consumers

•

develop and assess a detailed implementation
proposal

•

make its formal recommendation.

National will then legislate to require the separation and
give the Commerce Commission the powers needed to
oversee and enforce its implementation.
This process will be specific to the supermarket
sector via the Grocery Industry Competition Act.
National is not proposing a general power for the
Commerce Commission to break up businesses across
the economy.
If the Commission concludes that a practical separation
would not enhance competition for the benefit of
consumers, National will not proceed.
The ultimate test is the net benefit to the Kiwi shopper.

•

the likely improvement in competitive behaviour

•

the reduction in market power

•

the ability of new competitors to enter and expand

Our bottom line is the Kiwi shopper.

•

likely changes in the behaviour of PAK’nSAVE, New
World and Four Square

•

efficiency and duplication costs

•

supply-chain resilience

The purpose of this policy is not to break up a
business for the sake of it. It is to create stronger
competition while preserving viable local grocery
businesses, so supermarkets have to fight harder for
New Zealanders’ business.

•

rural and regional access

•

impacts on suppliers and owner-operators

•

implementation costs and practical feasibility.

That is ultimately a competition assessment.
The Commerce Commission is better placed to make that
judgment independently than politicians are to design
a supermarket restructure around the Cabinet table.
The Commission does not currently have a specific
statutory mandate to recommend this form of
structural separation.

What this means for shoppers

That means competing harder on price, service, range
and convenience. It means competing for sites and
opening stores in places where rivals already operate.
And it means trying new store formats and finding new
ways to win customers.
The best long-term protection for shoppers is not
politicians setting grocery prices or taxpayers owning
supermarkets. It is strong businesses competing hard
against each other.
National has worked to make it easier for new competitors
to enter and expand, and we will keep doing that.

National will therefore amend the Grocery Industry
Competition Act 2023 in our first 100 days to provide
that mandate.

But we also have to be realistic about the market we
have today and how long it could take a new national
competitor to emerge.

National will also provide the Commerce Commission
with $5 million to carry out this work, ensuring it has the
resources needed to undertake the detailed analysis,
consultation and implementation work required.

The work undertaken to date tells us structural
separation of Foodstuffs is the option worth pursuing.

•

take account of the existing CBA and analysis

National will pursue that separation, subject to an
independent Commerce Commission assessment that it
can be implemented in a way that enhances competition
for the benefit of New Zealand consumers.

•

obtain the additional information it needs using its
investigative and information-gathering powers

If the Commerce Commission recommends separation,
National will act by legislating to require a separation.

# More medicines and earlier care

Published by the New Zealand National Party as a PDF policy document. Source: <https://assets.national.org.nz/web/prod/More%20medicines%20and%20earlier%20care.pdf?v=1791237531>.
The text below is the verbatim text layer of the PDF extracted with `pdftotext` (reading order). Line breaks follow the
PDF; tables and multi-column layouts may read out of order in this section, so a second rendering that preserves the
page layout (`pdftotext -layout`) follows it. Nothing has been added, removed or paraphrased.

## Full text (reading order)

Building the Future:

More medicines and earlier care
Over this term, National has reduced wasteful spending
to invest in the frontline, putting patients back at the
heart of the health system with faster access to care
and the largest ever funding boost for new cancer and
other life-saving medicines. Now, National will lock in
that progress and go further.
Responsible fiscal management is paying a dividend.
Together, National and hardworking Kiwis have put
New Zealand back on a path to surplus, and National
will maintain that discipline by bringing money
back home. We will reduce foreign aid outside the
Pacific, where we will continue to support our closest
neighbours and strongest interests. Every dollar saved
will be put to work for Kiwis fighting cancer and other
serious illnesses, with no new taxes.
A re-elected National Government will deliver a further
$604 million uplift in Pharmac’s medicines budget, paid
for by these savings. The last time National made this
investment, it delivered 66 new medicines benefiting
hundreds of thousands of Kiwis, including 33 new
cancer treatments.
National will also back new ways to bring the latest
treatments to New Zealand through more clinical trials
and locally produced CAR-T cell therapy. Money that
was once spent offshore will instead be invested in
cutting-edge care, ensuring more Kiwis benefit from
world-class treatment here at home.

A re-elected National Government will:
•

Deliver a further $604 million uplift in
Pharmac’s medicines budget, building on
National’s track record of expanding access to
new cancer and other life-saving medicines.

•

Turn responsible fiscal management into
more medicines, by reducing foreign aid
outside the Pacific.

•

Set a national target for clinical trials in
New Zealand, so more Kiwis can access the
newest treatments sooner, with a focus on
cancer and rare disorders.

•

Unlock CAR-T cell therapy by supporting
New Zealand’s medical sector to develop and
produce this life-changing cancer treatment
here at home.

Authorised by J de Joux, ps@national.org.nz

Preventing serious illness
The best time to beat cancer and chronic disease is
before it takes hold. A re-elected National Government
will expand screening and prevention, building on
the progress achieved this term. National’s package
brings hundreds of thousands more Kiwis into free
cancer screening, trials new ways to find prostate and
lung cancer early, and helps more Kiwis get active and
avoid chronic diseases like diabetes. That means more
cancers caught when they are most treatable, and more
New Zealanders staying healthy.

A re-elected National Government will:
•

Lower the free bowel screening age to 50
by 2029, backed by additional colonoscopies,
so bowel cancer is caught earlier when it is
most treatable.

•

Complete the free breast screening
extension to age 74 by 2029, finishing the
job National has started so more women have
access to early detection.

•

Launch new screening pilots for prostate
and lung cancer, so more cancers are found
earlier.

•

Deliver free cervical screening for all women
aged 25 to 69 from March 2027, so cervical
cancer can be stopped before it starts.

•

Establish the Healthy Kiwis Programme,
expanding active prescriptions with a target
to double the number of people receiving
them by 2030, helping more Kiwis get active,
stay healthy, and avoid chronic diseases
like diabetes.

Increasing the medicines budget
When National entered Government in 2023, Labour
had left behind a funding cliff in Pharmac’s budget,
putting New Zealanders’ access to medicines at risk.
National filled that gap, then went further with a record
$604 million uplift in Pharmac’s medicines budget,
delivering 66 new medicines benefiting around
250,000 Kiwis, including 33 new cancer treatments.
But there’s more to do. Too many New Zealanders
are still missing out on medicines available in other
countries, making their fight against cancer and other
serious illnesses even harder.
A re-elected National Government will invest that same
$604 million again, largely paid for by reducing foreign
aid outside the Pacific.
For Kiwis, this means even more people can access
the medicines they need. Pharmac will be able to
fund new cancer and other life-saving medicines that
aren’t currently available here, and widen eligibility for
treatments that are already funded so more people
benefit from them.

A re-elected National Government will:
•

Deliver a further $604 million uplift in
Pharmac’s medicines budget, building on
National’s track record of expanding access to
new cancer treatments and other medicines
for New Zealanders.

Clinical trials for more Kiwis
Clinical trials are one of the best ways for Kiwis to get
the newest treatments, often years before they are
publicly available. For someone facing cancer, a trial
can be a chance to try a promising new medicine they
could not get any other way. It matters even more
for people living with a rare disorder, where so few
treatments are funded that a trial can be one of the only
options available.
Trials are good for New Zealand too. Between 2013 and
2018, trials of new medicines added more than $150
million a year to our economy and supported more than
700 jobs. However, companies wanting to run a trial
here often face a slow and confusing approvals process
that changes from district to district, adding cost and
delay. As a result, trials are too often taken to other
countries, and New Zealanders miss out.

A re-elected National Government will:
•

Set a national target that within ten years, 5
per cent of New Zealanders being treated for
cancer will have part of their care delivered
through a clinical trial, where a trial is right for
them and they want to take part, aligning with
Australia.

•

Set up a single national front door for clinical
trials, so companies have one clear place to
go and patients can be matched to trials more
easily, including those with a rare disorder
who often struggle to find a relevant study.

•

Simplify and standardise the approvals
process, so a trial approved once can run
right across the country, while keeping strong
protections for patient safety.

Unlocking CAR-T cell therapy for cancer
patients
CAR-T cell therapy works by taking a patient’s own
immune cells, reprogramming them to recognise and
attack their cancer, and returning them to the body to
do the job. For some people with rare or aggressive
cancers that have not responded to other treatments,
it can be life-changing. New Zealanders who need
this therapy currently rely on having their cells sent
overseas to be made, which is hugely expensive, yet
New Zealand has the scientists, clinicians, and knowhow to do it here.
A re-elected National Government will back BioOra, a
New Zealand-based commercial-stage biotechnology
company, with a $25 million co-investment to expand
its cell therapy manufacturing, research, and clinical
facilities in Christchurch and produce CAR-T right here
at home. BioOra’s Christchurch precinct could supply
the whole country, anchoring a high-tech industry
in the South Island, supporting skilled jobs, and
keeping New Zealand at the cutting edge of the fight
against cancer.

A re-elected National Government will:
•

Co-invest $25 million with BioOra to expand
its cell therapy manufacturing, research, and
clinical facilities in Christchurch, so Kiwis
who need CAR-T can be treated at home
rather than sent overseas.

The Prevention Package
The best time to fight cancer and chronic disease is
before it takes hold. National’s Prevention Package will
find more cancers early and keep more Kiwis healthy
and out of hospital.

Catching bowel cancer earlier
New Zealand’s rate of bowel cancer is among the
highest in the world, with more than 3,300 Kiwis
diagnosed every year and over 1,200 losing their
lives to it. National has already lowered the screening
age from 60 to 56 as first steps towards aligning with
Australia, but we are not stopping there.
Early detection is the difference between survival and
tragedy. People whose bowel cancer is found and
treated at an early stage have a 90 per cent chance
of long-term survival. National will take the next steps
to lower the screening age to 50, bringing hundreds
of thousands more Kiwis into the programme. Taking
steps to lower the screening age to 50 is expected to
prevent 1,149 cancer cases over ten years.

A re-elected National Government will:
•

Extend free bowel screening, by lowering the
age by two years every year to reach 50 in the
next term of Government, so we catch bowel
cancer earlier when it is most treatable.

•

Continue the roll out of free bowel cancer
tests for people of any age with symptoms, so
cancer is found sooner no matter how old a
patient is.

•

Deliver additional colonoscopies to increase
system capacity.

Earlier detection for breast and prostate
cancer
Breast cancer is New Zealand’s most commonly
diagnosed cancer in women, with nearly 3,900
new cases a year, and the risk grows with age. Free
mammograms currently stop at 69, leaving older
women to pay for screening themselves or go without.
National has already begun extending free breast
screening to women aged 70 to 74, and a re-elected
National Government will finish the job.

Kiwi men deserve the same focus on early detection.
Prostate cancer is the most common cancer among
New Zealand men, with more than 4,000 diagnosed
and more than 700 deaths each year, making it the
second biggest cause of cancer death for men after
lung cancer. Found early, more than 90 per cent of men
survive at least five years, but that falls below 40 per
cent once the cancer has spread.
Unlike breast, cervical, and bowel cancer, there is no
organised screening programme for prostate cancer, so
whether a man gets checked is too often left to chance.
National will pilot organised screening in the two
districts with the highest demand, allowing Health New
Zealand to gather evidence for a potential nationwide
programme, based on a proposal from the Prostate
Cancer Foundation.

A re-elected National Government will:
•

Complete the free breast screening
extension to age 74 by 2029, ensuring older
women have access to early detection and
life-saving preventative care.

•

Launch a prostate cancer screening pilot in
two high-demand districts, offering men aged
50 to 70 regular screening to evaluate what
works for a potential nationwide programme.

Free cervical screening for all women aged
25 to 69
Cervical cancer is among the most preventable
cancers, because nearly every case is caused by HPV,
a common virus the screening test picks up well before
any cancer develops. When it is caught early, around
91 per cent of women survive, but that falls to around
19 per cent once it has spread.
Unlike breast and bowel screening, cervical
screening is not free for every woman. That’s despite
successive Parliamentary Reviews since 2018 having
recommended it.

As announced in September, National has funded free
cervical screening for all women aged 25 to 69 from
1 March 2027, meaning an estimated 786,000 women
will no longer have to pay.

A re-elected National Government will:
•

Establish the Healthy Kiwis Programme to
deliver active prescriptions, with a target to
double the number of people receiving them
by 2030, helping more Kiwis get active, eat
well, and avoid chronic diseases like diabetes.

•

Work with Bowel Cancer New Zealand to
determine how the CHALLENGE exercise
programme could be made available
for bowel cancer patients, with evidence
suggesting it can reduce the risk of death by
37 per cent in bowel cancer patients who have
completed surgery.

Earlier detection for lung cancer
Lung cancer is New Zealand’s biggest cancer killer,
claiming more than 1,700 lives every year, more
than breast cancer, prostate cancer, and melanoma
combined. Most people are only diagnosed once the
disease is advanced and the chance of a cure is slim.
Screening can change that. International trials have
found that low-dose CT scans for people at high risk
reduce lung cancer deaths by 20 to 25 per cent, and
Australia began screening through its own national
programme in July 2025.
A re-elected National Government will deliver a lung
cancer screening pilot in Bay of Plenty and Hawke’s
Bay, offering low-dose CT scans to people at high risk,
such as current and former smokers. The pilot will test
the best way to find, invite, and screen those most at
risk, catching more lung cancers early and building the
evidence for a potential nationwide programme.

Keeping Kiwis active, healthy, and out of
hospital
New Zealand is facing a chronic disease epidemic.
The number of Kiwis with type 2 diabetes is set to
nearly double by 2040, yet most cases are preventable,
and billions are spent every year treating disease that
could be stopped before it starts. Beating this epidemic
means getting Kiwis moving and eating well.
Active prescriptions do exactly that. A GP or practice
nurse prescribes exercise and healthier eating, and a
trained coach then provides free, personalised support
over several months to help the changes last. National
introduced the scheme in 1998 to get Kiwis active and
healthy, and it works. The evidence shows that 85 per
cent of patients are more active after receiving their
prescription, as are 80 per cent of child patients, and
patients see significant improvements in HbA1c, blood
pressure, and BMI. Yet only 26,000 people a year
receive this support, a fraction of those who need it.
National will expand active prescriptions through a
new Healthy Kiwis Programme, working with local
providers across the country, and setting a target for
Health New Zealand to double the number of people
receiving them by 2030. That means more Kiwis getting
the support they need to stay healthy, fewer cases of
chronic disease, and less pressure on our hospitals.

Fiscal impact
The Pharmac uplift will be paid for by bringing money
back home from foreign aid, with the remaining funded
from future operating allowances.
Since 2017, MFAT’s budget has grown from $1.05
billion to nearly $2 billion a year and its staff numbers
have risen by more than 34 per cent. Millions of
dollars have gone towards, among other things, smart
agriculture systems in Latin America and the Caribbean,
workshops with indigenous farmers in Patagonia, and
installing livestock emissions equipment at universities
in South Africa.
National will reduce New Zealand’s International
Development Cooperation (IDC) budget, which funds
our foreign aid, and associated administration costs
by 10 per cent, saving $431.2 million over the forecast
period. Aid to the Pacific, which makes up around
66 per cent of IDC funding, will be fully protected,
reflecting the importance of our closest neighbours and
strongest interests.
National will also make MFAT more efficient. When other
government agencies found savings in the 2026 round
of baseline reductions, MFAT was exempt. National
will now bring MFAT into line with the rest of the public
sector, catching up through a 2 per cent baseline
expenditure reduction that saves a further $45.6 million
over the forecast period.
The Prevention Package will be funded through
existing baseline health funding and future operating
allowances. Under National, the expanded breast
screening age, free cervical screening for all women
aged 25 to 69, and a lung cancer screening pilot
are already funded, and National is committed to
protecting that funding and delivering these services
for New Zealanders.

colonoscopy, so the earlier years are the busiest

# National backs the Waikato

Published by the New Zealand National Party as a PDF policy document. Source: <https://assets.national.org.nz/web/prod/National%20backs%20the%20Waikato.pdf?v=1792365832>.
The text below is the verbatim text layer of the PDF extracted with `pdftotext` (reading order). Line breaks follow the
PDF; tables and multi-column layouts may read out of order in this section, so a second rendering that preserves the
page layout (`pdftotext -layout`) follows it. Nothing has been added, removed or paraphrased.

## Full text (reading order)

Building the Future:

National backs
the Waikato

Building the Future:

National backs the Waikato
Waikato is New Zealand’s productive heartland.
It is where much of our food is grown, our energy
is generated, our exports are made and our freight
moves through. Hamilton and the surrounding
towns are growing quickly, while rural and coastal
communities depend on strong connections and
reliable services.
National is backing that growth with the infrastructure
Waikato needs for the future.
That investment is anchored by two major projects.
National is extending the Waikato Expressway from
Cambridge to Piarere with $1.773 billion of funding,
and building the new Waikato Medical School
in Hamilton, which will provide 120 additional
medical training places each year from 2028.
But the investment goes much further. We are
progressing Hamilton Southern Links, expanding
Hamilton Airport, strengthening transport resilience
in the Coromandel, adding classrooms and specialist
education capacity, increasing health capacity,
supporting more housing, and backing major
productive infrastructure across the region.
We also invested a record $1.9 billion into the
Waikato’s roads through the 2024-27 National
Land Transport Fund, ensuring the region’s roads
are up to standard. Construction has also begun
on replacing the SH25 Pepe Stream bridge, the
SH25 Ramarama Stream Bridge and the SH27
Ohinekaua Stream bridge – improving the resilience
of the wider Waikato state highway network and
keeping local communities, freight and emergency
services moving.

Authorised by J de Joux, ps@national.org.nz

We are building the housing our most vulnerable in the
Waikato needs, with more than 900 additional social
houses being delivered in the Waikato under National.
We are also working to make Waikato communities
safer. Ram raids have fallen sharply from their peak,
theft and robbery are down, Police foot patrols have
more than doubled, and tougher laws are giving Police
stronger tools to target gangs and repeat offenders.
There is more to do. National will keep building the
infrastructure Waikato needs to grow, while making
sure families, businesses and communities can share
in the benefits..

A re-elected National Government will:
• Deliver Cambridge to Piarere, creating a
safer, faster and more reliable connection
through one of New Zealand’s most important
economic corridors.
• Continue to progress Hamilton Southern
Links, and further explore options for a staged
delivery of this important project, so some of
the benefits can be felt, sooner.
• Deliver the Waikato Medical School, building
a stronger pipeline of doctors for rural and
regional New Zealand.
• Keep investing across the region, in transport,
health, education, housing and productive
infrastructure.
• Keep Waikato communities safer, with visible
Police, tougher consequences for repeat
offenders and continued pressure on gangs
and retail crime.

Two big builds for Waikato’s future
Waikato is growing, and National is investing in the
infrastructure the region needs for decades to come.
At the heart of that programme are two major projects:
extending the Waikato Expressway from Cambridge
to Piarere and building New Zealand’s new medical
school in Hamilton.
Together, they will strengthen the connections and
workforce that underpin Waikato’s future growth.

Extending the Waikato Expressway
National is getting on with the next major extension
of the Waikato Expressway.
Budget 2026 invested $1.773 billion in the Cambridge to
Piarere Road of National Significance, a new 16-kilometre,
four-lane expressway from the end of the existing Waikato
Expressway to the SH1/SH29 intersection at Piarere.
This is one of New Zealand’s most important freight and
economic corridors, connecting Auckland, Waikato and
the Bay of Plenty with the central and lower North Island.
Early works for the project began in January, both major
construction contracts are now in procurement, and
the first phase of construction is expected to begin in
early 2027.

University of Waikato, backed by $82.85 million from
the Government and more than $150 million from the
University and philanthropic partners.
From 2028, the school will provide 120 additional
medical training places every year, with a strong focus
on primary care and rural health. Students will spend
their first year studying in Hamilton before undertaking
three years of clinical training across regional and
rural communities.
In Waikato, that training will stretch from Waikato Hospital
to North Waikato, Hauraki and Thames-Coromandel,
South Waikato, Waipā and the King Country. That
means more doctors training in the communities that
need them, helping build a stronger pipeline of GPs and
frontline clinicians for rural and regional New Zealand.
National is also planning ahead for the wider region’s
future health needs. A 13-hectare site has now been
secured at Drury for a future major health facility,
following work specifically identifying the rapid
growth of South Auckland and north Waikato.
Combined with the new Medical School, this is about
building health capacity ahead of growth rather than
waiting for existing services to come under even
more pressure.

For Waikato families this means safer, faster, and
more reliable journeys. For farmers, manufacturers
and exporters it means a stronger connection to ports,
markets and customers.

What National is delivering:

Building New Zealand’s new medical school

• Construction underway on the Waikato
Medical School, creating 120 additional doctor
training places every year from 2028.

National is also making one of the biggest investments
in New Zealand’s rural and regional health workforce in
a generation.
National campaigned on the Waikato Medical School
in 2023, after the previous Labour Government
dismissed the project. Now, National is delivering it in
Government. Construction is underway on the New
Zealand Graduate School of Medicine at the

and north Waikato.

Building across Waikato
A productive region needs infrastructure that can
keep up.
Across Waikato, National is upgrading key transport
links, expanding health and education capacity, and
backing the infrastructure that supports more homes,
jobs and investment. From Hamilton to the Coromandel
and the King Country, we are making sure the region
has what it needs to keep moving forward.

Connecting the region
• Progressing Hamilton Southern Links, a major
future transport connection linking the Waikato
Expressway at Tamahere with western Hamilton
and opening up access to new housing, businesses
and Hamilton Airport. The route has been designated,
the investment case was endorsed by the new NZTA
board in 2025, and initial site investigations have
been completed.
• Expanding Hamilton Airport, supporting a
255-metre runway extension, apron and turning-bay
expansion and upgraded lighting, strengthening
Waikato’s ability to move people and freight.
• Began construction of bridge replacements: SH25
Pepe Stream bridge, the SH25 Ramarama Stream
Bridge and the SH27 Ohinekaua Stream bridge,
supporting a more resilient transport network
for Waikato.
• Delivered a new Road of Regional significance in
the Waikato, improving safety and reliability at the
State Highway 1 and State Highway 29 intersection,
building a new roundabout to replace the former
T-intersection.

• Fixing the roads Waikato already has, including the
accelerated SH1 maintenance programme between
Tīrau and Waiouru, which has rebuilt or resurfaced
more than 120 lane kilometres of state highway.
• Extended rail connectivity from Hamilton to Auckland,
with NZTA extending the Te Huia trial by 12 months
until June 2027.

Infrastructure for growing communities
• Delivering more social homes, with 929 net
new social homes added across Waikato since
November 2023.
• Fewer Waikato families are living in emergency
housing, with the number of households falling from
564 in November 2023 to 120 in September 2026,
a 79 per cent reduction.
• Unlocking new housing in Hamilton, by approving
an Infrastructure Funding and Financing levy for
Te Awa Lakes, helping to deliver the water and
roading infrastructure needed for 1,500 new homes.
• Building more classrooms where rolls are growing,
including four new classrooms at Hamilton East
School, two at Te Wharekura o Kirikiriroa and four
more at Berkley Normal Middle School.
• Expanding specialist education, with four new
classrooms at Hamilton North School and new
satellite classrooms at Te Aroha College and Fairfield
Intermediate, giving more students with high and
complex needs access to purpose-built learning
spaces closer to home.

• Adding health capacity, with a new 28-bed
assessment ward being built next to Waikato
Hospital’s emergency department and due for
completion in 2027, Hospital in the Home being
expanded to support up to 40 patients receiving
hospital-level care in their own homes, 10 new
forensic mental health beds opened at Waikato
Hospital alongside eight community step-down
beds, a new 64-bed acute mental health facility due
to open shortly, and extra security staff in Waikato
Hospital’s emergency department around the clock.

with a new infusion service at Te Kūiti Hospital
reducing the need for King Country patients to
travel to Hamilton for cancer treatment, and the new

• Backing local manufacturing, with Green Steel
at Hampton Downs approved through Fast-track.

New Zealand’s domestic infrastructure supply chain.
• Unlocking billions in future exports at Waihi,
with the Waihi North project extending mining
operations and supporting significant new
investment and economic activity in the region.

ageing water network to support Fieldays, which

consenting and detailed design of a new four-lane
road at Ruakura, helping complete the Ruakura
Inland Port and opening up land for new homes
and businesses in Hamilton’s east.

Waikato needs, progressing Southern Links
and investing in safer, more resilient roads
across the region.
• Keep infrastructure ahead of growth,
delivering more classrooms, health capacity,
housing and essential services as Hamilton
and Waikato’s fastest-growing communities
expand.
• Keep unlocking productive infrastructure,
getting worthwhile manufacturing, energy,
mining and development projects moving faster.
• Keep investing across the whole region, from
Hamilton and the Waikato growth corridor to
rural communities and the Coromandel.

Law and order: safer Waikato communities
Waikato businesses and communities were hit hard by
the surge in ram raids, retail crime and gang offending.
National has focused on restoring consequences and
putting Police back into communities. Ram raids in the
Waikato Police District have fallen 79 per cent from
their 2022 peak, while between 2023 and 2025 theft
across the Waikato region fell 11 per cent, robbery,
blackmail and extortion fell 6 per cent, and burglary
fell 2 per cent. Police foot patrols have increased
106 per cent.
Retailers are also getting a more targeted response.
Waikato’s dedicated Retail Crime Teams laid 172
charges in their first six weeks, targeting prolific
offenders responsible for repeated harm to local
shops and businesses.
National has also banned gang patches in public,
introduced dispersal notices and non-consorting
orders, toughened sentencing for gang offenders,
and put nearly 1000 additional gang members
behind bars.

National will
• Keep driving down ram raids and retail crime,
targeting the repeat offenders causing the most
harm to local businesses.
• Keep Police visible in Waikato communities,
building on the 106 per cent increase in
foot patrols.
• Keep the pressure on gangs, enforcing the
gang patch ban, dispersal notices and nonconsorting orders, and putting more serious
gang offenders behind bars.

# National Electrify NZ - Home Energy Fund policy document

Published by the New Zealand National Party as a PDF policy document. Source: <https://assets.national.org.nz/web/prod/National%20Electrify%20NZ%20-%20Home%20Energy%20Fund%20policy%20document.pdf?v=1782343598>.
The text below is the verbatim text layer of the PDF extracted with `pdftotext` (reading order). Line breaks follow the
PDF; tables and multi-column layouts may read out of order in this section, so a second rendering that preserves the
page layout (`pdftotext -layout`) follows it. Nothing has been added, removed or paraphrased.

## Full text (reading order)

Building the Future: Our Plan to Electrify NZ
Over this term, National has made tremendous progress bolstering New Zealand’s energy security –
by enabling greater development of renewable energy through comprehensive RMA reform, ending
Labour’s oil and gas ban, and securing strategic reserves of coal, diesel, and LNG.
Now National is focused on helping Kiwis to become more energy independent and reduce their
power bills by supporting them to electrify their own homes, farms, and small businesses.
A re-elected National Government will continue our plan to Electrify NZ by:
• Launching the Home Energy Fund – a central government and council-backed financing
platform offering long-term loans, secured against the home and repaid through rates, so
households can invest in solar, batteries, insulation and other energy resilience measures
without large upfront costs.
• Enabling electrification in the new planning system – clear, national permitted-activity
rules so Kiwis can install rooftop and ground-mounted solar, batteries and micro-hydro
schemes on their own property without a consent.

Home Energy Fund
Kiwi families are under pressure from rising power bills. Rooftop solar, batteries, insulation and
modern electric appliances can ease that pressure and make homes more resilient – but high
upfront cost put them out of reach for many households, and existing green loans from commercial
banks are limited.
The Ratepayer Assistance Scheme, long advocated for by Local Government New Zealand (LGNZ)
and Rewiring Aotearoa, offers a practical, market-based answer by providing a low-interest loan
secured against a homeowner’s property and repaid over time on their rates bill.
A re-elected National Government will implement a narrower version of the Ratepayer Assistance
Scheme, called the Home Energy Fund – a national financing platform jointly owned by central
government and participating councils that offers ratepayers low-interest, long-term loans secured
against their property.
The Home Energy Fund pays the approved installer upfront, and the homeowner repays the lowinterest loan over ten years, either through a charge on their rates bill or on sale of their property.
Because these loans are secured by property and backed by Crown and local government balance
sheets, they can be offered at low, competitive interest rates. Council participation will be voluntary,
but based on advocacy from LGNZ, we expect strong interest from councils across New Zealand.
Energy resilience investments eligible for support through the Home Energy Fund include:
• Residential solar and battery storage,
• Insulation, heat pumps, and other investments in residential electrification.
Establishing the Home Energy Fund will require an amendment to the Local Government Act and a
one-off Crown equity investment of $7 million for a 20% shareholding in the new entity, with the
balance funded by participating councils and the LGFA. Loans from the Home Energy Fund will be
available to ratepayers with at least 20% equity in their property.

Enabling electrification in the new RMA
This term, National delivered on our plan to Electrify NZ – turbo-charging new renewable energy
projects by requiring resource consent decisions within one year and consents that last 35 years,

while cutting red tape holding back transmission and distribution upgrades. Four renewable energy
projects have also been consented through Fast Track.
Those reforms are supporting a robust pipeline of new generation, but Kiwis still face costly,
confusing rules to develop small-scale renewables on their own property, making the process slow
and expensive.
For example, Rewiring Aotearoa found Environment Canterbury has required ground-mounted solar
installations to apply for a water discharge consent, because rain runs off the panels and could
carry bird droppings. Hurunui District Council, meanwhile, requires consent for any free-standing
installation larger than 25m² - barely enough to power an average New Zealand home.
It’s not just solar that’s hard. Micro-hydro and battery storage also face fragmented and confusing
consenting requirements region to region.
There are huge opportunities to supercharge small-scale renewables like solar and micro-hydro on
Kiwis’ own land. New Zealanders should be able to draw on the abundant natural resources on their
own property with as little red tape as possible.
That’s why the next National-led Government will go further. We will set clear, national rules so that
small-scale renewables – rooftop and ground-mounted solar, micro-hydro and battery storage – are
largely permitted as of right on your own property.
Specifically, National will:
•
•
•
•

Let property owners install rooftop solar without a consent, even where height limits or
landscape overlays would otherwise get in the way.
Make small-scale on-farm ground-mounted solar a permitted activity with standard rules
to manage genuine effects and sensible safeguards to protect land that is environmentally
significant.
Allow small-scale battery storage not enclosed by an existing building as of right,
subject only to standard rules managing genuine effects.
Permit small run-of-river micro-hydro for on-site use, where it stays below a set size and
meets standard environmental conditions that protect the river, fish passage, and other water
users.

# National KiwiSaver policy document

Published by the New Zealand National Party as a PDF policy document. Source: <https://assets.national.org.nz/web/prod/National%20KiwiSaver%20policy%20document.pdf?v=1782016131>.
The text below is the verbatim text layer of the PDF extracted with `pdftotext` (reading order). Line breaks follow the
PDF; tables and multi-column layouts may read out of order in this section, so a second rendering that preserves the
page layout (`pdftotext -layout`) follows it. Nothing has been added, removed or paraphrased.

## Full text (reading order)

Building the Future: Enhancing KiwiSaver for Everyone
Strengthening New Zealanders’ financial security is central to National’s plan to fix the basics and
build the future. At the heart of that plan are hardworking New Zealanders and their families, who
deserve to get ahead when they work hard and make responsible choices for their future.
That’s why in November last year, National promised to continue lifting default KiwiSaver
contributions to a combined 12%, matching Australia by 2032.
Default contributions are already rising, increasing to 3.5% on 1 April 2026. Under National’s plan
they would continue to rise by 0.5% in 2028, and then each year thereafter, until 1 April 2032, when
employee and employer contribution rates reach 6%.
Kiwis can expect those changes to mean a significant uplift in their future savings, giving them greater
financial security in retirement.
Now National is announcing further changes to support New Zealanders with their financial security
when they need it most, whether that’s raising a family or approaching retirement, and to strengthen
the KiwiSaver system so that more Kiwis are saving for their future.
These include:
•

leave for everyone – from 1 July 2027.

July 2027.

Compulsory savings: Making every New Zealander a KiwiSaver
For the vast majority of Kiwis in work, KiwiSaver is working. According to Retirement Commission
research from 2024, 90% of eligible, paid employees are contributing to their KiwiSaver. However,
rates of contribution are lower among low-income, part-time, and self-employed workers.
Ensuring every New Zealander is financially prepared for retirement is a top priority. Since National
released its last KiwiSaver policy in November, we have received feedback that Kiwis believe New
Zealand is best served by shifting KiwiSaver to a compulsory savings model, where everyone is

guaranteed to be more financially prepared for retirement, whether they work part-time, are selfemployed, or just need a nudge to save a little more today in preparation for tomorrow.
That’s why, if re-elected, National will make contributions to KiwiSaver (or an equivalent scheme)
compulsory for all workers from 1 July 2028. Contributions will be made at the prevailing default rate
as part of the agreed glidepath, lifting combined default contributions to 12% by 2032, matching
Australia.
The following exceptions will apply to this policy:
•

Employees already saving through another defined contribution superannuation scheme managed
through their employer will be excluded.

•

Individuals receiving paid parental leave for the period they are out of work will also be excluded,
recognising that the Government would now automatically meet the employer contribution for
parental leave recipients, irrespective of whether they are contributing.

•

Individuals who wish to suspend their contributions would be required the meet the hardship test,
currently applied for individuals who wish to make an early withdrawal from their KiwiSaver.

•

Self-employed individuals would only be required to contribute the equivalent of the employee
contribution. This means someone who is self-employed from 1 July 2028 will be required to
contribute 4% of their income to their KiwiSaver (not the combined rate of 8%).

Fiscal impact
Government contribution
By requiring more individuals to contribute to their KiwiSaver, there is a direct fiscal impact to the
Crown with a higher number of individuals becoming eligible for the annual Government contribution,
worth $260.72.
According to the Retirement Commission, those contributing to KiwiSaver represent 80% of people in
paid employment. The forecast cost of additional contributions reflect eligibility for the government
contribution and conservatively assume new contributors receive the same average government
contribution as current contributors.
Cost to the Crown as an Employer
As an employer in its own right, compulsion will present an additional modest fiscal impact for the
Crown, as higher employee contributions are matched by additional employer contributions.
In Budget 2026, when default contributions rose from 3% to 3.5%, these costs were largely managed
within agency baselines, with funding only made available for the Ministry of Education to meet the
cost of higher KiwiSaver contributions for the education workforce.
Additional ESCT
In Budget 2025, Treasury and Inland Revenue estimated that the increase in default KiwiSaver
contributions would net the Crown average additional net revenue of $163 million per annum.
We expect these changes to similarly generate some additional revenue for the Crown, although this
revenue is highly sensitive to assumptions on the income profile of those not currently contributing to
KiwiSaver. To present the most conservative estimate on the net cost of this policy, we have opted
not to offset the fiscal impact by any additional revenue from higher employer superannuation
contribution tax.

$1500 Baby Boost Payment and Automatic Enrolment at Birth
At the heart of National is a belief in New Zealand as a property-owning democracy, where every Kiwi
has a real stake in the future of our economy. Making that a practical, financial reality for every child
growing up in New Zealand today should be a priority.
That’s why if re-elected National, enrolment in KiwiSaver at birth will be automatic, and matched with
a $1,500 Baby Boost payment to kickstart their retirement savings, which will benefit from decades of
compounding returns.
Example
A $1,500 investment at birth, growing at a long-run average return of approximately 7% per annum,
will be worth around $5,000 by age 18, even if there were no further contributions made in that time.
Fiscal impact
The cost is calculated on the basis of approximately 60,000 births per annum in New Zealand. At
$1500 per newborn, the cost is approximately $90 million per annum. Last year there were 57,700
live births in New Zealand.

Paid Parental Leave Top-Up
Right now, the Government matches any KiwiSaver contributions made by someone on paid parental
leave, as if they were receiving an employer contribution on their weekly parental leave payments.
In reality, this comes at a time of financial pressure for many families as they adjust to life on a single
income and more expenses, so many parents choose not to contribute while on paid parental leave.
In the year to June 2025, when this policy took effect, only around 1 in 5 of those eligible continued to
contribute to their KiwiSaver while on paid leave with their new baby, meaning 4 in 5 missed out on
the matching contribution.
National believes strong families are the cornerstone of a more prosperous society, and that starts
with supporting every family to save for their future and build their own financial security.
Under National’s policy, from 1 July 2027, the Government will provide a KiwiSaver contribution to
people on paid parental leave even if the person is not contributing themselves. This contribution will
be made at the default rate applied against the amount of paid parental leave a person is receiving.
Example
Jess is 30 when she has her first baby in 2028 and 33 when she has her second in 2031. She
receives a maximum paid parental leave entitlement for 26 weeks after the birth of each baby.

During her first stint on paid parental leave, Jess will receive an additional $625 in her KiwiSaver.
During her second stint, she will receive an additional $952 in her KiwiSaver.
Assuming an annual average return of 7%, when Jess turns 65, these contributions are worth an
additional $15,000 in her KiwiSaver.
Fiscal impact
The cost of this policy is modelled as the cost of applying the full employer contribution on paid
parental leave payments, less ESCT, and the cost of the current policy to match contributions ($3.8
million in 2024/25).

Employer Contributions for Workers Over 65
Employers are not currently required to make compulsory KiwiSaver contributions for employees
aged 65 and over. While some employers continue contributing voluntarily, many do not, meaning
older workers can face an effective pay cut simply for reaching 65.
This rule is increasingly out of step with how New Zealanders work. Around 1 in 4 New Zealanders
aged over 65 remain in paid work, among the highest rates of older-worker participation in the OECD,
and many continue saving for their retirement.
If re-elected, National will require employers to pay the compulsory employer contribution for
contributing KiwiSaver members aged over 65, on the same basis as for all other employees, from 1
July 2027.
This directly implements a recommendation of the Retirement Commissioner, who called for
employer contributions to be required for those over 65 in the Commission’s 2024 review of
KiwiSaver settings.
Example
Jeff, aged 65, is earning $70,000 per year in 2027. He chooses to work three more years and retires
at age 68. With his employer now obliged to make a contribution to his KiwiSaver, Jeff now retires
with an additional $6300 in 2030.
Fiscal impact
Any fiscal impact is limited to the Crown’s own employees aged over 65 and is expected to be
modest and met within agency baselines.

# National’s 47-point plan to support Small Businesses

Published by the New Zealand National Party as a PDF policy document. Source: <https://assets.national.org.nz/web/prod/National%E2%80%99s%2047-point%20plan%20to%20support%20Small%20Businesses.pdf?v=1791324870>.
The text below is the verbatim text layer of the PDF extracted with `pdftotext` (reading order). Line breaks follow the
PDF; tables and multi-column layouts may read out of order in this section, so a second rendering that preserves the
page layout (`pdftotext -layout`) follows it. Nothing has been added, removed or paraphrased.

## Full text (reading order)

Building the Future:

National’s 47-point
plan to support
Small Businesses

Building the Future:

National’s 47-point plan to
support Small Businesses
Our small businesses are the backbone of our
economy. National has their back.

agreements, tax, ACC and leave right from day one, and
less paperwork for apprentices and seasonal workers.

From the local dairy to the mechanic, the family farm
to the manufacturer, café or tourism operator, small
businesses make New Zealand tick. They build our
homes, produce our food, keep our towns busy and
take Kiwi products to the world.

Unlike Labour, we will keep our successful Investment
Boost scheme, rewarding businesses that invest in their
next stage of growth.

Our Investment Boost policy has been a game changer.
Businesses can immediately deduct 20 per cent of
the cost of eligible new productive assets, giving them
a powerful incentive to invest in better equipment,
technology and premises.
We have restored 90-day trials for employers of every
size, given contractors greater certainty, and passed
the Employment Leave Act to replace the Holidays Act
with a simpler system.
We are making it easier for businesses to get paid,
expanding eInvoicing and opening banking to greater
competition. We have replaced the RMA, reformed
building rules and made it easier to use trusted
overseas products.
But there is more to do.
For too many owners, running a business still means
evenings spent on paperwork, uncertainty before
taking on another employee, months resolving a
straightforward dispute, delays getting approvals, fees
eating into every payment and opportunities overseas
that are simply too difficult to pursue.

National’s plan changes that.
We will make it easier for a small business to take the
leap and become an employer. National will introduce
a First Employee Support Package to help owners
navigate requirements around payroll, employment

Authorised by J de Joux, ps@national.org.nz

We will overhaul the way straightforward employment
disputes are handled, with a fast-track process, firmer
Authority timeframes, better use of mediation and a
system where the cost and process better match the
scale of the dispute.
We will give owners their time back through Tell
Government Once, simpler renewals, digital records
and the removal of outdated paper, newspaper, fax and
telex requirements.
We will help businesses keep more of what they earn
through faster payments, lower and more transparent
payment costs, modern banking and payments, better
access to government contracts and practical support
to adopt AI.
We will make it easier to grow by delivering planning
and building reforms, cutting duplicated technical work,
improving access to capital and connecting growing
firms with international investment.
And we will help more New Zealand businesses take
on the world, with intensive support for the Next 200
high-potential exporters, simpler digital trade tools,
faster border processes, another $1 billion of non-tariff
barriers targeted for removal and more markets opened
to Kiwi businesses.
This is a 47-point plan built around the reality of running
a small business: less time navigating government,
more confidence to employ someone, more room
to invest and grow, and more opportunities to sell to
customers here and around the world.

A.  Making it easier to employ and
train employees
National is making it easier for small businesses to
employ people and grow, with clearer rules and more
practical support for hiring and training.
We restored 90-day trial periods for employers of
every size, removed the 30-day rule so employers and
employees can agree individual terms from day one,
and introduced clearer contractor rules.
The Employment Leave Act has now passed, replacing
the Holidays Act from August 2028 with simpler
leave calculations and a two-year implementation
period. Health and safety reforms are also sharpening
the focus on preventing serious harm and making
obligations clearer for businesses.
Alongside this, skilled-trades residence, Earn as You
Learn manufacturing and industry-led school subjects
will help businesses find the skills they need and give
more New Zealanders practical pathways into work.

What National will do if re-elected…
Helping a sole trader become an employer
Taking on a first employee is one of the biggest steps
a small business can make. Overnight, an owner who
has spent years doing everything themselves becomes
responsible for payroll, employment agreements, leave,
tax, ACC and managing another person.
National wants more successful sole traders to have
the confidence to take that step.
We will introduce a First Employee Support Package
that brings the essentials together in one place.
This will ensure any new employer get the basics right
from day one and have somewhere to turn before a
small uncertainty becomes an expensive mistake.
We will also reduce penalties for genuine first-year
administrative errors where no worker has been
harmed and the employer moves quickly to put things
right. Workers’ pay, entitlements and safety protections
will remain unchanged.

Making repeat seasonal hiring easier
Growers, vineyards and other seasonal businesses often
bring back the same workers year after year. Both sides
may know the job and each other well, but still have to
repeat much of the same paperwork each season.
National will develop a standard recurring seasonal
agreement and a short renewal process so employers
and returning workers can confirm the next season’s
dates, terms and any changes without starting again
from scratch.

Each fixed term will still need a genuine seasonal
reason and existing employee rights will remain.

Making apprenticeship paperwork simpler
Employers training apprentices should be spending
their time teaching skills, not chasing paper records
and signatures.
National will work with training providers to ensure
approved digital competency records and electronic
supervisor sign-off are consistently accepted across
apprenticeships.
Building on systems already in use, this will make it
easier for apprentices, employers and assessors to see
what has been completed and what still needs to be
signed off.

Helping businesses prepare for the new
leave system
The Employment Leave Act is now law, but the new
system does not take effect until August 2028.
Employers must continue using the existing Holidays
Act rules until then.
Payroll systems will need updating, leave balances
converted and employers and employees will need to
understand how the new calculations work.
National will deliver that transition with early guidance,
worked examples and coordinated support for
employers and payroll providers.

National will:
1.	 Introduce a First Employee Support Package
with practical first-year guidance and reduced
penalties for genuine administrative mistakes;
2.	 Make repeat seasonal hiring easier with a
standard recurring seasonal agreement and
shorter renewal process, while retaining the
requirement for a genuine seasonal reason;
3.	 Make apprenticeship record-keeping simpler
with consistent digital competency records
and electronic sign-off; and
4.	 Deliver the transition to the new employment
leave system with early guidance, worked
payroll examples and coordinated
implementation support.

B. Backing businesses to grow
National wants to support small business to invest,
expand, and grow, so they can create more jobs and
contribute more to their communities and the economy.
Investment Boost is one of the biggest changes
National has made to support that investment. It is a
$6.6 billion investment in kiwi businesses. It allows
businesses to immediately deduct 20 per cent of the
cost of eligible new assets.
That could mean better tools or another vehicle for a
builder, new equipment for a café, or machinery that
allows a manufacturer to fill a larger order.
Early evidence suggests businesses are responding.
Inland Revenue found 40 per cent of surveyed
businesses that had invested and understood
Investment Boost said it had increased their
investment spending.

What National will do if re-elected…
Giving small businesses more room to grow
The compulsory GST registration threshold has
remained at $60,000 since 2009. Inflation has steadily
eroded its real value, meaning businesses are reaching
the threshold at a much earlier stage of their growth.

Crossing the threshold brings additional administration,
recordkeeping and pricing decisions, potentially
creating a hurdle for a business that is still getting
established.
National believes there is a strong case to look again at
whether the current threshold remains fit for purpose.
That’s why, in government, we will commission a
review of the GST registration threshold. The review
will focus on reducing unnecessary compliance and
removing barriers to small-business growth, while
carefully considering the fiscal cost and wider impacts
of any change.

National will:
5.	 Review the compulsory GST registration
threshold, examining options to reduce
compliance and remove barriers to smallbusiness growth; and
6.	 Keep Investment Boost, retaining the
immediate 20 per cent deduction for eligible
productive assets of any value and businesses
of every size.

C.  Resolving employment disputes
faster and more fairly
Employment disputes are stressful for everyone
involved. For a small-business owner, months spent
dealing with lawyers, paperwork and hearings can
mean thousands of dollars in costs and hours away
from customers and staff. For an employee, the same
delays can leave questions about income, reputation
and their next job hanging over them.
The system should be rigorous where the issues
are serious, but the cost and process should
be proportionate to the scale and complexity of
the dispute.
National will develop a faster pathway for minor matters
and reform the wider system so problems are resolved
earlier, cases keep moving and both sides get a
fair hearing.
This work will build on the Government’s 2026 review
of the employment dispute system, which specifically
sought feedback on the time and cost involved in
disputes, the role of employment advocates and where
the system could work better.

What National will do if re-elected…
A fast track for straightforward disputes
National will develop a simplified fast-track process
within the Employment Relations Authority, for suitable
minor employment disputes.
The new pathway will provide a simpler route to a
binding decision, with straightforward forms, clear
eligibility rules and firm decision timeframes. The aim is
to match the process to the scale of the dispute, rather
than requiring every disagreement to work through the
same pathway.

Serious, complex or precedent-setting cases will remain
on the appropriate existing pathway, and fair-hearing
and challenge rights will be preserved.

Resolve problems earlier
Mediation is already a standard part of the employment
dispute system. We want to make use of the tools
already available to resolve straightforward disputes
earlier, before they become drawn out and expensive.
The law already provides options such as mediator
recommendations and, where the parties agree,
binding decisions. But these options are not routinely
offered or well understood.
National will require the Employment Relations
Authority to clearly explain and offer these resolution
options in suitable minor disputes, while preserving
each party’s choice about whether to use them. We
will also ensure prompt access to mediation, with
exceptions where mediation is inappropriate or urgent
action is required.

Keep Authority cases moving
Where a dispute does reach the Employment Relations
Authority, parties should be able to expect steady
progress and a timely determination.
National will require the Authority to issue
determinations within one month of the investigation
meeting or final submissions, except in genuinely
exceptional circumstances. Public holidays and
recognised court or Authority closedown periods,
including the Christmas and New Year period, will be
excluded when calculating that timeframe.

We will also track cases across the full process, from
filing through case management and investigation to
the final decision. The Authority’s case-management
powers will be strengthened to narrow the issues
genuinely in dispute, direct the production of relevant
information and deal efficiently with repetitive or
unnecessary procedural applications.
National will review the Authority’s ability to enforce its
own decisions, and whether their current powers are fit
for purpose.

Stop people having to give the same
evidence twice
Evidence given in the Authority can currently need to
be heard again if a matter progresses further. This is an
additional layer of cost and duplication that parties and
witnesses just don’t need.
National will require the Authority to keep a reliable
record of oral evidence, with appropriate privacy and
access safeguards. Courts will retain the ability to hear
evidence again where fairness or the circumstances
require it.

Better representation, without pricing
people out
Employees and employers should be able to get
affordable help with an employment dispute, but
paid professional representation should meet basic
standards of competence, conduct and transparency.

National will develop proportionate regulation of paid
employment advocates, including standards of conduct
and competence, clear information about fees and a
proper complaints process.

Ensuring collective bargaining has genuine
workplace support
Under current New Zealand law, a union can initiate
collective bargaining without first demonstrating
support from a minimum number or proportion of the
employees whose work would be covered by the
proposed agreement.
National will change this by requiring a minimum level
of employee support before new collective bargaining
can be initiated. The proposal would require support
from the lesser of 10 employees or 20 per cent of the
employees proposed to be covered, with a minimum of
two employees.
Comparable jurisdictions already use employeesupport tests. In the United Kingdom, a union
generally needs membership of at least 10 per cent
of the proposed bargaining unit to apply for statutory
recognition. In Australia, where an employer has not
agreed to bargain, the Fair Work Commission can
require bargaining where a majority of the employees
proposed to be covered want to bargain.

Earlier certainty over who is an employee
National has already introduced the contractor
gateway, which came into force in February 2026.
Where all of the gateway criteria are met, a worker is
treated as a contractor. Where they are not, the existing
common-law test continues to apply.
But where employment status remains genuinely
disputed, resolving that question early can prevent
the rest of the dispute becoming more complicated
and expensive.
National will create a clearer early process for
determining disputed employment status under section
6 of the Employment Relations Act, consistent with the
contractor gateway. The objective is to give both sides
earlier certainty about which rights and obligations
apply before they incur the cost of litigating the rest of
the dispute.

Employment law people can actually
navigate
New Zealand’s employment framework has
accumulated across multiple statutes over many years.
We currently have a system where obligations are
spread across a range of Acts, making it particularly
difficult for small businesses and employees without
specialist legal support to work out what applies.
National will progress an Employment Relations
Consolidation Bill in the next parliamentary term. The
purpose will be to bring the core employment-law
framework into a clearer and more coherent legislative
structure, reduce unnecessary cross-references and
make rights and obligations easier to find.

Health and safety rules that make sense on
the shop floor
The same principle applies to health and safety. A
workshop, café or construction business should be able
to understand what it needs to do to keep people safe.
National will rewrite priority health and safety codes
and guidance in plain English, with practical examples
developed alongside small businesses, workers and
industry experts. Too often, outdated and difficult-tounderstand guidance adds an unnecessary layer of
compliance difficulty.
This will support the Government’s wider health and
safety reforms by making expectations clearer and
helping businesses focus their effort on the risks that
can actually cause harm.

National will:
7.	 Develop a fast-track process for suitable minor
employment disputes, through a simplified
Employment Relations Authority pathway, with
clear eligibility, proportionate procedures,
firm decision timeframes and fair-hearing
safeguards;
8.	 Make better use of mediation to resolve minor
disputes early, including requiring mediator
recommendations and available binding
options to be clearly explained and offered in
suitable cases;
9.	 Require Employment Relations Authority
determinations within one month of the
investigation meeting or final submissions,
and track delays across the full process from
filing to decision;
10.	 Require the Authority to record oral evidence
so it can be reused where lawful and fair,
reducing unnecessary repetition;
11.	 Strengthen the Employment Relations
Authority’s powers to keep cases moving, and
deal with unnecessary procedural delays;
12.	 Review the Employment Relations Authority’s
enforcement powers, including whether it
should be able to enforce more of its own
orders without requiring parties to begin
avoidable proceedings in another court;
13.	 Introduce proportionate regulation of paid
employment advocates, covering conduct,
competence, transparent fees and complaints;
14.	 Require a minimum level of employee
support before new collective bargaining can
begin, proposing a threshold of the lesser
of 10 employees or 20 per cent of those
