D.  Giving business owners their time
back
For many small-business owners, the paperwork starts
when the working day ends. After serving customers,
managing staff and paying suppliers, there are still
forms to complete, licences to renew and records
to update.
Each requirement might seem small on its own.
Together, they take time and money away from the
business and time away from family.
National will make everyday compliance simpler.
Businesses should be able to provide information once,
use reliable digital tools and have a strong compliance
record recognised. Requirements should be clear,
practical and proportionate to the risks involved.

What National will do if re-elected…
Tell government once
Changing a business address or contact details
should be straightforward. Owners should not have
to work through a list of agencies updating the same
information in different systems.
National will develop a Tell Government Once service
built around the New Zealand Business Number and
existing government systems. Businesses will be able
to update core details in one place and securely share
those changes with participating agencies, including
Inland Revenue, ACC, the Companies Office and
relevant licensing bodies.
National will also explore this service integrating
with Councils where practical, with any necessary
information-sharing changes supported by clear
privacy rules and business control over the
information shared.

Simpler renewals for reliable businesses
A café can have separate renewal dates for food
registration, alcohol licensing, outdoor dining and
signage. Keeping track of different forms, invoices
and deadlines creates work throughout the year.
National will require councils to offer a coordinated
approach for relevant permits, licences and registrations.
Where possible, we will streamline approvals, aligning
approval lengths, ensuring businesses don’t have to
renew more often than necessary.
We will also introduce automatic or simplified renewals
for suitable low-risk approvals where a business has a
strong compliance record and its circumstances have
not materially changed.
For hospitality businesses, National will also deliver the
alcohol-licensing reforms already announced, including
simpler applications and renewals, longer renewal periods
for suitable licences and changes to the fee structure.

Letting accountants help with statutory
declarations
Many small businesses already rely on their chartered
accountant for trusted advice and official paperwork.
They should also be able to complete a statutory
declaration with that professional rather than arranging
a separate appointment elsewhere.
National will progress Suze Redmayne’s members
bill, first introduced by Carl Bates, to allow eligible
chartered accountants to administer statutory
declarations, with appropriate professional and
identity safeguards.
This is a specific extension of who can take a declaration.
Remote statutory declarations are already permitted
subject to legal requirements, and this reform will build
on those existing options rather than duplicate them.

Making digital the default
Businesses increasingly keep records, sign
documents and serve customers digitally. Government
requirements should make it easy to use reliable
technology rather than forcing businesses back
onto paper.
National will make clear that secure and accessible
electronic records can satisfy document-retention
requirements wherever a physical original is not
genuinely necessary. We will also remove remaining
statutory exceptions and inconsistent agency practices
that unnecessarily require paper.
That will include modernising physical-display rules
for alcohol licences and vehicle consumer information
where accessible digital alternatives can provide
the same information to customers and enforcement
officers. We will also make clear that suitable electronic
proof of delivery, including app confirmations,
photographs and secure tracking records, can meet
relevant requirements, and that accurate electronic
hazardous-substance records can be used where
they remain readily accessible onsite, including in
an emergency.
National will replace unnecessary compulsory
newspaper notices with searchable online publication,
while keeping appropriate ways to inform affected
communities. We will also remove obsolete fax, telex
and other paper-based requirements that create a real
compliance burden.
Where digital options already exist, we will make their
acceptance clearer and more consistent.

Clearer fire-safety guidance
Small-business owners should be able to understand
their fire-safety obligations without needing to become
experts in the system.
National will publish clearer guidance on existing
evacuation requirements, approved schemes and
available templates, helping businesses understand
what applies to them and how to comply.
The objective across these reforms is the same:
less time navigating government processes, fewer
unnecessary forms and more time spent running and
growing the business.

National will:
18.	 Build a Tell Government Once service around
the NZBN, so core business information
can be updated once and shared across
participating agencies and councils;
19.	 Make business renewals simpler and better
coordinated by aligning renewal dates
where practical and introducing automatic
or simplified renewals for suitable low-risk
businesses with strong compliance records;
20.	 Implement the announced alcohol-licensing
reforms to simplify applications and renewals,
extend suitable renewal periods and reform
fees;
21.	 Allow eligible chartered accountants to
administer statutory declarations, making it
easier for small businesses to complete official
paperwork through a trusted professional they
already use;
22.	 Remove unjustified paper-retention
requirements and publish consistent guidance
on accepting lawful electronic records and
evidence;
23.	 Modernise remaining licence and vehicleinformation display rules where accessible
digital alternatives preserve consumer and
enforcement access;
24.	 Replace unnecessary compulsory newspaper
notices with searchable online publication and
appropriate community notification;
25.	 Remove obsolete fax, telex and paper
requirements that impose a real compliance
burden; and
26.	 Publish clearer small-business guidance
on fire evacuation requirements, approved
schemes and available templates.

E.  Improving cashflow and lowering
costs for businesses

What National will do if re-elected…

Labour’s Business Payment Practices Act would have
required large businesses to report their payment
practices without requiring them to pay suppliers
any sooner. National repealed it and instead put the
responsibility on government to lead by example, while
committing to work with BusinessNZ on an industry-led
prompt-payment code.

Payment fees take a slice out of every sale. The
Commerce Commission’s implemented interchange-fee
reductions were expected to lower merchant service
fees by around $90 million a year, while proposed
caps on commercial credit cards could deliver another
$40 million in annual savings.

Government agencies are now expected to pay
95 per cent of domestic eInvoices within five business
days and other domestic invoices within 10 working
days. Results reported in July showed agencies paid
95.9 per cent of more than 1.6 million invoices within
10 working days.
National will build on these reforms by continuing to
publish agency payment performance, addressing
persistent delays and ensuring prompt-payment
requirements flow through government supply chains.
We are also making invoicing easier. eInvoicing
sends invoices directly between accounting systems,
reducing manual entry, mistakes and opportunities for
invoice fraud. By July, around 113,000 businesses were
registered to receive eInvoices, up from 52,000 earlier
in the year. Research estimates full adoption could
deliver up to $800 million a year in productivity gains.

Lower-cost, more competitive payments

National will make merchant fees, terminal charges and
other payment-service costs easier to compare, with
the disclosure obligation sitting with providers rather
than small businesses. We will also monitor whether
regulated savings are reaching businesses and support
further evidence-based fee reductions.

Helping independent repairers compete
Modern vehicles increasingly require access to
manufacturers’ information to diagnose and repair
faults. National will progress Dan Bidois’ motorvehicle repair-information reform to give independent
workshops better access to that information.
A regulated market for manufacturers’ repair
information would help independent repairers compete,
give customers more choice and reduce avoidable
delays getting work vehicles back on the road, with
appropriate safety, security and commercial safeguards.

Putting useful technology within reach
Small-business owners can see the potential of AI, but
often lack the time or expertise to work out where to
start. The AI Advisory Pilot helps businesses identify
useful applications and put them into practice, cofunding up to 50 per cent of eligible expert support.
Around 150 businesses have already joined, another
120 places have been announced, and around 650
businesses received co-funded support for AI-related
courses between July 2025 and June 2026.

Giving smaller firms a fair shot at government
work
Government procurement reforms introduced in
December 2025 reduced the main rulebook from 71
rules to 47 and introduced a minimum 10 per cent
weighting for economic benefits to New Zealand in
covered procurement evaluations.
National will monitor the reforms to ensure capable
smaller New Zealand suppliers have genuine
opportunities to compete. Requirements around
insurance, experience and reporting should be
proportionate to the size and risk of the contract
being offered.

National will:
27.	 Build on the Government’s prompt-payment
reforms by holding agencies to account for
low performance, tackling persistent delays
and enforcing fair payment terms through
procurement supply chains;
28.	 Complete the industry-led prompt-payment
programme and expand eInvoicing with
BusinessNZ, accounting providers and
business organisations;
29.	 Keep driving down payment costs by
improving fee transparency, monitoring

and supporting further evidence-based
reductions;
30.	 Complete the rollout of modern business

workshops better access to manufacturers’
information; and

support for small businesses, including the AI
Advisory Pilot.

F.  Backing the businesses that build
and produce
A builder will not take on another apprentice without
confidence the next job can proceed. A manufacturer
cannot fill a bigger order without the machinery and
space to produce it. For these businesses, delays cost
money and can mean missed opportunities.

National has also opened the door to more trusted
overseas building products. Recognition of Australia’s
WaterMark scheme alone made more than 90,000
plumbing products available under the recognised
pathway, increasing choice and competition for builders
and customers.

What National will do if re-elected…

National is making it easier to invest, build and expand
through clearer rules, faster decisions and better
access to the tools businesses need to grow. Fasttrack approvals are already helping significant housing,
infrastructure and productive projects move through a
more coordinated process.

Faster approvals and less duplicated work

The replacement planning system will bring more
consistent national rules and fewer unnecessary
consents, with an estimated 15,000 to 22,000 fewer
consent and permit applications and $13.3 billion in
administration and compliance savings over 30 years.

National will require regulators to accept and reuse
relevant, appropriately certified reports where they
remain current and fit for purpose. Further information
can still be required where site conditions, the project
or the risks have materially changed.

Building reforms will also consolidate consenting
functions, halve Project Information Memorandum
processing times from 20 to 10 working days and
introduce proportionate liability backed by professional
indemnity insurance and home warranties.

We will continue to recognise trusted overseas
building products and standards where they meet
New Zealand’s requirements. Builders should have
access to a wider range of reliable products, and
customers should benefit from stronger competition.

National will implement the replacement planning system
and carry the building reforms through into practice.
We will also tackle repeated requests for the same
technical information.

Finance for the next stage of growth
National will carry through capital-market reforms that
make it easier for growing firms to raise equity and
debt, with requirements proportionate to the offer and
appropriate protections for investors.
We will continue attracting investment that brings
productive capacity, skills and international connections
into New Zealand. The goal is more businesses able
to buy better equipment, develop new products,
reach new customers and create skilled jobs in
their communities.

National will:
33.	 Deliver the replacement planning system with
consistent national rules, fewer unnecessary
consents and practical support through the
transition;
34.	 Deliver building-consent reforms that enable
greater consolidation of consenting functions
and more consistent decisions;
35.	 Cut Project Information Memorandum
processing times from 20 to 10 working days
as part of the building-system reforms;
36.	 Deliver proportionate building liability, backed
by professional indemnity insurance and
home warranties;
37.	 Require regulators to reuse current, relevant
certified engineering and geotechnical reports
where they remain fit for purpose;
38.	 Continue expanding recognition of trusted
overseas building products and standards that
meet New Zealand’s requirements;
39.	 Deliver capital-market reforms to make it
easier for growing businesses to raise equity
and debt; and
40.	 Use Invest New Zealand to connect
productive businesses with international
investment, skills and commercial partners.

G.  Taking more New Zealand
businesses to the world
A small New Zealand business can have a product the
world wants but lack the contacts, time or expertise to
navigate an unfamiliar market. National will help more
firms make their first export sale and turn promising
overseas demand into regular orders.
National signed the New Zealand - India Free Trade
Agreement in April. It has now been ratified and will
enter into force on 20 October 2026, giving exporters
better access to a market of 1.4 billion people.
The agreement will eliminate or reduce tariffs on 95
per cent of our current exports to India. Fifty-seven per
cent will be tariff free from day one, including sheep
meat, wool and more than 95 per cent of forestry and
wood exports.
National has also expanded access through
agreements with the UAE, brought the NZ-EU FTA into
force ahead of schedule, concluded negotiations with
the Gulf Cooperation Council, and continued removing
non-tariff barriers holding exporters back.

What National will do if re-elected…
Backing the next 200 exporters
National’s Next 200 program will provide intensive
support to 200 high-potential small and mediumsized businesses ready to begin exporting or expand
significantly. Each will receive a dedicated NZTE
relationship manager, tailored market intelligence,
overseas introductions and help with regulatory and
customs requirements.
We will give NZTE a sharper role in identifying
commercial opportunities and connecting smaller
firms with buyers. Support should help an owner work
through the practical steps from initial interest to a
completed order.

Make trade rules easier to use
National will introduce three AI-powered tools: an FTA
tariff adviser, a rules-of-origin navigator and a marketaccess requirements tool. Owners will be able to
describe their product and destination in plain English
and find the relevant official requirements, with access
to specialist help where needed.

We will expand paperless trade, digital certification and
automated customs processes, including pursuing realtime electronic certification with the United Kingdom
and other close partners.
A trusted-exporter fast lane will build on Customs’
existing Secure Exports Scheme. We will make its
benefits easier for eligible smaller firms to use.
National will pursue the removal of a $1 billion in nontariff barriers by 2030, working with businesses to
identify the certification, standards and market-access
problems stopping otherwise competitive products
from reaching customers.

More markets and stronger supply links
National will pursue the goal of doubling export
value by 2034, help businesses use the India
agreement and progress the Gulf agreement into
force. We will pursue the next group of priority trade
negotiations where they offer meaningful opportunities
for New Zealand exporters.
We will modernise existing agreements, including
services access with China, expand digital trade
arrangements and support expansion of the CPTPP
and RCEP. Our goal of lifting services to 35 per cent
of export value by 2030 recognises the opportunities
for smaller technology, creative and professional
businesses to sell internationally.
We will pursue essential-supplies agreements with
like-minded partners, using the Singapore agreement
as a model. Reliable access to fuel, machinery parts
and other critical inputs helps a small business
keep operating when international supply chains
are disrupted.

National will:
41.	 Establish the Next 200 program, providing
intensive NZTE support for 200 high-potential
small and medium-sized exporters;
42.	 Create an AI-powered export navigator
covering tariffs, rules of origin and marketaccess requirements, linked to official
information and specialist support;
43.	 Expand paperless trade and digital
certification, including pursuing real-time
electronic certification with close trading
partners;
44.	 Create a trusted-exporter fast lane through
the Secure Exports Scheme, making it easier
for eligible smaller firms to participate and
reducing duplicated documentation.
45.	 Remove a further $1 billion in non-tariff barriers
by 2030, prioritising restrictions identified with
New Zealand exporters;
46.	 Open more markets for small businesses
by helping firms use the India and Gulf
agreements, pursuing the next group of
priority markets, and expanding digital and
services trade arrangements; and
47.	 Strengthen New Zealand’s trade resilience by
pursuing essential-supplies agreements that
help businesses maintain access to critical
goods during disruption.

# National's Budget Responsibility Rules

Published by the New Zealand National Party as a PDF policy document. Source: <https://assets.national.org.nz/web/prod/National's%20Budget%20Responsibility%20Rules-1.pdf?v=1788512439>.
The text below is the verbatim text layer of the PDF extracted with `pdftotext` (reading order). Line breaks follow the
PDF; tables and multi-column layouts may read out of order in this section, so a second rendering that preserves the
page layout (`pdftotext -layout`) follows it. Nothing has been added, removed or paraphrased.

## Full text (reading order)

BUILDING THE FUTURE:

NATIONAL’S BUDGET
RESPONSIBILITY RULES
While in Government, National has prioritised a return to balanced budgets, so we can reduce debt as a share of the
economy and keep taxes low for every New Zealander.
In a more volatile international environment, which has prolonged New Zealand’s economic recovery, that has required
responsible economic and fiscal management, including a total of $50 billion in savings achieved across the last three
Budgets.
That approach is working. The forecast return to surplus was brought forward a year in Budget 2026, while a targeted
response to the global fuel shock was funded from within existing allowances. The Government’s ongoing programme of
savings has also enabled greater investment in frontline services, like health, education, and law and order.
But the job isn’t done. The books have now been in deficit for seven years running. Getting back to surplus isn’t an
optional extra, it’s essential to New Zealand’s international economic credibility. Prior to Budget 2026, both Fitch
and Moody’s moved their outlook on New Zealand’s sovereign credit rating to negative. At the same time, the cost of
government debt has risen worldwide. Long-term bond yields in the United States are at their highest levels since 2007,
and since 1998 in the United Kingdom.
For New Zealand, the rising cost of borrowing matters more here than in many other countries, because we do not have
a large domestic savings pool to absorb our own government debt. Higher levels of debt, and a higher cost of servicing
our debt, is ultimately a risk to our financial resilience and national security.
Against that backdrop, New Zealand must focus on remaining competitive and attractive to capital markets. Keeping
debt down and getting back to surplus is the best option we have of achieving that objective and ensuring the cost of
borrowing continues to be affordable for households, businesses, and the government.

Three fiscal rules
For those reasons, credible and consistent fiscal policy is paramount.
That’s why a re-elected National Government will maintain three fiscal rules:
•
•
•

Prioritising a return to surplus in 2028/29, and maintaining a surplus over time, sufficient to see the debt curve bend
down.
Bending debt down below 40 per cent of GDP, and maintaining debt below 40 per cent over time.
Keeping taxes low by right-sizing government, with core Crown expenditure as a share of the economy declining
towards 30 per cent of GDP.

Getting back to surplus
Running a consistent operating surplus is critical to New Zealand’s economic credibility. An operating surplus means dayto-day expenditure is funded from the revenue we have available, instead of additional borrowing.
A re-elected National Government will prioritise returning the books to surplus by 2028/29, and maintain a surplus over
time, so that debt as a share of the economy continues to decline.
National will get back to surplus by prioritising spending restraint, not by introducing new taxes on hard-working New
Zealanders. Where revenue comes in ahead of forecast, as it did at Budget 2026, that upside will contribute to reducing
the deficit.
Equally, National will not over-react to forecast changes in the other direction: a downside surprise will not trigger sharp
cuts to frontline services.

Bending debt down
National will keep government debt at prudent levels so New Zealand can absorb the shocks that inevitably come. As of
BEFU 26, net core Crown debt is forecast to peak at 46.1 per cent of GDP in 2027/28 and then fall to 44.4 per cent by the
end of the forecast period.
A re-elected National Government will keep it on that downward trajectory towards 40 per cent of GDP, and then
maintain debt below 40 per cent of GDP over time.
This matters more for New Zealand than for most countries. We are a small, commodity-exporting economy, exposed to
natural disasters and reliant on offshore lenders.
Historically New Zealand has had lower government debt than comparable countries as insurance against that exposure.
That buffer was eroded considerably under the last Labour Government.
Rebuilding it is what allows a future government to respond to the next earthquake, pandemic, or global shock without a
fiscal crisis. In a more volatile world, where government bond yields have risen significantly in recent years, maintaining
low levels of debt also protects New Zealand against the prospect of international financial shocks.

Keeping taxes low by right-sizing government
A re-elected National Government means an ongoing commitment to keep taxes low for working New Zealanders, which
means a greater role for Kiwis to determine their own future on their own terms.
The only affordable way to achieve that is an ongoing focus on fiscal discipline, where frontline services are prioritised
over back office expenditure and the overall size of government as a proportion of the economy continues to fall.
When Labour took power in 2017, core Crown expenditure was around 28 per cent of GDP. By the time they left office in
late 2023, this had risen to 34 per cent of GDP, driving large deficits and a steady stream of new taxes.
To keep taxes low and return to surplus, National is on a mission to right-size government, by restoring government
spending as a share of the economy to historic norms, at 30 per cent of GDP over time.
To achieve that, National will maintain tight operating allowances, and support additional expenditure for frontline
services through an ongoing programme of reprioritisation and reductions in lower-priority expenditure.

Investing in the infrastructure New Zealand needs
Fiscal discipline is not an argument against investment. National will continue to invest in the roads, hospitals, schools
and defence capability the country needs.
Capital investment is lumpy by nature, so new spending will be offset where possible by capital savings and better use
of assets the Crown already owns, and every project will be tested against a clear value-for-money framework. Capital
spending adds to debt, so it must be disciplined by the same rules: if it is not, debt never turns down.
Consistent surpluses are also critical to National’s mission of investing in infrastructure. By achieving a consistent surplus
over time, governments have room to invest in infrastructure, funded through borrowing, while continuing to bend the
debt curve down. The only way to reduce debt sustainably over time while continuing to run an operating deficit would
be to underinvest in capital assets, like roads, schools, and hospitals.

Authorised by J de Joux, ps@national.org.nz

```text
and since 1998 in the United Kingdom.

For New Zealand, the rising cost of borrowing matters more here than in many other countries, because we do not have
a large domestic savings pool to absorb our own government debt. Higher levels of debt, and a higher cost of servicing
our debt, is ultimately a risk to our financial resilience and national security.

Against that backdrop, New Zealand must focus on remaining competitive and attractive to capital markets. Keeping
debt down and getting back to surplus is the best option we have of achieving that objective and ensuring the cost of
borrowing continues to be affordable for households, businesses, and the government.

Three fiscal rules

For those reasons, credible and consistent fiscal policy is paramount.

That’s why a re-elected National Government will maintain three fiscal rules:

•   Prioritising a return to surplus in 2028/29, and maintaining a surplus over time, sufficient to see the debt curve bend
    down.
•   Bending debt down below 40 per cent of GDP, and maintaining debt below 40 per cent over time.
•   Keeping taxes low by right-sizing government, with core Crown expenditure as a share of the economy declining
    towards 30 per cent of GDP.

Getting back to surplus

Running a consistent operating surplus is critical to New Zealand’s economic credibility. An operating surplus means day-
to-day expenditure is funded from the revenue we have available, instead of additional borrowing.

A re-elected National Government will prioritise returning the books to surplus by 2028/29, and maintain a surplus over
time, so that debt as a share of the economy continues to decline.

National will get back to surplus by prioritising spending restraint, not by introducing new taxes on hard-working New
Zealanders. Where revenue comes in ahead of forecast, as it did at Budget 2026, that upside will contribute to reducing
the deficit.

Equally, National will not over-react to forecast changes in the other direction: a downside surprise will not trigger sharp
cuts to frontline services.

Bending debt down

National will keep government debt at prudent levels so New Zealand can absorb the shocks that inevitably come. As of
BEFU 26, net core Crown debt is forecast to peak at 46.1 per cent of GDP in 2027/28 and then fall to 44.4 per cent by the
end of the forecast period.

A re-elected National Government will keep it on that downward trajectory towards 40 per cent of GDP, and then
maintain debt below 40 per cent of GDP over time.

This matters more for New Zealand than for most countries. We are a small, commodity-exporting economy, exposed to
natural disasters and reliant on offshore lenders.

Historically New Zealand has had lower government debt than comparable countries as insurance against that exposure.
That buffer was eroded considerably under the last Labour Government.

Rebuilding it is what allows a future government to respond to the next earthquake, pandemic, or global shock without a
fiscal crisis. In a more volatile world, where government bond yields have risen significantly in recent years, maintaining
low levels of debt also protects New Zealand against the prospect of international financial shocks.

Keeping taxes low by right-sizing government

A re-elected National Government means an ongoing commitment to keep taxes low for working New Zealanders, which
means a greater role for Kiwis to determine their own future on their own terms.

The only affordable way to achieve that is an ongoing focus on fiscal discipline, where frontline services are prioritised
over back office expenditure and the overall size of government as a proportion of the economy continues to fall.

When Labour took power in 2017, core Crown expenditure was around 28 per cent of GDP. By the time they left office in
late 2023, this had risen to 34 per cent of GDP, driving large deficits and a steady stream of new taxes.

To keep taxes low and return to surplus, National is on a mission to right-size government, by restoring government
spending as a share of the economy to historic norms, at 30 per cent of GDP over time.

To achieve that, National will maintain tight operating allowances, and support additional expenditure for frontline
services through an ongoing programme of reprioritisation and reductions in lower-priority expenditure.

Investing in the infrastructure New Zealand needs

Fiscal discipline is not an argument against investment. National will continue to invest in the roads, hospitals, schools
and defence capability the country needs.

Capital investment is lumpy by nature, so new spending will be offset where possible by capital savings and better use
of assets the Crown already owns, and every project will be tested against a clear value-for-money framework. Capital
spending adds to debt, so it must be disciplined by the same rules: if it is not, debt never turns down.

Consistent surpluses are also critical to National’s mission of investing in infrastructure. By achieving a consistent surplus
over time, governments have room to invest in infrastructure, funded through borrowing, while continuing to bend the
debt curve down. The only way to reduce debt sustainably over time while continuing to run an operating deficit would
be to underinvest in capital assets, like roads, schools, and hospitals.

                                                                                              Authorised by J de Joux, ps@national.org.nz
```

# National's Economic Plan

Published by the New Zealand National Party as a PDF policy document. Source: <https://assets.national.org.nz/web/prod/National%27s%20Economic%20Plan.pdf?v=1790557287>.
The text below is the verbatim text layer of the PDF extracted with `pdftotext` (reading order). Line breaks follow the
PDF; tables and multi-column layouts may read out of order in this section, so a second rendering that preserves the
page layout (`pdftotext -layout`) follows it. Nothing has been added, removed or paraphrased.

## Full text (reading order)

Building the Future:

National’s Economic Plan

Building the Future:

Our Economic Plan,
designed for you

Introduction
New Zealand is the best country on Planet Earth.
We have the resources, the institutions and, above
all, the people, to realise that promise.

National’s Economic Plan is about
your future.

But success is not guaranteed. The future must be built.
Kiwis are among the hardest workers in the world, but
we don’t get as much bang for every hour worked or
dollar invested as our international counterparts.

1. No new taxes, by getting the books back in order.
2. Rewarding hard work, with more jobs and
higher wages.
3. Building your financial security.

Over the last 40 years New Zealand has developed
a productivity problem. National is fixing it.
We have refocused the education system on the core
skills our kids need, banged on doors to open up new
markets for our exporters, slashed red tape, sped
up consenting, and incentivised businesses to grow
and innovate.
National’s Economic Plan means more jobs and higher
wages. It means more money coming into communities.
It means more doctors, nurses and teachers, and better
schools and hospitals.
We are making good progress. Inflation is down from
a 32-year high. Interest rates have fallen. Business
confidence is up. Investment is increasing. Construction
projects are getting started faster. And public spending
is back under control.

All this means growth is expected to average 2.7%, with
220,000 new jobs being created by 2030 and wages
growing faster than inflation.
There is a lot more to do.
I have no doubt we can build a future for New Zealand
where hard work is rewarded, where families can get
ahead, kids get the education they deserve, and high
quality health and other public services are available
when needed.
Our best years are ahead of us. Let’s grasp the
opportunity.

Rt Hon Christopher Luxon
National Party Leader

Authorised by J de Joux, ps@national.org.nz

Overview

National’s Economic Plan, at a glance

1

Responsibly managing the books

2

Reducing red tape and supporting innovation

3

Delivering world-class education

4

Driving trade and investment

5

Building infrastructure for the future

Delivering a surplus in 2028/29. Getting debt below 40% of GDP over time. Financial security
to manage the next crisis. Simplifying tax rules to support investment.

Replacing the RMA. Ending the war on farmers. Simplifying employment rules. Extending
support for research and innovation.

An hour a day of reading, writing and maths. Replacing NCEA. More trades-training.

New trade deals. Securing the next billion customers for our farmers, growers and exporters.
Boosting tourism. Investment Boost providing support to invest.

More investment in intergenerational infrastructure - roads, hospitals, classrooms and
energy generation. Major projects fast-tracked. 30-year infrastructure plan.

What this means for you
Rewarding hard work

Building your financial security

220,000 new jobs forecast by 2030. Wages
growing faster than household bills. Keeping a
lid on inflation and interest rates. Lower Student
Loan repayments. No new taxes.

A bigger KiwiSaver nest egg. A $1,500 KiwiSaver
Baby Boost for all newborns. Helping first
home buyers get on the property ladder.

Don’t put it all at risk
Nine new taxes to pay for Labour’s $18 billion hidden bill
Labour has made ‘free’ election promises totalling $18 billion. As well as a Capital Gains Tax, there are
eight other new taxes being proposed by Labour and their mates that Kiwis would end up paying for.

1. Responsibly managing the books
Getting the books in order helps keep interest rates down, supporting investment
and financial stability - and means we can deliver our promise of no new taxes.
Simpler tax rules

Surplus in 2028/29

Debt under 40%

that reduce compliance costs
and reward investment

so Government spending
doesn’t push inflation up

of GDP over time, so we don’t
saddle our kids with more costs

Financial resilience is critical to growth, particularly in a more volatile world. Businesses invest when they can see
what’s coming: stable prices, sensible interest rates and a government that won’t come back for more of their money.
When governments borrow and spend big, inflation rises and interest rates stay higher for longer. National has
taken the opposite approach. With a global fuel shock pushing prices up again, the last thing businesses need is a
government adding to the pressure.
As a small trading nation, New Zealand is more exposed than most when disaster strikes or the world economy
turns. Bending down debt rebuilds our buffers for the next crisis, and it helps keep borrowing costs down to help
drive investment.
A stable, predictable tax system matters just as much. That’s why we introduced Investment Boost, have ruled out
new taxes, and are stripping out compliance costs that tie businesses up in paperwork.

What we’ve delivered

• $50 billion reprioritised across three Budgets, and
new spending coming in below operating allowances
every single year.
• Refocused the Reserve Bank on a single job: keeping
prices stable.
• Inflation down from a 32-year high of 7.3 per cent.
• Budget 2026 reduced the Government’s planned
borrowing programme by $6 billion, the first reduction
in five years.
• Investment Boost, helping businesses invest and
hire with tax relief on new assets.
• Stopped the Ute Tax, Labour’s brightline test
extension, and the Auckland Fuel Tax, and scrapped
Labour’s Rentals Tax.
• Let startups defer tax on employee shares, making it
easier to attract and keep talent.
• Loosened the thin capitalisation rules, helping
investors to fund New Zealand’s growth.

What we’re doing next

• Returning the books to surplus in 2028/29 and
staying there, so government spending doesn’t put
pressure on inflation and interest rates.
• Getting net core Crown debt below 40 per cent
of GDP over time.
• Right-sizing government, with Public Sector reform
to get core Crown expenditure below 30 per cent
of GDP.
• No new taxes, including no capital gains tax, and
keeping Investment Boost, so businesses can plan
and invest with confidence.
• Reducing tax compliance, such as employers no
longer needing detailed FBT log books for work
vehicles, and innovative firms getting R&D tax credits
during the year, not after it.
• Doubling the threshold before overseas shares are
caught by the foreign investment fund rules, helping
attract skilled people and investment.
• More to come before November 7…

2. Reducing red tape and supporting innovation
Reducing red tape, backing competition and supporting research and innovation,
so New Zealand businesses can invest, grow, create jobs and lift wages.
Red tape cut
by replacing the RMA and
introducing Fast-track

Science and innovation

War on farmers ended

reforms focused on impact
and commercialisation

with common sense changes to
reduce compliance and red tape

Governments don’t create wealth. That’s done by our farmers getting up early to milk the cows and our growers
producing the best food in the world. It’s our dairy owners and our tradies, our rocket companies and our film
makers. Every job, every pay rise and every dollar of tax starts with a Kiwi with an idea and a willingness to have a go.
National backs Kiwi businesses to grow, and we’ll do everything we can to make it easier to build, invest, hire and
export. That means cutting through tangled regulations and slow consents that have held us back for too long.
It means backing competition. And it means supporting the research and innovation that creates well-paid jobs.

What we’ve delivered

• Fast-track, a one-stop consenting process for major
projects.
• Backing innovation with the biggest reforms of the
science system in more than 30 years, focusing on
impact and commercialisation.
• Aligned tertiary research funding with economic
growth priorities.
• Strengthening competition settings to make it easier
to enter markets, compete and expand.
• Ended the war on farmers, by restoring common sense
to winter grazing, limiting farm to forest conversions,
ending the Ute Tax, enabling flexible land use, and
keeping agriculture out of the ETS so we don’t shut
down farms or send production overseas.
• Restoring 90-day trials, and replacing the Holidays
Act to simplify compliance.
• Changed immigration settings to ensure New Zealand
is attracting the skills we need.
• Invested in pest and weed management, like additional
funding to tackle Wilding Pines, as this has long
term benefits for tourism and productive farming.
• Elevate NZ Venture Fund supporting startups to
scale and grow.

What we’re doing next

• Implementing the replacement of the RMA, which
will roughly halve the number of consents needed
and provide much more certainty when a consent
is required.
• Increasing competition for Government
procurement, by opening up currently closed
supplier panels to give new businesses a fairer
shot at more than $50 billion of annual government
purchasing.
• Ensuring regulation across the Reserve Bank, MBIE
and the Financial Markets Authority is coordinated
to reduce bureaucracy and remove barriers to the
introduction of new fin-tech.
• Plain English re-write of Health and Safety Codes to
make compliance more straightforward.
• More to come before November 7…

3. Delivering world-class education
A world class education system that creates opportunities for Kiwi kids and is
the foundation for a high-wage, high-productivity economy.
Teach the Basics

Replace NCEA

Trades Academy

Brilliantly, with an hour a day
of reading, writing and maths

with clear grades, and exams
in every subject

places doubled, reaching
20,000 by 2030

New Zealand’s prosperity depends on the knowledge, skills and ambition of our young people. For too long,
achievement in reading, writing and maths went backwards, while employers struggled to find the skills they needed.
We are turning that all around.
National is rebuilding our education system around what works: Teaching the Basics Brilliantly with structured literacy
and maths, a knowledge-rich curriculum, regular assessment and reporting to parents, and better pathways into
future training and work.
Early results show the plan is working. Maths and writing achievement has improved at Year 6, the first time results
have significantly improved in years.

What we’ve delivered

• An hour a day of reading, writing and maths.
• New knowledge-rich curriculum with clear year-byyear expectations.
• Banned cellphone use in schools.
• Structured literacy, phonics checks and a structured
approach to maths.
• Maths textbooks and workbooks, science kits and
more classroom resources.
• Regular assessment and more detailed reporting
to parents.
• Stopped open-plan classrooms.
• Halved the cost of building new classrooms.
• Restored regional polytechnics so training happens
close to home.
• Established eight Industry Skills Boards, ensuring
learners and apprentices are job-ready.

What we’re doing next

• Replacing NCEA. In its place will be clear A+ to E
grades and an exam in every subject.
• Embedding the new curriculum across every year
level and every subject.
• Doubling the number of Trades Academy places to
20,000 by 2030.
• Rolling out nine new industry-developed vocational
subjects and courses.
• Banning social media for under-16s.
• More to come before November 7…

4. Driving trade and investment
Trade means more money coming into Kiwi communities, more jobs and
higher wages.
Free trade deals

Doubling exports

Investment Boost

to help unlock the next billion
customers for Kiwi businesses

on track for 2034, with export
income up $20 billion already

tax relief helping businesses
invest and hire

New Zealand will never get rich selling only to itself. National is hustling on the world stage to open doors for our
farmers, growers, and exporters - because New Zealand’s products are the best in the world and more exports
means more money flowing directly into Kiwi communities.
National is delivering new free trade deals. Our plan will help Kiwi farmers, growers and exporters secure
New Zealand’s next billion customers overseas. We are backing tourism to get more money flowing into local
communities. And we are making it easier to invest so that our businesses can grow and create more well-paid
jobs for Kiwis.

What we’ve delivered

• Completed a Free Trade Agreement with India,
brought the NZ-EU deal into force ahead of schedule,
New Zealand’s first Free Trade Agreement in the
Middle East with the UAE, and negotiations with the
six nation Gulf Cooperation Council.
• Exports up from $94 billion to $114 billion, bringing
more money and jobs into Kiwi communities.
• Completed 23 trade missions to 18 countries.
• Eliminated $733 million of non-tariff barriers.
• Tourism numbers up 24% since 2023.
• Active Investor Plus has driven around $4.8 billion of
new investment.
• Established Invest New Zealand to support new
investment that drives growth and jobs.
• Major Events and Tourism package to drive economic
activity.

What we’re doing next

• Securing New Zealand’s next billion customers
by pursuing trade, with trade negotiations with
seven priority markets including Brazil, Switzerland,
Argentina and the European Free Trade Association all designed to double the value of exports by 2034.
• Reducing red tape at the border for exporters,
targeting removal of $1 billion of non-tariff barriers
with a focus on expanding paperless trade and
digitalised systems.
• Resetting the International Visitor Levy, so regions
receive a direct return from the visitors they host
without needing new taxes.
• Ensuring foreign investment fund settings and IRD
rules are not preventing Active Investor Plus visa
holders from staying in New Zealand and contributing
to the economy.
• Growing the pool of investment capital available
to grow the New Zealand economy by increasing
Kiwisaver balances.
• More to come before November 7…

5. Building infrastructure for the future
Fixing the system to deliver roads, power, water, schools and hospitals.
Energy supply

Roads of National

Health and Education

cutting consenting red tape to
supercharge new generation

Significance, and other major
transport projects

new schools and hospital
upgrades to meet your needs

National is the party of infrastructure. Roads, rapid transit, hospitals, schools, defence, fibre, and energy. The
infrastructure services New Zealanders rely on every day get built when National is in government.
New Zealand has a significant infrastructure deficit, and when we do invest it can be expensive compared to other
countries. National is fixing both of these problems, while also getting on with building tens of billions of dollars of
infrastructure to grow the economy, lift productivity and wages, support jobs, and ensure Kiwis can live better lives.

What we’ve delivered

• Independent 30-year National Infrastructure Plan.
• Four Roads of National Significance under
construction – Ōtaki to north of Levin, the Hawke’s
Bay Expressway, Takitimu North Link, and SH29
Tauriko West.
• Started construction on over $20 billion of
Government infrastructure projects.
• Funded over 1,600 new classrooms and delivered
8,500 net new social homes.
• Hospital builds or upgrades underway in Dunedin,
Auckland, Whangārei, Nelson, Palmerston North,
Wellington, Hawke’s Bay, and Tauranga.
• Started and finished the Auckland City Rail Link.
• South Island transport funding up by 42 per cent.
• Replacing the failed Resource Management Act,
making it easier to get things built.
• Over 30 projects approved under Fast-Track,
representing tens of thousands of jobs and billions
in investment, with more in the pipeline.
• Sped up new renewable generation with our Electrify
NZ changes, which has seen New Zealand’s largest
windfarm approved in five months, not five years.

What we’re doing next

• Completing the next tranche of the Roads of National
Significance, with the Northern Expressway and
Cambridge to Piarere beginning construction by
early 2027.
• Continuing to deliver hospitals, schools, public
transport and other infrastructure Kiwis need.
• Requiring new data centres to bring new generation
with them.
• Legislating requirements for asset management
plans, and long-term capital plans.
• Finishing off the job we started fixing our planning
system.
• Requiring the Infrastructure Commission to
internationally cost-benchmark government-led
infrastructure builds including transport, schools,
and hospitals to ensure taxpayer money is spent
wisely.
• More to come before November 7…

What it means for you

Rewarding hard work
National’s Economic Plan means more jobs and higher wages. It means inflation
under control. It means if you work hard, you can get ahead.
220,000 new jobs

No new taxes

Low inflation

expected by 2030, creating
more opportunities here in NZ

so you can get ahead

so a hard-earned pay rise isn’t
swallowed by bills

A job is how a young person gets a start, and how a family gets ahead. When more Kiwis are in work and wages rise
faster than prices, everything else gets easier: paying the mortgage, saving for the future, giving your kids a shot.
Making work pay means ensuring three things. First, that the economy is designed to create more jobs and lift
wages. Second, that the tax and welfare systems reward effort rather than penalise it. And third, that the cost of
everyday life is under control, so a hard-earned pay rise isn’t swallowed by bills.
Simply put, our plan is to encourage work, not tax it.

What we’ve delivered

• Tax relief for hardworking Kiwis, helping 1.9 million
families by $60 a week on average.
• Inflation down from a 32-year high, allowing
mortgage rates to fall.
• Supporting parents to work, with the FamilyBoost
childcare tax credit helping around 100,000 families
with up to $120 a week.
• Provided $50 a week in temporary, targeted support
to those most affected by the Middle East fuel crisis.
• Rents increasing at their lowest level in 25 years.
• Restored work expectations in the welfare system
with sanctions for those who don’t meet their
obligations, and a $1,000 bonus for young people
who move into work.

What we’re doing next

• No new taxes.
• We’ve set the conditions for job creation, with
220,000 new jobs expected by 2030.
• Wages expected to rise faster than inflation.
• Implementing a Rates Cap, to stop wild increase in
council costs.
• Extending Paid Parental Leave from 26 to 30
weeks, and letting parents take leave together or in
overlapping blocks.
• Helping Kiwis keep more of what they earn
by reducing weekly mandatory student loan
repayments, while cracking down on overseas
borrowers who don’t repay.
• More to come before November 7…

What it means for you

Building your financial security
Helping you become financially secure, at every stage of life.
KiwiSaver compulsory

First home buyers

$1,500 Baby Boost

with contributions rising
to 12%

buyers helped with a lowdeposit loan

KiwiSaver Baby Boost for all
newborns, to get them started

New Zealanders save less than Australians. That means we can be less prepared for retirement, but also that we can
be less financially secure whatever our stage of life.
National is supporting Kiwis to build their financial security, whether that means buying a first home, paying back
your student loan, taking time with a new baby, or retiring with dignity.

What we’ve delivered

• Lifted KiwiSaver contributions from 3 to 3.5 per cent.
A young worker on a moderate wage can now expect
to retire with nearly $900,000.
• Increased NZ Super for a couple by more than $180
a fortnight.
• Helping home buyers by freeing up land for housing
and reducing building costs, while helping reduce
mortgage rates by getting on top of inflation.

What we’re doing next

• Making KiwiSaver compulsory, and lifting
contributions to 6 per cent each for employers and
employees by 2032, matching Australia.
• Enrolling every newborn in KiwiSaver with a $1,500
Baby Boost.
• Making Government KiwiSaver contribution while
on Paid Parental Leave, and requiring employers to
keep contributing for workers over 65.
• Extending 5% deposits to more first-home buyers by
increasing current income caps.
• More to come before November 7…

The choice

Don’t put it all at risk
Labour have $18 billion of ‘free’ election promises, the only catch is nine
new taxes.
$18 billion Hidden Bill

Nine new taxes

Capital Gains Tax

to pay for all of Labour’s ‘free’
election promises

proposed by Labour and its
coalition partners

would punish Kiwis who do
the right thing and save and
invest

Despite ruling it out as Prime Minister, Chris Hipkins is now campaigning on hitting Kiwis with a 28% Capital Gains
Tax that will hit rentals, baches and businesses that own their own premises. And it will hit KiwiSaver funds that
invest in New Zealand businesses that owns commercial or residential property.
Labour is also proposing a $5 billion tax increase on businesses by scrapping Investment Boost.
The problem is, Labour cannot govern on its own. Between them, Labour, the Greens, Te Pāti Māori and The
Opportunities Party have proposed nine new taxes.

The nine new taxes
The tax

Who is proposing it

What it means

Capital Gains
Tax

Labour

A 28 per cent tax on capital gains, hitting the bach, the rental
and the business that owns its own premises.

Asset Tax

Greens, Te Pāti Māori

A 2.5 per cent annual tax on assets over $10 million, including
the businesses that employ New Zealanders.

Inheritance
Tax

Greens

A 33 per cent tax on large inheritances.

Gift Tax

Greens

A 33 per cent tax on large gifts.

45 per cent

Greens

A new top income tax rate of 45 per cent on income above
$160,000.

Rentals Tax

Greens

Removing interest deductibility on rentals, after restoring it
coincided with rent increases falling to their lowest in two decades.

Land Tax

TOP

An annual tax of 1.75 per cent on the value of your land,
including the family home, or 0.75 per cent on the value of a farm.

Digital Tax

Greens, Te Pāti
Māori, Labour

A tax on digital services Kiwis use every day.

Business Tax

Labour

Scrapping Investment Boost, a $5 billion tax increase on the
businesses that invest in new equipment.

```text
what’s coming: stable prices, sensible interest rates and a government that won’t come back for more of their money.
When governments borrow and spend big, inflation rises and interest rates stay higher for longer. National has
taken the opposite approach. With a global fuel shock pushing prices up again, the last thing businesses need is a
government adding to the pressure.
As a small trading nation, New Zealand is more exposed than most when disaster strikes or the world economy
turns. Bending down debt rebuilds our buffers for the next crisis, and it helps keep borrowing costs down to help
drive investment.
A stable, predictable tax system matters just as much. That’s why we introduced Investment Boost, have ruled out
```

# National's Education Manifesto

Published by the New Zealand National Party as a PDF policy document. Source: <https://assets.national.org.nz/web/prod/National's%20Education%20Manifesto.pdf?v=1791664336>.
The text below is the verbatim text layer of the PDF extracted with `pdftotext` (reading order). Line breaks follow the
PDF; tables and multi-column layouts may read out of order in this section, so a second rendering that preserves the
page layout (`pdftotext -layout`) follows it. Nothing has been added, removed or paraphrased.

## Full text (reading order)

Building the Future:

Education Manifesto 2026

Building the Future:

Education Manifesto 2026
Our vision
Every child deserves an education that opens doors.
The knowledge to understand the world, the skills
to contribute to it, and the confidence to build a
successful future.
National’s vision is a world-leading education system
that raises achievement and gives every young
New Zealander the opportunity to succeed.
A child’s background, postcode, or learning needs
should never set the limit on what they can achieve.
We believe in high expectations for every child,
excellent teaching in every classroom, and additional
support when needed.
A great education is the foundation of opportunity
for individuals and of stronger economic growth and
prosperity for New Zealand.
That starts in the early years, with children developing
the language, skills and confidence they need for school.

Authorised by J de Joux, ps@national.org.nz

It continues through a clear, knowledge-rich curriculum,
effective teaching, regular assessment, and warm,
dry classrooms.
It means parents knowing how their child is progressing,
teachers having the training and resources to teach
well, and young people leaving school with credible
qualifications and pathways into further study, training
and employment.
Over the past three years, National has begun a
transformation of education. We have restored a focus
on the basics and backed teachers with the tools to
deliver them.
Encouraging results are beginning to emerge. Our
next term will build on that foundation: helping children
arrive at school Set Up for Success and giving them
More Time Learning once they get there.

1. Reforms to date
When National came into Government, too many
children were missing school or reaching secondary
school without strong foundations in reading, writing
and mathematics. The curriculum lacked clarity,
assessment was inconsistent, and teachers were too
often left without the resources and specialist support
they needed.
The warning signs had been clear for years.
New Zealand’s PISA mathematics score fell from

523 in 2003 to 479 in 2022 equating to a loss of
two years of learning for our 15-year-olds in 2022
compared to 15-year-olds in 2003.
Our response has been to put ambition, achievement
and evidence at the centre of the education system,
with a target of 80 per cent of Year 8 students at
or above the expected level in reading, writing and
mathematics by 2030.

Teaching the Basics Brilliantly
Our focus

What we have delivered or funded

Strong foundations

An hour a day of reading, writing and mathematics; structured literacy
and a new mathematics curriculum.

Practical classroom resources

More than one million mathematics books and resources, alongside
decodable readers, teacher guides and curriculum support.

Clear information for parents

20- and 40-week phonics checks and twice-yearly assessment in
reading, writing and mathematics for Years 3–8.

Support where it is needed

Nearly $750 million for the largest expansion of learning support in a
generation, alongside targeted literacy and mathematics intervention.

Better places to learn

Around $2.7 billion across three Budgets for school property, with nearly
1,600 additional classrooms and learning spaces fully funded.

Focused classrooms

Phones away during the school day, and end to open plan classrooms
and a renewed focus on attendance and learning.

A clear, knowledge-rich national
curriculum

Knowing how every child is
progressing

National has rebuilt the curriculum around the
knowledge and skills children should learn, year by
year. Internationally benchmarked content and clear
progressions give teachers, parents and students
greater certainty about what success looks like.

Parents deserve clear information about their child’s
learning. Teachers need to identify gaps early and
know what to teach next. National has made regular
assessment and clear reporting a core part of the
education system.

New primary English and mathematics content
was introduced from the beginning of 2025. We
have developed the wider Years 0–13 curriculum
and are supporting implementation with practical
teaching materials.

• Phonics checks at 20 and 40 weeks of schooling
to identify children who need additional reading
support.

Maths workbooks, textbooks and teacher guides, literacy
resources, science and music kits, and lesson-planning
support help teachers spend more time teaching.
A nationally consistent curriculum gives every child
access to a world-leading education, wherever they live
and whichever school they attend.

Transforming reading, writing and
mathematics
We have required an hour a day each of reading,
writing and mathematics in primary and intermediate
schools and mandated structured literacy, including
phonics.
Children are explicitly taught the building blocks of
reading, alongside vocabulary, fluency, comprehension,
spelling, and writing.
We have invested in teacher training, decodable books,
and classroom resources to make these changes
work. Structured mathematics gives children a clear
sequence of learning and the practice they need to
master essential skills.
For children who need additional help, we have expanded
structured literacy intervention and mathematics support.
Intensive small-group teaching in reading and maths,
together with writing and mathematics acceleration
programmes give students the opportunity to catch
up before gaps become entrenched.

• Twice-yearly assessment in reading, writing, and
mathematics for Years 3–8 provides a consistent
picture of progress.
• The free SMART assessment tool supports teachers
with marking and reporting, alongside the option of
using PAT.
• Early mathematics checks, including the Year 2
numeracy check and Year 5 multiplication and division
check, strengthen our focus on essential skills.
• The Parent Portal gives families practical guidance
and resources to support learning at home.
The Curriculum Insights and Progress Study now
measures reading, writing and mathematics annually
at Years 3, 6 and 8. This gives New Zealand a clearer
national picture and helps direct support to the
students that need it most.

Backing teachers and school leaders
National has refocused professional development on
literacy, mathematics and assessment, strengthened
expectations for initial teacher education, and invested
in support for aspiring and new principals.
We have expanded opportunities to train in schools
so more New Zealanders can learn on the job. From
2027, the School On-site Teacher Training programme
will offer up to 660 places, rising to 704 each year from
2028, with a focus on secondary teaching where the
need is greatest. Participants will receive a $20,000
grant from next year.

We are also helping with the cost of teacher registration
and practicing certificates through to 2028. Stronger
subject knowledge, an understanding of the science of
learning and practical classroom preparation will help
ensure beginning teachers are ready to succeed.

The largest expansion of learning
support in a generation
National has invested nearly three-quarters of a billion
dollars in learning support. High expectations must be
matched by the help children need to meet them.
• Learning Support Coordinators for all schools with
Year 1–8 students from 2028.
• More than 560 additional early-intervention teachers
and specialists, and learning support extended from
ECE through to the end of Year 1.
• Guaranteed, uncapped funding for every child
verified for the Ongoing Resourcing Scheme.
• 1000 specialist places at any one time provided by
the private sector to ease pressure on waitlists.
• Additional teacher-aide hours and training to
support children with behavioural, emotional and
neurodiverse needs – building to two million extra
hours every year from 2028.
• Funding for three new special schools and 142
specialist classrooms, alongside accessibility
improvements.
This expansion will help identify needs sooner, support
families earlier and give teachers greater access to
specialist expertise.

Warm, dry classrooms and better
value for school property
Doing the basics brilliantly also means providing safe,
warm, and dry classrooms. National inherited 352
school property projects without the funding to deliver
them and classrooms costing around $1.2 million each.
We commissioned an inquiry and changed how school
property is planned, funded, and delivered.
Across three Budgets, this Government has invested
around $2.7 billion in school property. Nearly 1,600
additional classrooms and learning spaces have been
fully funded, providing more than 23,000 additional
student places. In 2024, 583 classrooms were
delivered, 31 per cent more than in 2023.
Repeatable designs and offsite construction have
brought the cost of most classrooms below $650,000,
close to half the inherited cost. More than $330 million
saved through this approach has been reinvested in
school property.
Maintenance funding has increased by $880 million
over our first two Budgets, more than twice the
previous 6 years combined. We have raised the base
rate for five-year property funding by 50 per cent,
from $30 to $45 per square metre, and doubled the
minimum allocation for small schools from $45,000 to
$90,000 as schools enter their new funding cycles.
The New Zealand School Property Agency began
operating on 1 October 2026. Its dedicated board brings
commercial and construction expertise to building,
managing and maintaining school property, supporting
a long-term approach that gives school communities
greater certainty and drives better value for money.

Credible qualifications and pathways
for young people
National is replacing NCEA with qualifications that
parents, employers and tertiary providers can trust.
A clear senior secondary curriculum and stronger
subject-based assessment will give students the
knowledge and skills they need for their next step.
The new Foundational Award in literacy and numeracy
will be introduced at Year 11 in 2028, followed by the
New Zealand Certificate of Education at Year 12 in
2029 and the New Zealand Advanced Certificate of
Education at Year 13 in 2030.
Nine new industry-led subjects will strengthen
vocational pathways and connect school learning
with the world of work. We are also expanding Trades
Academies, with places set to nearly double to 20,000
by 2030. Young people should have rigorous, credible
options that match their strengths and aspirations.

Results: raising achievement
There is still a very long way to go, but the evidence is
beginning to show an encouraging change in direction.
Teachers and school leaders are putting the reforms
into practice, and children are starting to benefit.

Curriculum Insights: improvements in primary
mathematics and writing
The 2025 Curriculum Insights and Progress Study
found statistically significant improvements at Year 6.
The proportion meeting or exceeding expectations rose
from 30 to 36 per cent in mathematics and from 33 to
38 per cent in writing: gains of six and five percentage

points respectively. Reading results were broadly stable
but early phonices results in year one and two were
encouraging. These findings show both the progress
being made and why our work must continue.

Phonics: stronger foundations from the start
In the first year of national phonics checks, the
proportion of children at or above expectations after
20 weeks at school rose from 36 per cent in Term 1 to
58 per cent in Term 3 of 2025.
These checks help teachers identify children who need
support early and show encouraging progress in the
foundations of reading.

PISA: a narrowing equity gap
PISA 2025 shows New Zealand remains above the
OECD average in reading, mathematics and science, with
overall achievement stabilising after years of decline.
Most encouragingly, the gap between advantaged
and disadvantaged students narrowed in all three
subjects, driven by gains among students from the
most disadvantaged backgrounds.
Those students made gains equivalent to around a year
of learning in science, three terms in mathematics and
six months in reading.
These are the first positive results across the education
system we have seen in a very long time. While they
are only early indicators, we cannot risk losing this
progress. The reforms need time to embed, and
teachers need continued support to deliver them.
National will stay the course, build on what is working
and keep raising achievement for every child.

2.  Our 2026 policy: Set Up for Success
Every parent wants their child to start school ready
to learn, ready to participate and confident about
the next step. The early years lay the foundations
for everything that follows. National’s Set Up for
Success policy will give parents and educators a
clearer, shared picture of the knowledge, skills and
developmental milestones children should be building
before school.

Clearer milestones and earlier support
National will establish clearer developmental
milestones throughout early childhood education and
require progress to be reported to parents. Families
should know what their child is learning, how they are
progressing, and how they can help at home.

Clearer expectations will make it easier to recognise
when a child needs additional help, provide that
support earlier and strengthen the transition from
early childhood education to school.

Where additional support is needed, children will
be connected with the expanded Early Intervention
Service. Earlier identification and a stronger handover
to school will help more children get the right support
at the right time.

A School Start Check for every child

More interaction, fewer screens

National will introduce a School Start Check, completed
in early childhood education before a child starts
school, or on school entry for children who have not
had one. It will help parents, early childhood educators,
and schools understand each child’s strengths and
where additional support is needed.

Technology has a place, but young children need rich
language, conversation, books, movement, and direct
interaction with adults and other children to build
strong foundations for learning.

The check will cover foundations such as oral
language, following instructions, recognising
their name, pencil grip and early letter formation,
interacting with others and taking turns, and growing
independence in self-care, including toileting. Children
with additional needs will be supported according to
their circumstances.

A re-elected National government will introduce:
• No screens or individual devices use in early
childhood education.
• Tight limits on screen and individual-device use
in Years 1–3, with age-appropriate limits for older
primary students.
• Make the writing component of twice-yearly primary
assessments completed on paper.
Set Up for Success will give parents greater clarity,
educators shared expectations and children a stronger
start to their school journey.

3.  Our 2026 policy: More Time Learning
National will give more young people time to build
the knowledge and skills they need for a successful
future, and make the school calendar more consistent
for families.

Lifting school leaving requirements
National will require students to stay at school until they
complete Year 11 or turn 16, whichever is later.
Currently, students can leave school when they turn 16.
Many reach that birthday during Year 11, allowing them
to leave before completing Year 11.
For these students, this will mean staying until the end
of Year 11. Those who turn 16 in Year 12 will still need to
stay until they turn 16.
We are replacing NCEA, beginning in 2028, with new
qualifications backed by a clear senior secondary
curriculum and stronger subject-based assessment.
Our expectation is clear. Students should complete a
full Year 11 of compulsory science, English and maths,
and have the opportunity to gain the new Foundational
Award in literacy and numeracy.

The existing early leaving exemption will remain for
a very small number of students each year.
Strong literacy and numeracy skills support employment
and further learning. Completing Year 11 gives students
the opportunity to build those skills and gain the
Foundational Award.

Consistent school dates and more
time learning
National will set consistent school start and finish dates.
Parents have told us how frustrating different dates can
be, leaving families juggling childcare and taking extra
leave from work.

Building on our progress
Set Up for Success will help children arrive at school
ready to learn. More Time Learning will build on that
start, raising achievement, closing the equity gap and
giving every young person the opportunity to succeed
at school and go on to live the life they want.

# National's Fiscal Plan

Published by the New Zealand National Party as a PDF policy document. Source: <https://assets.national.org.nz/web/prod/National%27s%20Fiscal%20Plan.pdf?v=1791759269>.
The text below is the verbatim text layer of the PDF extracted with `pdftotext` (reading order). Line breaks follow the
PDF; tables and multi-column layouts may read out of order in this section, so a second rendering that preserves the
page layout (`pdftotext -layout`) follows it. Nothing has been added, removed or paraphrased.

## Full text (reading order)

National’s plan for the government’s books
Maintaining a strong set of government books matters
for New Zealanders. It is essential to delivering lasting
prosperity for New Zealand and is one of the most
practical things a government can do for household
budgets.
Spending restraint helps take pressure off inflation and
keep taxes low. When government debt is at moderate
levels, interest rates are lower, the cost of financing this
debt is less, and New Zealand has fiscal headroom when
the next earthquake, severe weather event or global
economic shock hits us.
When National entered government in 2023, we
inherited a very difficult set of books, with ongoing
budget deficits. Over the previous six years, government
spending had gone up 70 per cent, and government
debt had tripled. The interest costs on this debt were
rising fast, and today taxpayers are still paying the
equivalent of four Dunedin Hospitals every year just to
cover them.
National introduced much-needed fiscal discipline. We
did so by carefully prioritising where taxpayers’ money
is spent, stopping spending in low-value areas and
reinvesting it in the frontline services New Zealanders
rely on such as hospitals and schools. In total, we have
reprioritised around $50 billion over three Budgets to
invest in frontline services, rather than increasing taxes
to find the revenue.

Operating and capital allowances
National will continue with $2.4 billion operating
allowances for future Budgets. Operating allowances are
the maximum amount of net new operating funding – on
average, per annum – the government intends to spend
in each Budget, in areas that are under its direct control.
$2.4 billion makes for very tight allowances, but National
has shown in its three Budgets so far that it can manage
within these.
In contrast, new operating spending in the previous
Government’s last two Budgets averaged $7.2 billion.
National will also continue with $3.5 billion capital
allowances for Budgets 2027 and 2028, and $5 billion
capital allowances thereafter. Capital allowances are
the net new one-off funding the Government intends
to allocate to capital projects in each Budget.

Election commitments
The following table shows how National’s election
commitments fit into these operating and capital
allowances.
By far the biggest commitments are in the health system.
Health policies make up 88 per cent of all National’s
spending commitments, reflecting New Zealand’s ageing
population and National’s focus on delivering quality
health care for all.

As a result of our careful economic management,
independent Treasury forecasts show that overall
government spending is coming down as a proportion
of the economy, a return to surplus is expected soon,
and after next year the government debt curve bends
down rather than up.

A total of $7.5 billion operating is left unallocated over
the four years. This is to cover net new operating
spending in that period, over and above the election
commitments specified in the table. In addition, a total
of $14.2 billion remains to be allocated from capital
allowances in future Budgets.

Under a National Government, this fiscal repair will
continue.

These unallocated amounts from the operating and
capital allowances are there to cover, for example:

A re-elected National Government will:
•

not impose new taxes

•

continue investing in health, schools, law and
order, roads, defence capability and other
frontline services New Zealanders rely on

•

reprioritise spending and show ongoing restraint
so that overall government expenditure comes
down towards 30 per cent of GDP

•

return to surplus in 2028/29 and stay there, and

•

keep government debt on a downward trajectory
towards 40 per cent of GDP and maintain debt
below 40 per cent of GDP
over time

Authorised by J de Joux, ps@national.org.nz

•

any future increases in funding for education,
social services and law and order

•

pay rounds for teachers and police

•

new investments in state highways, hospitals, school
buildings, police stations, courthouses
and defence capability.

National does not need to find any new funding for pay
equity. A contingency for the costs of future pay equity
settlements in the public sector is already in
the accounts. However, Treasury estimates show that
a future government seeking to reinstate the previous,
more expensive pay equity regime would need to
account for around $11 billion in additional costs, over
and above the contingency already set aside for the
current scheme.

next general election.

Tax relief
National recognises that the last few years have been
tough for New Zealand households and businesses. In
2024, the Government adjusted personal income tax
thresholds for the first time in 14 years. Alongside other
increases in government assistance, this delivered
an additional $60 a fortnight on average to around
1.9 million households.
But, as is always the case, inflation and wage growth
mean people are paying a slightly higher proportion of
their income in tax every year. The median full-time wage
and salary earner, for example, is now earning $82,000
a year, which puts them in the second-highest, 33 per
cent, income tax bracket.

While National’s fiscal plan shows a pathway to potential
tax relief for working New Zealanders, now is not the
time to cut taxes. The responsible thing to do now is
reduce debt and invest in frontline services, especially
health and infrastructure.
That approach means future generations are not left
paying off debt. It strengthens New Zealand’s resilience
to global shocks and gets the balance right between
economic responsibility and investing in the services
people rely on.
Once the books are back in the black and surpluses are
growing, a National Government will be in a position
to consider tax relief. But the priority is making the
forecasts a reality by delivering a return to surplus and
less debt.
