# National's Fishing Policy_2

Published by the New Zealand National Party as a PDF policy document. Source: <https://assets.national.org.nz/web/prod/National%27s%20Fishing%20Policy_2.pdf?v=1791665038>.
The text below is the verbatim text layer of the PDF extracted with `pdftotext` (reading order). Line breaks follow the
PDF; tables and multi-column layouts may read out of order in this section, so a second rendering that preserves the
page layout (`pdftotext -layout`) follows it. Nothing has been added, removed or paraphrased.

## Full text (reading order)

Building the Future:

Fishing

The health of our ocean matters to every New Zealander.
It is part of who we are, provides us food, recreation,
well-being, and a place for families and communities
to connect.
For a family in Auckland, it might mean taking the tinny
out from Half Moon Bay on a summer morning to try
for a snapper. For a group of friends in Whakatāne
or Gisborne, it might mean heading out to get a few
kingis. For a fishing crew in Nelson, it’s their job and
their income.
Recreational fishing generates around $1.7 billion of
economic activity per year, the seafood industry’s
economic output is around $6.4 billion per year, and
the annual worth of the boating and marine industry is
around $3 billion.
We must strike the balance between environmental,
recreational, customary and commercial interests and
look after the long-term health of the whole ocean. We
need to understand the asset, manage it well, and hand
it on to future generations in better condition than we
found it.
In the last three years we have passed the Hauraki
Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Act 2025,
the most significant expansion of marine protection
in more than a decade. And we have delivered
five new marine reserves as part of the South-East
Marine Protection Network, Te Au Roa o Te Rakihouia
protecting 308 square kilometres of unique marine
habitat and sea life.

Authorised by J de Joux, ps@national.org.nz

We want fish stocks managed at healthy and abundant
levels, not simply kept above minimum sustainability
limits. Our decisions will be guided by the best available
science, data and evidence, while upholding property
rights and the Crown’s Treaty settlement obligations.

A re-elected National Government will:
1.

Protect the Hauraki Gulf – including a new
Marine Reserve off Waiheke Island, further
expand the Goat Island Marine Reserve,
and banning commercial fishing in High
Protection Areas.

2. Support recreational fishers – including
ensuring fishers have a seat at the table
in fishing reforms, and preventing the
commercial sale of Marlin.
3. Preserve our seamounts – including
reviewing bottom trawling with an aim to
increase protections from 32% to 50% of our
EEZ by 2040.
4. Invest in innovation – with a $20 million Fish
Tech Innovation Fund in partnership with the
seafood sector.
5. Take an inclusive and principled approach to
fisheries management reform.
6. Ratify the High Seas Treaty in the next term
of Government.

1. Protecting the Hauraki Gulf
The Hauraki Gulf is loved by many Kiwis. It is
a place to swim, boat and fish. It is also a vital
hub for tourism, transport and commercial activity.
It is central to Auckland’s identity and way of life,
and National understands the strength of
that connection.
Since coming into Government, we have passed
the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection
Act 2025, delivering the most significant expansion
of marine protection in more than a decade by
tripling marine protection. The Act recognises the
Gulf’s importance to mana whenua, recreational
and commercial fishers, tourism operators and
communities across the Auckland region. It
expands two existing marine reserves, creates
five new Seafloor Protection Areas and 12 new
High Protection Areas.
The decision to allow bottom trawling in some
designated trawl corridors in the Gulf has been
controversial. While this has provided limited access
to the commercial sector, the widespread concern
of environmental groups and the recreational fishing
population has not gone unheard. So, we will review
that also. We believe a consistent approach to
protection of the Gulf is best for all users and that
removing exceptions to the original intent of the
protections is needed.
We have invested in removing the kina barrens to
help restore the kelp forests in the Hauraki Gulf, which
are critical to a healthy ocean. National will build on
these protections.

National believe the waters of the Gulf are best utilised
by those who fish, dive, swim, or collect kaimoana
recreationally. It is Auckland’s playground and the
centrepiece of some of New Zealand’s most iconic
aquatic events.

A re-elected National Party will:
•

Establish the Hākaimangō-Matiatia Marine
Reserve off Waiheke Island, a new 23.5km2
marine protected area in the Hauraki Gulf
Marine Park.

•

Further expand the size of the Goat Island
/ Te Hāwere-a-Maki Marine Reserve, home
to one of the most diverse marine habitats in
the country and an educational, scientific and
tourism hub with 350,000 visitors per year.

•

Ban commercial fishing in the Hauraki Gulf’s
High Protection Areas by removing the
exemptions for ringnet fishers.

•

Keep the ban on harvesting shellfish
and marine species from rockpools and
continue to impose higher penalties and
strict enforcement. National will keep this
ban in place as long as necessary for these
ecosystems to recover and won’t support it
being removed before then.

•

Develop a sustainable fisheries plan in
the wider Hauraki Gulf Marine Park in
partnership with industry and interested
stakeholders, review bottom trawling
corridors, incorporating new innovation and
methodologies and updated environmental
biomass data.

2. Supporting recreational fishers
Enjoying time on the water and catching a feed
is part of what makes us Kiwis. At least 600,000
New Zealanders fish recreationally, now and then.
We are fortunate to have a charter fishing industry
that drives local coastal economies, provides expert
access to deep-water fishing grounds, and makes
recreational boating accessible to everyday kiwis
and our tourists.
Too often we only identify serious problems once a
stock has already declined to a level where drastic
restrictions are required. National will work with
the wider fishing sector to investigate how we can
improve fisheries data in New Zealand. A more
proactive management system would mean that
emerging stock pressures should be identified
earlier, and management responses occur sooner.
As a result, fish stocks will remain healthy and
productive for future generations. Better information
would mean less risk of stock collapse, and more
certainty for recreational fishers, commercial
operators, iwi and our coastal communities.
National will protect the marine environment so
it keeps providing for recreational sport and
customary fishers.

A re-elected National Party will:
•

Rule out a licence for recreational sea fishing.
Fishing for a feed is a Kiwi right. We will not
introduce or require a licence or permit for
recreational fishing in the sea. Existing licences
for freshwater sports fish are not affected.

•

Support the Billfish Accord. National will
prevent the commercial sale of Marlin, so it
stays as a world-class sport fishery.

•

Increase penalties and enforcement,
including instant fines for those exceeding
catch limits. If we want our fish to be there for
our children and grandchildren, we all need
to take only what we need and stick to the
limits. Those who don’t follow the rules – no
matter whether customary, recreational or
commercial – should face consequences.

•

National will increase Honorary Fisheries
Officers to 200 to crack down on illegal
fishing and strengthen patrols and targeted
enforcement to catch offenders and protect
our fisheries. Higher fines reinvested into their
monitoring and enforcement training programs.

Honorary Fishery Officers have similar powers to paid fishery officers,
including the authority to search, question and seize. They also help educate
recreational fishers about the rules. Most spend more than 100 hours a year
in the role, and together they complete between 11,000 to 14,000 inspections
each year, around 40 percent of recreational compliance work.

3.	 Protecting our Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) and seamounts
There are over 1,900 seamounts and seamount-like
features in New Zealand’s EEZ waters. They support
diverse ecosystems and rare species such as stony
corals, black corals, gorgonian corals and hydrocorals.
Over 70,000 people signed the Live Ocean petition
calling for greater protection for seamounts. National
will act to protect more of these biodiversity hotspots
in our EEZ through a targeted, balanced and scienceled approach.
Spatial management measures will seek to protect
habitats and ecological values that are vulnerable,
while avoiding unnecessary impacts on the value
of the existing fishing catch, and the Crown’s Treaty
settlement obligations with regard to the Fisheries
Settlement. Our proposed approach will retain the
flexibility to review settings as scientific understanding,
environmental conditions and fisheries change over
time rather than applying a blanket ban.
Transparent, reliable data is essential to public
confidence in how much fish is harvested and how our
fisheries are managed. We must balance commercial,

recreational and customary interests while protecting
this shared resource for future generations. Commercial
fishing is a significant contributor to New Zealand’s
economy, earning close to $2 billion in exports each
year and supporting 9000 jobs and incomes in
regional communities.

A re-elected National Party will:
•

Increase protection of the EEZ and preserve
of our seamounts with an aim to increase
protected areas from 32% to 50% by 2040.

•

Prioritise vulnerable corals and seamounts
for protection based on a balanced and
science-led approach.

•

Uphold the Crown’s Treaty fisheries
settlement obligations.

Seamounts and seamount-like features include seamounts defined as
submarine features greater than 1000m in height from base to peak, as well
as other submarine features, such as underwater mounts of lesser elevations,
including hills, knolls, banks, rises and peaks along oceanic ridge systems
greater than 100m in height.

4.	 $20 million Fish Tech Innovation Fund
Commercial fishing is an important part of
New Zealand’s economy. It supports thousands of
jobs in coastal communities and provides high-quality,
locally caught seafood for New Zealanders and export
markets alike, with close to $2 billion in annual export
earnings. While some people catch their own fish,
most New Zealanders enjoy seafood from their local
supermarket or fish and chip shop. Ensuring the longterm sustainability of our fisheries is critical for both
coastal communities and consumers.

The Fund will be targeted towards better fishing gear
and practices, including reducing the impact of bottom
trawling. It will also target science and research into
biomass data to improve the responsiveness of the
Quota Management System.

Mitigation technology, properly designed and properly
adopted, can change outcomes. There is good
evidence this approach works. Since 1 October 2024,
New Zealand’s surface longline vessels have been
required to use hook-shielding devices or the “three
out of three” seabird mitigation measures: tori lines,
setting lines at night, and weighted lines. Seabird
captures across all fishing methods fell to 505 in the
third quarter of 2025–26, down from 767 in the same
period a year earlier.

Fish Tech Innovation Fund

National will establish the Fish Tech Innovation Fund
in partnership with the seafood sector, matching
dollar-for-dollar any investment from the sector,
up to $10 million.

By backing science and innovation and working with
the sector, we can improve environmental outcomes
while supporting a sustainable and productive
fishing industry.

Total fund

$20 million

Government

$10 million over four years (from the
Primary Sector Growth Fund)

Seafood sector

$10 million, matched dollar for dollar

Focus

Better fishing gear and methods, aiming
for less seabed contact and less bycatch

A re-elected National Party will:
•

Establish a $20 million Fish Tech Innovation
Fund with the seafood sector to support new
innovation that reduces seabed contact and
protects sensitive habitats.

5.	 Sensible fisheries
management reforms

6.	 High Seas Treaty and
International Agreements

National will deliver better ecosystem outcomes
through fisheries law reform by making sure our
legislation has the confidence of New Zealanders.
Fisheries management and the Quota Management
System must be fit for purpose and effective in a
changing climate.

Many of the fish stocks we depend on move across
national boundaries and into the high seas. That gives
New Zealand a strong interest in international fisheries
agreements that work.

National will convene a multi-stakeholder forum
to properly examine and test all aspects of the
proposed Fisheries Amendment Bill in order to
achieve a balanced and acceptable package of
fisheries reform legislation.

National support the following principles
for any fisheries reform:
•

Transparent data is critical to building community
trust in how much we harvest and how we manage
our fisheries.

•

Improving the effectiveness of the Quota
Management System should be central to the
reforms.

•

Commercial and recreational interests must be
balanced in a way that protects this asset for those
who come after us.

The High Seas Treaty, formally the Agreement on
Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ),
came into force on 17 January 2026. It makes it
possible to set up marine protected areas in the high
seas, regulate the use of marine genetic resources, and
assess the environmental impact of current and future
human activity.
So far 103 Parties have ratified the Agreement and
145 countries have signed it. New Zealand has signed
but not yet ratified. A re-elected National Party would
ratify it.

A re-elected National Party will:
•

Ratify the High Seas Treaty in the next term
of Government.

# National's Plan for Hunting and Fishing

Published by the New Zealand National Party as a PDF policy document. Source: <https://assets.national.org.nz/web/prod/National%27s%20Plan%20for%20Hunting%20and%20Fishing.pdf?v=1785105126>.
The text below is the verbatim text layer of the PDF extracted with `pdftotext` (reading order). Line breaks follow the
PDF; tables and multi-column layouts may read out of order in this section, so a second rendering that preserves the
page layout (`pdftotext -layout`) follows it. Nothing has been added, removed or paraphrased.

## Full text (reading order)

Building the Future: Our Plan for Hunting
and Fishing
Hunting and fishing are part of the Kiwi way of life. They put food on the table,
bring families and communities together, support regional jobs and tourism,
and connect New Zealanders with the outdoors.
Over this term, National has given hunters and fishers
a stronger voice in government and delivered practical
progress to improve access and game management.
A re-elected National Government will build on this by:
•

recognising valued introduced species in law;

•

  stablishing a clearer framework for wild animal
e
management;

•

s  trengthening the Game Animal Council and
modernise Fish & Game;

•

  xpanding hunter-led conservation and protect
e
recreational access; and

•

 growing hunting-related jobs and exports.

Recognising valued introduced species
New Zealand’s wild animals are managed through
a fragmented collection of laws, agencies and plans.
Responsibilities are often unclear, while species valued
by hunters, anglers and local communities can be
treated simply as pests.
A re-elected National Government will establish a
coordinated wild animal management framework and
formally recognise valued introduced species in law.
This will include introduced species that provide
recreational, economic, environmental or cultural value
to New Zealanders. They will not be treated as pests
by default simply because they were introduced.
Management will remain practical and evidence
based. Action will still be taken where populations
cause unacceptable environmental damage,
but species will be managed according to
local conditions.

Strengthen the Game Animal Council and Fish
& Game
National will strengthen the Game Animal Council
as the statutory manager of valued game animals.
The Council will have a clearer role in managing
herds of special interest, developing national and
regional game animal management plans, and
supporting practical hunter-led conservation. It
will also help coordinate recreational, guided and
commercial hunting on public conservation land,
improving monitoring and reducing conflict between
different users.
National will also pass legislation to modernise Fish
& Game New Zealand. The reforms will simplify
administration, strengthen accountability to licence
holders and ensure resources are directed to the
regions, habitats and fisheries where they are
most needed.
Expand hunter-led conservation
This term, National delivered two herds of special
interest. This reflects that National believes that
hunters should play a greater role in managing
animal populations and protecting the places in
which they hunt.
A re-elected National Government will seek proposals
for additional herds of special interest, building on
the wapiti and sika models. The final selections will
be evidence-based and require strong local and
hunter support.
National will also replace the outdated Tahr Control
Plan 1993 with a modern management plan developed
alongside the tahr hunting community.

Protect recreational access
Access to public land, rivers, lakes and the coast
is fundamental to hunting and fishing. National
recognises this, this is why National launched an
Access Charter to ensure better access for recreational
hunting and fishing on public conservation land across
New Zealand.
A re-elected National will strengthen the Charter by
adding the Game Animal Council, Land Information
New Zealand and the Overseas Investment Office
as signatories.
We will change the current policy that generally
prevents recreational hunting on Crown land
managed by Land Information New Zealand.
Suitable Crown land that would ordinarily be
accessible to the public will be opened for hunting and
fishing under rules similar to those applying on public
conservation land. Existing arrangements for Crown
pastoral leases and other land that is not ordinarily
publicly accessible will remain unchanged.
National will also ensure existing recreational access
is protected when sensitive land is purchased by
overseas investors and improved where practical.
Growing hunting-related jobs and exports
Hunting supports the economy. guides, outfitters,
taxidermists, accommodation providers, tourism
operators and rural businesses throughout regional
New Zealand.
National will promote New Zealand’s premium
guided-hunting offer in key overseas markets and
simplify trophy-export permits, veterinary certification,
taxidermy requirements and customs processes.
National will also develop clearer rules for recreational
hunting, guided hunting, aerial hunting and commercial
wild animal recovery. These activities serve different
purposes and should be managed in ways that reduce
conflict and protect conservation, recreational and
economic outcomes.

Authorised by J de Joux, ps@national.org.nz

Other initiatives to ensure as many New Zealanders
can go hunting and fishing as possible
Investigate options for sustainable funding of national
hunter training programmes, alongside the Firearms
Safety Authority, to help deliver the training and
education of the next generation of hunters.
Direct Fish and Game regions to review their existing
regional boundaries to better align with
the Government’s Resource Management Act and
local government reorganisation reforms, as well as
to resolve existing issues in cross-boundary
catchment management.
Partner with DOC and community organisations to
maintain and enhance access to public conservation
huts and facilities.
Give hunters and fishers a voice by replacing an
existing Conservation Authority and Conservation
Board seat with a permanent representative from the
hunting and fishing sector.
Ensure that the Outdoor Access Commission’s
public access maps are considered as part of the
Government’s investment into a new planning and
environmental online management system.
Simplify the consenting system for shooting ranges
to more accurately reflect a risk-based approach
and implement a pre-existing right to operate where
there is no ability to complain if someone moves to
the nuisance.
Pilot a Government-backed biodiversity credit
to recognise the environmental benefits of
hunter-led conservation.

# National’s plan for Kiwi kids

Published by the New Zealand National Party as a PDF policy document. Source: <https://assets.national.org.nz/web/prod/National%E2%80%99s%20plan%20for%20Kiwi%20kids.pdf?v=1792535730>.
The text below is the verbatim text layer of the PDF extracted with `pdftotext` (reading order). Line breaks follow the
PDF; tables and multi-column layouts may read out of order in this section, so a second rendering that preserves the

## Full text (reading order)

Fixing the Basics. Building the Future.

National’s plan for
Kiwi kids

Fixing the Basics. Building the Future.

National’s plan for Kiwi kids
From Monday 26 October, Kiwis will be able to vote
on New Zealand’s future.
National has a plan to help you secure your future,
whether you’re a young person starting out, a parent
raising your family, or in your retirement.
This election, there is a clear choice between sticking
with National’s plan for a more secure future, no matter
the stage of your life, with a growing economy, less
debt, more jobs and higher wages.
Or going back to Labour – propped up by the Greens,
Te Pati Maori and TOP – who will undo the progress
New Zealand has made over the last three years,
leaving you to pay for it through at least nine new
taxes costing households $2,263 each year.

Authorised by J de Joux, ps@national.org.nz

Under our plan for Kiwi kids, every child will get the
best possible start in life. By sticking to National’s
plan, we will deliver a future where children get the
education they need to set them up for success; and
an economy that has been responsibly managed so
they are not burdened with our debt.
Labour will undo the progress we have made
in education by removing the requirement to
teach one hour a day of reading, writing and
maths, scrapping twice yearly assessments in
Primary Schools, and undoing NCEA changes.

What we’ve delivered to date
Improved childhood immunisation. Lifted immunisation
rates to 92 per cent from 77 per cent.
Strong foundations. An hour a day of reading,
writing and mathematics; structured literacy and
a new mathematics curriculum.
Practical classroom resources. More than
one million mathematics books and resources,
alongside decodable readers, teacher guides
and curriculum support.
Clear information for parents. 20- and 40-week
phonics checks and twice-yearly assessment in
reading, writing and mathematics for Years 3–8.
Support where it’s needed. Nearly $750 million
for the largest expansion of learning support in
a generation, alongside targeted literacy and
mathematics intervention.
Better places to learn. Around $2.7 billion across
three Budgets for school property, with nearly
1,600 additional classrooms and learning spaces
fully funded.
Focused classrooms. Cell phones banned
during the school day. An end to open plan
classrooms and a renewed focus on attendance
and learning.

Better vocational education. National has restructured
the vocational education system to give regions
and industry a greater role in training decisions,
so young people can train for real jobs relevant to
their community.
A focus on improving child safety by implementing
all of the recommendations in the Dame Karen
Poutasi Review.

The results so far
The latest Progressive Achievement Test (PAT) data,
shows a significant improvement in mathematics,
and improvements in reading comprehension
and vocabulary.
The results show primary and intermediate students
made the equivalent of four months’ additional
progress in mathematics between 2024 and 2026,
signalling a turnaround in achievement.
The results also show statistically significant
improvements in reading comprehension and
vocabulary, equivalent to approximately one month’s
additional progress in each area over the last year.
After a prolonged period of declining reading
results, we are finally seeing a statistically
significant improvement.

Our 2026 election policies for Kiwi kids
• $1,500 Baby Boost and automatic enrolment in
KiwiSaver. From 1 July 2027, National will enrol
every child born into KiwiSaver at birth and give
them a $1,500 Baby Boost payment to kickstart their
retirement savings, which will see them benefit from
decades of compounding returns.
• End screen use in ECE and tightly limit it in primary
schools (years 1-3). Technology still has a place
in education, but it should enhance learning, not
become the default way children learn. We will also
place a renewed emphasis on handwriting because
it is an important part of learning to read and write.
• Require ECEs to report on children’s progress
against developmental milestones so you can see
how your child is progressing.
• Introduce a School Start Check at ECE before
children transition to primary school.
• Clearer developmental milestones throughout ECE
and report this progress to parents.

• Replace NCEA with a new national qualification
system. We are replacing NCEA, beginning in
2028, with new qualifications backed by a clear
senior secondary curriculum and stronger
subject-based assessment.
• Lifting the school leaving age. National will
require students to stay at school until they
complete Year 11 or turn 16, whichever is later.
• Consistent school dates. National will set consistent
school start and finish dates. Parents have told us
how frustrating different dates can be, leaving families
juggling childcare and taking extra leave from work.
• Ban under-16s from social media. To protect
children from online harm.
• More warm dry classrooms. Installing acoustic
panels, ceiling insulation bales, and carpet with
built-in underlay across schools nationwide to
improve warmth and noise reduction.

• Keep teaching the basics brilliantly. One hour
of reading, writing and maths every day; the core
learning areas to help raise achievement and
give every young New Zealander the opportunity
to succeed.

• Learning support coordinators in all schools and
more teacher aides. Delivering the most substantial
boost to learning support in a generation with
substantial increases to teacher aide hours and
providing Learning Support Co-ordinators for all
schools with Year 1-8 students.

• Accelerated Maths. National will expand the Year
7-10 Maths Acceleration Programme by an additional
40,000 students to reach 128,000 students across
three years.

• Expand trades training. To help young people
move into apprenticeships, employment and
other structured pathways from education
into employment.

Fixing the Basics. Building the Future. Party Vote National.

National’s plan for
Retirement

Fixing the Basics. Building the Future.

National’s plan for Retirement
Seniors have spent a lifetime contributing to
New Zealand, and they deserve the security,
respect, and opportunities to enjoy the retirement
they have earned.
From Monday 26 October, Kiwi seniors will be able
to vote on New Zealand’s future.
National is committed to recognising all that our
older generations have given to this country and
supporting them in retirement and into their old age. As
a society, we must ensure you feel included and valued
to live with dignity, respect and the security you deserve.
This election, there is a clear choice between sticking
with National’s plan for a more secure future, no matter
the stage of your life, with a growing economy, less
debt, more jobs and higher wages.
Or going back to Labour – propped up by the Greens,
Te Pāti Māori and TOP – who will undo the progress
New Zealand has made over the last three years,
leaving you to pay for it through at least nine new
taxes costing households $2,263 each year.
Many retirees have spent a lifetime paying off
their homes or have bought a rental property to top
up their Super to support them in retirement. Now,
these investments are at risk with TOP’s proposed
Land Tax – and Labour’s own Capital Gains Tax.

Authorised by J de Joux, ps@national.org.nz

The Land Tax would mean that if you have $500,000
worth of land in an urban centre, you will owe $8,750
a year in extra tax, on top of your rates bill.
And Labour’s Capital Gains Tax means an extra 28 per
cent could be taken off investments that have built your
retirement security.
There is no new money being proposed for seniors
to help offset these costs, leaving you thousands of
dollars worse off.
It’s unfair, and National won’t let it happen.
Don’t put it all at risk. By sticking to National’s plan,
we will deliver a better future for retirees. A future
where your finances are protected. A future where
we invest responsibly in health, so you have peace
of mind knowing you’ll get the care you need when
you need it.
A Labour-led coalition will undo the progress
we’ve made, putting our economy and your
savings at risk with reckless spending, more
borrowing and higher taxes; leaving no money
to invest in the frontline services you need.

National’s track record…
Increased superannuation to give couples an extra
$180 every fortnight in their back pockets.
Helped more seniors with their rates, ensuring
that every SuperGold Card holder earning only
NZ Superannuation, with rates higher than $2000,
can access the full rebate scheme.
Protected the Winter Energy Payment to help
superannuitants with their power bills.
Reduced inflation from record highs under Labour,
by getting government spending under control,
taking pressure off the cost of living.
Froze petrol tax for three years and scrapped the
Auckland Regional Fuel Tax, helping you get to where
you need to go, cheaper.
Made it easier for Kiwis to build a simple granny flat
by removing the need for both building and resource
consents in most cases for units up to 70 square metres,
supporting inter-generational living arrangements.
Progressed an upgrade to the SuperGold Card to
enable seniors to use it as a free, official form of photo
identification, making it easier to access banking, legal
and other essential services.
Invested a record amount in our Health system –
$34.2 billion this year. We are also providing
more elective surgeries like cataracts, hip and
knee replacements to shorten waiting times.
Targeted free prescriptions for seniors and extended
prescriptions for long-term, stable conditions to up to
12 months, saving you time and money.

Funded 66 new medicines, including 33 extra cancer
medicines, thanks to our $604 million funding boost,
with more medicines to come.
Hired over 2,100 new nurses and 900 more doctors,
and introduced a wave of hiring incentives to recruit
more GPs and nurse practitioners.
Provided a 24/7 digital health service so you can
contact a doctor or nurse using your phone, laptop,
or tablet at any time, day or night.
Increased numbers of urgent and after-hours clinics
across the country, including new 24/7 services.
Reduced violent crime and ram raids so you can feel
safer on the streets and in your own home.
Cracked down on gangs, banned gang patches in
public, and gave Police more powers and tools to
tackle criminals.
Introduced tougher sentences and brought back
consequences for crime such as restoring Three Strikes
for repeat offenders.
Ensured your grandchildren get the education
they deserve, requiring all kids to do an hour each
of reading, writing and maths every day at school,
as well as banning cell phones in schools.
Funded more accessible housing, with over
22 per cent of social and affordable houses funded
by this government being accessible, which
benefits seniors.

Our 2026 election policies for seniors
A re-elected National government will:
• Boost seniors housing by ring-fencing at least
20 per cent of all Housing Flexible Fund places
going forward for seniors’ housing – whether that
be affordable rentals (like Abbeyfield), social homes,
or other innovative solutions.
• Expand the granny flat rules so more can be built,
faster and cheaper, by allowing an attached garage
of up to 40sqm in addition to the 70sqm granny flat,
speeding up processing times by requiring PIMs
to be processed within five working days for all
standalone dwellings and limit fees to cost recovery,
removing the requirement for a primary dwelling,
exploring a new licensing class for builders to ensure
quality construction, and allowing tiny homes on
wheels to also access these rules.
• Strengthen protections against elder abuse and
financial exploitation by reviewing the Enduring
Powers of Attorney framework and considering
further measures including law changes to better
protect seniors from economic harm.
• Establish a 0800-SENIORS number, to give seniors
a single free helpline covering any issue to help
them navigate government services and receive
the Government support they are entitled to. The
helpline will sit in MSD and be managed within
existing baselines.

• Improve access to healthcare for seniors by
expanding access to medicines and cancer
screening, including extending free cervical
screening to age 69 and improving access to
breast cancer screening, helping older
New Zealanders stay healthier for longer.
• Increase your KiwiSaver by requiring employers
to continue KiwiSaver contributions for employees
over 65 from 1 July 2027. This change means a
65-year-old earning $70,000 per year in 2027, who
chooses to work three more years and retires at
age 68 will retire with an additional $6300 in 2030.
• Strengthen grocery competition, helping with the
price of food at the checkout by cracking down on
the supermarket duopoly.
• Low interest energy loans so you can install solar,
insulation, heat pumps and home batteries, saving
you money now on your electricity bills.
• Keep council rates affordable by introducing a Rates
Cap and refocus councils on core services.
• No new taxes, protecting your assets from Capital
Gains Tax and a Land Tax, which are two of the nine
new taxes Labour and the left coalition are proposing.
• Protect the country’s finances by returning to
surplus in 2028/29 and government debt below
40 per cent of GDP over time, supporting the funding
of public services.

Fixing the Basics. Building the Future. Party Vote National.

# National's plan for Young Adults

Published by the New Zealand National Party as a PDF policy document. Source: <https://assets.national.org.nz/web/prod/National's%20plan%20for%20Young%20Adults.pdf?v=1792709954>.
The text below is the verbatim text layer of the PDF extracted with `pdftotext` (reading order). Line breaks follow the
PDF; tables and multi-column layouts may read out of order in this section, so a second rendering that preserves the
page layout (`pdftotext -layout`) follows it. Nothing has been added, removed or paraphrased.

## Full text (reading order)

Fixing the Basics. Building the Future.

National’s plan for
Young Adults

Fixing the Basics. Building the Future.

National’s plan for Young Adults
From Monday 26 October, Kiwis will be able to vote
on New Zealand’s future.
National has a plan to help you secure your future,
whether you’re a Kiwi kid, a young person starting
out, a parent raising your family, or in your retirement.
This election, there is a clear choice between sticking
with National’s plan for a more secure future, no matter
the stage of your life, with a growing economy, less
debt, more jobs and higher wages.
Or going back to Labour – propped up by the Greens,
Te Pati Māori and TOP – who will undo the progress
New Zealand has made over the past three years,
leaving you to pay for it through at least nine new
taxes costing households $2,263 each year.

Authorised by J de Joux, ps@national.org.nz

Under our plan for young adults, we’ll deliver a future
where you have the best opportunity to get ahead
in life without having to move abroad. A future with
a stronger economy, meaning more jobs and higher
wages. A future where it is easier to pay off a student
loan and buy your first home. A future where you get
the services you rely on – all with no new taxes.
Labour will undo the progress we’ve made in
the economy and spend recklessly, meaning
more taxes and more borrowing, leaving young
Kiwis to pay off our debt. That will raise inflation,
which in turn leads to higher unemployment and
higher interest rates on your mortgage.

What we’ve delivered to date
Tax relief: National introduced personal income tax
cuts in July 2024, which increased the take home pay
of hard-working Kiwis.
Support for young jobseekers: National introduced
community job coaches for up to 10,000 young
people looking for work. This helps our young people
with career planning, barriers to work and pathways
to employment.
Driver licence assistance: National is helping jobseekers
obtain licences, which is an important employment
requirement in many industries. More than 21,000
young people have already benefitted.

The results so far
National believes a strong economy is the foundation
for a successful life for young people.
We have made a lot of progress. New Zealand is
growing faster than the US, the UK, Canada, and
Australia. Exports are up $20 billion, inflation is down
from a 32-year high, and 220,000 new jobs are
expected with wages growing faster than prices.
More Kiwis are returning home, with a 14 per cent
increase in Kiwis moving back to New Zealand from
Australia last year.
We have made it easier to buy a first home with 5 per cent
deposits and first home buyers were at a record 26 per
cent of the property market in 2026 – that is 24,800
young Kiwis into their first homes in the past year. And
for tenants, rent increases are at a 25-year low, whereas
under Labour, rents went up $180 per week.

Our 2026 election policies for
Young Adults
• Lower student loan repayments: National will
reduce the student loan repayment rate for Kiwis
living in the country, leaving graduates with more
take-home pay. This gives young people more
income for rent, savings, a first home deposit or
starting a business.
• Wider access to 5 per cent home loan deposits:
National will expand access to the First Home Loan
Scheme so more eligible buyers can purchase with
a 5 per cent deposit, rather than the conventional
20 per cent.
• Paid Parental Leave extension: National is extending
paid parental leave from 26-30 weeks to give
parents more time with their newborn.
• Stronger KiwiSaver and $1500 Baby Boost:
KiwiSaver will become compulsory, contribution
settings will be higher, and a $1500 Baby Boost
contribution will be made for each eligible newborn.
• A welfare system focused on work: Provide
more intensive employment support for long-term
jobseekers, alongside stronger expectations.
• No new taxes: Give workers, households and
businesses greater certainty.

Fixing the Basics. Building the Future.
Party Vote National.

# National's South Island Plan

Published by the New Zealand National Party as a PDF policy document. Source: <https://assets.national.org.nz/web/prod/National%27s%20South%20Island%20Plan.pdf?v=1786659579>.
The text below is the verbatim text layer of the PDF extracted with `pdftotext` (reading order). Line breaks follow the
PDF; tables and multi-column layouts may read out of order in this section, so a second rendering that preserves the
page layout (`pdftotext -layout`) follows it. Nothing has been added, removed or paraphrased.

## Full text (reading order)

BUILDING THE FUTURE:

NATIONAL’S PLAN FOR
THE SOUTH ISLAND
The South Island is now a powerhouse of the New Zealand economy – producing the food, fibre, energy, technology
and visitor experiences the country needs and the world flocks to buy. In total, the South Island’s economy is worth
almost $100 billion a year, or around 22 per cent of the New Zealand economy, and its ports carry around a third of New
Zealand’s goods exports.
The Government’s growth agenda has already been supporting the South Island’s economic success. National’s
ambitious programme of RMA reform has unshackled development of new energy and new homes, while making life
easier for farmers and growers. Ongoing investment in the infrastructure southern towns and cities need to grow has
supported exports, tourism and urban growth. And after a sluggish post-COVID recovery, National’s pro-growth agenda
for tourism has encouraged tens of thousands of additional visitors to come to towns and cities like Queenstown,
Christchurch, Wanaka, Dunedin and Nelson.
But there is still more to do. Productive firms and growing towns can still be held back by unreliable transport links, rules
and regulations, and shortages of workers and homes. A single bridge closure can cut off a community or force freight
through a long detour.
National is not starting from scratch. We have brought government spending under control, delivered tax relief for
working New Zealanders, cut red tape for businesses and made it easier to build the homes, infrastructure and energy
projects our country needs. Business confidence has rebounded and the economy is growing again, giving businesses
greater confidence to invest, expand and employ more people.
National has also shown that responsible economic management and better public services can go hand in hand. By
getting the Government’s books back under control, National has been able to invest in the roads, hospitals, schools,
Police and other essential infrastructure New Zealanders rely on, including in the South Island.

A re-elected National Government will:
•
•
•
•

Build the transport and regional connections the South Island needs to move people, goods and visitors reliably.
Grow Southern exports across agriculture, tourism, and mining and resources.
Secure the energy new industrial investment needs, with substantial new demand matched by new generation,
storage and network capacity.
Strengthen the frontline health, education, and law and order services growing communities rely on.

Infrastructure: connecting the South
The South Island needs infrastructure that keeps communities connected and supports future growth. Distance means a
failed road or bridge can isolate a town, and a single vulnerable corridor can put freight, tourism and emergency access
at risk. National is investing in the transport and regional connections that remove weak points in the network and make
better use of the assets already being built.

What we’ve done
National is delivering record transport investment across the South Island through the 2024–27 National Land Transport
Programme, with South Island funding up 42 per cent on the previous three-year period:

•

$38.5 million to replace Christchurch’s Pages Road Bridge, and construction underway on the second Ashburton
Bridge for completion by the end of 2027.
$4.5 million for the first stage of the Rangiora Eastern Link, a $12.6 million pedestrian and cycle bridge over SH6
in Queenstown, and replacement of SH82’s Waihao North River and Elephant Hill Stream bridges, the first already
complete and under budget.
Canterbury’s Roads of Regional Significance, the SH1 Rolleston Access Improvements (estimated at $180–200 million
and expected to be complete by the end of 2028), the SH76 Brougham Street upgrade (main works expected to be
complete by late 2027) and the SH75 Halswell Road improvements, alongside early works on the Belfast to Pegasus
Motorway and Woodend Bypass Road of National Significance.
More than $150 million through Budget 2026 to strengthen vulnerable South Island state highways: around $20
million for SH60 Tākaka Hill, $40 million for SH6 Haast to Hāwea, $30 million for SH6 Cromwell to Frankton, $20
million for SH6 Frankton to Kingston and $40 million for SH94 Te Anau to Milford Sound. This sits alongside Crown
Resilience Programme repairs at SH73 Candys Bend, $5 million for the SH6 Gates of Haast and $7 million to progress
the fix for the SH6 Epitaph slip site.
A $3.9 billion nationwide Pothole Prevention Fund, ring-fenced for resealing, rehabilitation and drainage
maintenance, with 98 per cent of potholes now repaired within 48 hours and more than 20 lane kilometres of new
roads delivered across the West Coast, Otago and Southland.
A $9.8 million Regional Infrastructure Fund loan to upgrade Hokitika Airport, $4.6 million to upgrade port and wharf
infrastructure at Greymouth and Jackson Bay, and Coastal Shipping Resilience Fund co-investment of $5.3 million in
the reconstruction of Greymouth Wharf and $3 million in the ASP Rangitata at Timaru.
$24.3 million towards a new Chatham Islands supply vessel, and loans to Air Chathams ($17.2 million), Sounds Air
($4.5 million) and Golden Bay Air ($1.1 million) to protect important regional air connections.
A new Nelson–Tasman weather radar, on track for delivery in 2027, and a fixed-price contract signed for two new
Cook Strait ferries.
Major flood resilience investment through the Regional Infrastructure Fund, protecting the towns, farms and
freight routes that flooding puts at risk: $16.6 million to upgrade the Wairau River schemes in Marlborough, almost
$17 million for Motueka River and Tasman stopbanks, $10.8 million for Nelson’s Maitai and flood repair projects,
$10.8 million for Mataura River protection at Gore and Mataura, $8.5 million for Westport Harbour and Buller River
stopbank infrastructure, $6 million for the Waiho River stopbank on the West Coast, and river protection upgrades
across Canterbury, Otago and Southland – from the Rangitata and Ashley to the Taieri and Oreti.
Critical roading projects listed in the Fast-track Approvals Act, giving them access to a one-stop consenting pathway:
the Ashburton Second Urban Bridge, the SH1 Woodend Bypass (Belfast to Pegasus) and the Hope Bypass in Tasman.

What we’re doing next
A re-elected National Government will make a series of new investments in priority South Island projects. National will
invest $50 million in the shared road and rail connections needed for the proposed Rolleston intermodal freight hub.
Rolleston sits at the junction of the Main South Line, the Midland Line to the West Coast and State Highway 1, making
it the natural place to consolidate freight moving between Canterbury’s producers, the port and the rest of the island.
Crown funding will be conditional on a final business case, committed freight customers and binding private coinvestment, so taxpayers only contribute where the private sector is genuinely committed.
Queenstown is also one of the fastest-growing parts of the country and SH6 and 6A is its single most important piece
of road. This is the corridor that carries workers to the airport, freight to the supermarkets, and visitors to the town
that earns this country billions in export revenue. It needs to work, but instead, its chronically congested. A re-elected
National government will support innovative public transport solutions like Gondolas, as well as practical road-widening
to improve connectivity and efficiency along this stretch of road.
National also acknowledges that the South Island’s roading network is especially vulnerable, with its mountainous
terrain, active faults, and braided rivers. When a bridge or a corridor goes, there is often no second option - only a
several-hundred-kilometre detour, or no journey at all. Building resilience into our roads is how we make sure a single
event doesn’t shut down a whole region.
A re-elected National government would target transport funding in the next Government Policy Statement on Land
Transport to the most critical parts of the network, where disruption would have the greatest consequences for
communities, freight, emergency response, and the economy. This would include prioritising bridge replacements on key
routes on the South Island State Highway Network.

•
•

Invest $50 million in the shared road and rail connections for the Rolleston intermodal freight hub.
Ensure that congestion reducing Gondola solutions in Queenstown can access existing public transport funding in
the NLTF.
Commit $25m to four-lane the remaining portion past Hansen Road down to the Five Mile roundabout in
Queenstown.
Use the next Government Policy Statement to improve the network’s most critical links, including South Island state
highway bridge replacements.

The South Island’s prosperity is built on selling to the world. Its ports carry around a third of New Zealand’s goods
exports, and its farms, vineyards, mines and visitor businesses earn the income that pays for the services New
Zealanders rely on. National is backing each of the South Island’s major export sectors.

Agriculture
What we’ve done
•
•
•
•

Reformed the RMA to make life easier for farmers and growers, and introduced legislation giving high-country
farmers greater freedom to invest and diversify across around 1.2 million hectares of Crown pastoral land.
Listed new water storage projects in the Fast-track Approvals Act, including Klondyke Storage on the Rangitata
Diversion Race and the Balmoral water storage facility and fish screen on the Hurunui, granting access to a one-stop
consenting pathway.
$109 million through Budget 2026 to tackle wilding pines nationally, with Canterbury, Otago and Marlborough
among the priority regions, alongside Rural Support Trust funding and Mayoral Relief Fund payments for farming
communities hit by severe weather in Clutha, Hurunui, Kaikōura, Southland and Nelson Tasman.
$1.2 million through AgriZeroNZ for North Canterbury start-up Āmua, developing technology to cut nitrous oxide
emissions and nitrate leaching.

What we’re doing next

giving farmers and growers the certainty they need to invest in food and fibre production. The new system will replace
case-by-case litigation with clear, consistent national rules – so a farmer in the Amuri Basin or a grower in Central Otago
spends less time and money on process, and more on production.
National will also implement the new Crown pastoral land settings, so high-country farmers can invest and diversify with
confidence across the 1.2 million hectares of Crown pastoral land that supports so much of the South Island’s food and
fibre production.

Complete and implement the replacement of the RMA, giving farmers and growers certainty to invest.

Tourism
What we’ve done
Tourism is New Zealand’s second-largest export earner, and the South Island is at the heart of it. International visitors
spent $18.1 billion in the year to March 2025, up $1.2 billion or 7 per cent on the year before, and the sector now supports
around one in nine New Zealand jobs. For towns like Queenstown, Wanaka, Tekapo and Hokitika, visitor spending is
not a supplement to the local economy – it is the local economy, sustaining the cafés, guiding businesses, transport
operators and accommodation providers that employ thousands of Southerners.
National has backed that industry with marketing, infrastructure and events. Almost $3 million of directly targeted South
Island campaigns through the Regional Tourism Boost is bringing more international visitors south, including Great
South’s Southern Way campaign and the ChristchurchNZ-led Discover Different campaign across Canterbury and the
West Coast.
Alongside the marketing, National has invested in critical tourism infrastructure, including more than $4 million
in improvements to the Milford Road corridor and $15.2 million into the Milford Opportunities Project through the
International Visitor Levy and the Department of Conservation’s capital works programme. National has also invested
$3.8 million in public toilet facilities in Queenstown Lakes and Mackenzie districts, $2 million for the Dunedin Tunnels
Trail, $200,000 for the Waimate Trail, and made ongoing investment in the Great Rides.
Events matter too, filling beds and restaurants, and giving smaller centres a reason to be on the map. National has
backed more than 120 South Island events through the Regional Events Promotion Fund, worth more than $1.9 million
across two rounds, alongside major events support including Supercars in Christchurch, Crankworx, the Winter Games,
Warbirds Over Wanaka and the inaugural Snow League World Challenge, which will be held at Cardrona next month.
The results have been impressive. In the year to January 2026, South Island regions recorded an average 10 per cent
increase in international visitor days, and visitor spending rose in every South Island region in the year to March 2026,
with Southland recording the strongest turnaround, from a 5 per cent fall in 2025 to 13 per cent growth in 2026.

supercharge our town centres, by enabling more mixed-use, and cutting red tape to make it easier for things like cafés
and stores to open in our small towns. A small visitor town should not need to design bespoke planning rules from
scratch for an old bank to become a café or a main-street shop to add accommodation upstairs. Standard provisions
will let councils adopt sensible settings off the shelf, so towns can revitalise their centres and welcome new visitor
businesses.

businesses operating on conservation land, and publish regional performance so operators can see decisions being
made on time. The Bill also enables access charging for international visitors at key sites such as Aoraki / Mt Cook and
Milford Sounds. The revenue generated from these charges can assist with maintaining tourism infrastructure and
biodiversity at these popular sites.

•

Provide standardised planning provisions through standardised zoning to enable growth in our small-towns.

success: OceanaGold’s Macraes mine in Otago is the country’s largest gold mine, employing around 700 people and
producing more than five million ounces over its 35-year history, while the West Coast produces around 90 per cent
of New Zealand’s alluvial gold. In Buller, the Stockton mine (New Zealand’s largest opencast mine) exports premium
steelmaking coal. Together, gold and metallurgical coal account for around 80 per cent of New Zealand’s mineral
exports, and the Government has set a goal of doubling mineral exports to $3 billion by 2035.

benefits qualifying them to access the Fast-track regime.

protection available. A National Standard for on-farm quarries will let farmers take aggregate for tracks and maintenance
without unnecessary consenting costs.

•
•
•

Develop a new Government Policy Statement on Mining and Extraction under the Fast Track Approvals Act.

•
•

•
•

•

Complete and implement the replacement of the RMA, with more enabling rules for wind, solar and hydro

Finish fitting out Tower Three at Christchurch Hospital, delivering 96 additional beds for patients.

Deliver the remaining funded teaching spaces, nearly 100 more classrooms across the South Island.

•

Deliver a new Police station for Greymouth through Budget 2026.
Complete Phase 1 of the Christchurch Men’s Prison redevelopment, operational by mid-2030.

```text
Once the Conservation Amendment Bill is enacted, National will implement the new concession timeframes for visitor
businesses operating on conservation land, and publish regional performance so operators can see decisions being
made on time. The Bill also enables access charging for international visitors at key sites such as Aoraki / Mt Cook and
Milford Sounds. The revenue generated from these charges can assist with maintaining tourism infrastructure and
biodiversity at these popular sites.

National will:

•   Provide standardised planning provisions through standardised zoning to enable growth in our small-towns.
•   Introduce access charging for international visitors at Aoraki / Mt Cook and Milford Sounds, prioritising reinvestment
    in local conservation and tourism infrastructure.
•   Implement new conservation concession timeframes and publish regional performance.

Mining and resources

What we’ve done

Mining is a major South Island export earner and a backbone of regional economies on the West Coast and in Otago.
New Zealand produced 213,000 ounces of gold and 2.5 million tonnes of coal in 2024, and gold export revenues have
nearly tripled in three years to around $1.8 billion on the back of record gold prices. The South Island is critical to that
success: OceanaGold’s Macraes mine in Otago is the country’s largest gold mine, employing around 700 people and
producing more than five million ounces over its 35-year history, while the West Coast produces around 90 per cent
of New Zealand’s alluvial gold. In Buller, the Stockton mine (New Zealand’s largest opencast mine) exports premium
steelmaking coal. Together, gold and metallurgical coal account for around 80 per cent of New Zealand’s mineral
exports, and the Government has set a goal of doubling mineral exports to $3 billion by 2035.

•   Listed regionally and nationally significant South Island resource projects in the Fast-track Approvals Act, giving them
    access to a one-stop consenting process, including the Buller Plateaux Continuation coal expansion, the Bendigo–
    Ophir Gold Project in Central Otago, Macraes Phase Four, the Barrytown Mineral Sands Project near Greymouth, and
    quarry expansions at Miners Road and Southern Screenworks to supply the aggregate Canterbury’s growth requires.
•   Backed West Coast critical minerals processing with $50 million of Regional Infrastructure Fund investment: $30
    million for Westland Mineral Sands and $20 million for Taiko Critical Minerals in Greymouth.

What we’re doing next

To provide greater certainty to the minerals industry, a re-elected National Government will develop a new Government
Policy Statement on Mining and Extraction under the Fast Track Approvals Act. This new GPS will be modelled off similar
ones created for grocery competition, and will make clear that mining and extractive activities have regional and national
benefits qualifying them to access the Fast-track regime.

National will also develop National Standards under the replacement for the RMA for gravel extraction from rivers and
for on-farm quarries. A consistent national rule for river gravel extraction will support both aggregate supply and flood
management – gravel build-up raises riverbeds and flood risk, and extraction is often the most cost-effective flood
protection available. A National Standard for on-farm quarries will let farmers take aggregate for tracks and maintenance
without unnecessary consenting costs.

National will:

•   Develop a new Government Policy Statement on Mining and Extraction under the Fast Track Approvals Act.
•   Develop a National Standard for gravel extraction from rivers, supporting aggregate supply and flood management.
•   Develop a National Standard for on-farm quarries, cutting consenting costs for farmers.

Energy: powering Southern growth

The South Island has strong renewable resources and some of New Zealand’s best opportunities for new industrial
investment. It also faces long connection lead times, constrained local networks and communities vulnerable to outages.
National is unlocking new generation and making sure substantial new demand is matched by new supply.

What we’ve done

•   Reformed the RMA and delivered Electrify NZ so new electricity generation can actually get built.
•   Delivered fast-track approvals for four major new South Island generation projects: the 380MW Southland Wind Farm
    near Gore – set to be New Zealand’s largest wind farm, powering up to 150,000 homes; the 190MW Puke Kapo Hau
    expansion of the Mahinerangi Wind Farm west of Dunedin, including a 60MW battery; the 220MW Haldon Solar Farm
    near Twizel – the first solar farm approved through fast-track; and the 23MW Waitaha Hydro scheme on the West
    Coast, a project two decades in the making.
•   Re-consented the Tekapo Power Scheme through fast-track, securing hydro generation that powers more than
    228,000 households, and approved the Lake Pūkaki hydro storage and dam resilience works.
•   A further pipeline of South Island generation remains in the fast-track process, including the Kaihiku Wind Farm in
    Clutha (around 80 turbines) and major solar farms across the Mackenzie Basin and Waitaki.

What we’re doing next

A re-elected National Government will complete and implement the replacement of the Resource Management Act, with
more enabling rules for new renewable generation, so wind, solar and hydro projects are developed quickly and power
prices are kept down. Fast-track has shown what a difference process makes: the Southland Wind Farm was declined
under the RMA after years of process, then approved in around five months under fast-track. The new planning system
will make that speed the norm for renewable generation, not the exception.

A re-elected National Government will also require that new data centre projects are accompanied by new, firmed
generation, by applying an “additionality” test. Data centres are a significant economic opportunity for the South Island,
which offers abundant renewable energy and a cool climate, but they are also very large electricity users requiring
uninterrupted supply. Requiring new firmed generation alongside new data centres means the development of digital
infrastructure doesn’t put upward pressure on power prices for households and businesses, while giving energy
developers the committed customers they need to finance new generation.

National will:

•   Complete and implement the replacement of the RMA, with more enabling rules for wind, solar and hydro
    development.
•   Require new data centre projects to be accompanied by new, firmed generation, protecting households and
    businesses from higher power prices.

Frontline services: health, education, and law and order

Growth is only worth having if it comes with the services growing communities rely on. National has shown that
responsible economic management and better public services go hand in hand – and is investing in the hospitals,
schools and Police the South Island needs.

Health

What we’ve done

•   Begun construction on the New Dunedin Hospital, which will provide 351 beds expanding to 404 and be operational
    by 2031, and commenced redevelopment of Nelson Hospital, a new 128-bed inpatient building by 2029, $73 million
    in design and enabling works and a $10.6 million emergency department expansion.
•   Planning a $180 million expansion of health services and infrastructure in Otago Central Lakes, and building the $5
    million Clyde Primary Maternity Unit.
•   Rolling out urgent and after-hours care to 98 per cent of New Zealanders within a one-hour drive through the
    $164 million national programme, including 70 rural and remote sites, with the first two South Island sites already
    delivered at Twizel and Tākaka. The programme also delivers a new 24/7 urgent care service for Dunedin (opened
    in December), new daytime services for Invercargill and Timaru, and extended after-hours care for Ashburton,
    Alexandra, Gore, Golden Bay and Ōamaru.
•   Established the South Island’s first Rural Training Hub on the West Coast, so more doctors, nurses and midwives can
    train and build their careers in rural communities, alongside a new CT scanner now operational at Southland Hospital
    and mental health peer support in Christchurch Hospital’s emergency department.
•   Health targets are delivering across the South Island. In the April to June 2025 quarter, 83.7 per cent of cancer
    patients started treatment within 31 days, 87.4 per cent of children were fully immunised by age two, and 78.9 per
    cent of emergency department patients were admitted, transferred or discharged within six hours – with Canterbury
    up 8 percentage points and the West Coast up 17.7 on a year earlier, despite increased attendances. Progress has
    continued since: in the most recent quarter, to March 2026, 86.2 per cent of cancer patients nationally started
    treatment within 31 days, up from 84.6 per cent a year earlier, and childhood immunisation reached 83.5 per cent,
    up from 79.3 per cent.

What we’re doing next

A re-elected National Government will finish fitting out Tower Three at Christchurch Hospital, at an estimated cost of $70
million.

The building is currently being constructed with 96 beds included as shell space: the rooms are there, but not finished
off. National will complete them now, so all 96 beds are ready for patients straight away instead of waiting – adding real
capacity to the South Island’s largest hospital as Canterbury grows.

National will:

•   Finish fitting out Tower Three at Christchurch Hospital, delivering 96 additional beds for patients.

Education

What we’ve done

•   Funded 322 new teaching spaces across the South Island since Budget 2024, with 224 already delivered or under
    construction, alongside $148.3 million of redevelopment work across 14 schools.
•   A $161 million Canterbury school growth package, including a new primary school on Milns Road, a new school and
    52 additional classrooms in Selwyn plus a site for a future school, major expansions at Rolleston College, Lincoln
    Primary School, Ararira Springs and Te Rau Horopito, and new classrooms at schools from Woodend to Halswell.
•   $27 million for 18 new teaching spaces at Dunstan High School and Te Kura Whakatipu o Kawarau, with land secured
    at Ladies Mile for a future primary school as Queenstown grows.
•   New classrooms for smaller and rural communities – including South Westland Area School, Amuri Area School,
    Fiordland College, Heddon Bush School and Te Anau School – and major redevelopments at Twizel Area School,
    Ellesmere College, Alexandra Primary School, and Aurora and James Hargest Colleges in Invercargill.
•   Specialist classrooms at Ferndale School in Christchurch and Sara Cohen School in Dunedin, and replacement
    classrooms at Ashburton Intermediate and Maruawai College in Gore.

What we’re doing next

A re-elected National Government will deliver the remaining funded teaching spaces, nearly 100 more classrooms
already committed across the South Island, and complete the redevelopment programme underway across 14 schools.
That means the classrooms families have been promised in fast-growing communities like Selwyn, Rolleston and
Queenstown are built on time, alongside the rebuilds already underway in smaller centres from Twizel to Invercargill.

National will:

•   Deliver the remaining funded teaching spaces, nearly 100 more classrooms across the South Island.
•   Complete the redevelopment programme underway across 14 South Island schools.

Law and order

What we’ve done

•   Put more Police on the beat, strengthened consequences for serious and repeat offenders and given Police more
    tools to keep communities safe. The Government has met its national target of 20,000 fewer victims of violent crime
    ahead of schedule.
•   Signed the public-private partnership agreement for the first phase of the $700–800 million Christchurch Men’s
    Prison redevelopment, delivering 240 additional high-security beds, 52 specialist mental health beds and a new
    health centre – lifting the prison from 926 to 1,166 operational beds when Phase 1 opens.

What we’re doing next

Budget 2026 delivers a new Police station for Greymouth, giving the West Coast a modern base for frontline policing.
National will also complete Phase 1 of the Christchurch Men’s Prison redevelopment, with construction beginning this
year and the new facilities due to be operational by mid-2030 – so serious offenders face real consequences and
communities are kept safe.

National will:

•   Deliver a new Police station for Greymouth through Budget 2026.
•   Complete Phase 1 of the Christchurch Men’s Prison redevelopment, operational by mid-2030.

                                                                                         Authorised by J de Joux, ps@national.org.nz
```

documents/pdf-paid-parental-leave.md.text:
# Paid Parental Leave

Published by the New Zealand National Party as a PDF policy document. Source: <https://assets.national.org.nz/web/prod/Paid%20Parental%20Leave.pdf?v=1785023838>.
The text below is the verbatim text layer of the PDF extracted with `pdftotext` (reading order). Line breaks follow the
PDF; tables and multi-column layouts may read out of order in this section, so a second rendering that preserves the
page layout (`pdftotext -layout`) follows it. Nothing has been added, removed or paraphrased.

## Full text (reading order)

Building the Future:
Modernising Paid Parental Leave
Introduction
At the heart of National’s plan to build the future are
dedicated mums and dads, balancing long hours at
work with the excitement and pressure that comes with
raising young kids.
The arrival of a new baby is often one of the happiest
times in a family’s life, but it also comes with higher
costs and tough choices. Many parents are forced to
juggle the financial impact of taking time away from
work alongside a real desire to spend more time at
home with their babies.
Earlier this year, Christopher Luxon announced that a
re-elected National Government will look to take some
of that financial stress away by making unconditional
KiwiSaver contributions for new mums and dads who
choose to take paid parental leave: a Government
contribution at the default rate, applied against their
paid parental leave payments from 1 July 2027, even if
the parent isn’t contributing themselves.
Now, National is laying out a long-term vision to
modernise Paid Parental Leave as a whole and provide
new mums and dads with the financial flexibility they
need to spend more time at home with their new baby.
A re-elected National Government will:
•

Extend paid parental leave – from 26 to 30
weeks in three stages over the next term, as the
first step in National’s longer-term vision to extend
paid parental leave to 40 weeks.

Extending Paid Parental Leave
from 26 to 30 weeks
For working mums and dads, the first year of a child’s
life is one of the most important and special times
of their lives. It is when attachment forms, when
the foundations of language, health and emotional
development are laid, and when mums recover from
birth. It also supports mums through a postpartum
period that is often physically and mentally demanding.
Extra time to recover after having a baby will help
mums return to work with more confidence.
A new baby is also an expensive time for many
families, who juggle the costs that come with a
newborn while their household income comes under
strain from having one parent step away from work.
To address those pressures, National is laying out a
long-term vision to extend paid parental leave from six
months to nine months, with an initial increase of four
weeks over the next term.
Paid parental leave entitlements will increase from 26
weeks to 30 weeks over three Budgets:
Budget

Effective from

PPL entitlement

Budget 2027

1 July 2027

27 weeks (+1 week)

Budget 2028

1 July 2028

28 weeks (+1 week)

Budget 2029

1 July 2029

30 weeks (+2 weeks)

•

Shared parental leave – allowing parents
the flexibility to take their paid parental leave
entitlement at the same time, or in overlapping
instalments.

The phased approach is deliberate. Announcing the
full pathway up front gives families certainty to plan
around and gives employers time to prepare. To achieve
National’s vision of extending paid parental leave to nine
months (or 40 weeks), further increases are expected in
subsequent budgets, subject to fiscal conditions.

•

Protect full holiday pay for new parents – by
passing and protecting new employment leave
legislation that enhances rights to annual leave for
working mums and dads.

Each increase applies to parents whose entitlement
commences on or after the effective date. Policy on
maximum weekly rates and eligibility settings will be
unchanged.

Together, these three policies give families more time
with their new baby and more choice about how they
use it.

Authorised by J de Joux, ps@national.org.nz

Fiscal impact
The costings below are based on the gross cost of
paid parental leave forecast in BEFU 2026, net of the
additional PAYE revenue the Crown collects from paid
parental leave payments.
This policy has been designed to improve New
Zealand’s paid parental leave regime over time, with
increases staged so they are affordable within tight
operating allowances over multiple budgets.
Fiscal Year

The cost of each increase to paid parental leave
entitlements will be met from the annual operating
allowance in Budgets 2027, 2028, and 2029. The
largest extension of paid parental leave, scheduled
for 1 July 2029, is timed to coincide with the forecast
return to surplus that financial year.

2027/28

2028/29

2029/30

2030/31

Total

$27.0

$56.6

$119.0

$124.9

$327.4

Cost of extension ($m)

Shared parental leave
Right now, mums and dads can split their 26 weeks of
paid parental leave between each other, but the rules
prevent parents taking their paid parental leave at the
same time.
Under National’s policy, parents would have the option
to take all or some of their paid parental leave at the
same time. So instead of one parent taking 30 weeks
of paid leave, under this policy:
• both parents could take paid leave together for 15
weeks,
• both parents could take paid leave together for four
weeks, one parent could then take paid leave for ten
weeks, and then the other parent could take leave for
twelve weeks.
In short, under this policy new parents could mix
and match their combined right to 30 weeks of paid
parental leave as they see fit, with flexibility to take
leave together, then apart, then together again, in
whatever order and combination works best for them.
That flexibility is important. For some parents, it’s just
the opportunity to spend time together with their new
baby at home. For others, it will make a much bigger
difference: families welcoming twins or bringing a
premature baby home after weeks in neonatal care, or
mums who need their partner at home after a difficult
birth. Every family has different needs: this policy
recognises that and gives mums and dads the chance
to choose what will work best for their family.
In 2023, Nicola Willis introduced a members’ bill which
would have implemented these changes, but this
legislation was voted down at First Reading by the

Labour Party. Dana Kirkpatrick MP has sponsored the
legislation as a Member’s Bill in this term of Parliament.
This additional flexibility is not expected to generate
any significant costs for the Crown, because by itself
this policy does not increase paid parental leave
entitlements for each child born. Inland Revenue will
be expected to meet any administrative costs arising
from this change within baselines.
A re-elected National Government will:
Amend the Parental Leave and Employment Protection
Act 1987 to allow parents to divide their PPL
entitlement between them as they see fit, as provided
for in the Parental Leave and Employment Protection
(Shared Leave) Amendment Bill.

Full Holiday Pay for Parents
Returning to Work
Right now, working mums and dads who spend time
away from work are forced to take a big financial hit
when they later decide to take annual leave – for a
holiday, or a week away with their young child to meet
their grandparents.
That’s because under current legislation, annual
leave is currently paid based on a person’s average
weekly earnings over the previous 12 months. That
means a parent who takes a holiday in the months
after returning to work, including their first Christmas
break with their new baby, could see their holiday
pay reduced because they had spent time at home
caring for their child. In practice, that penalty fell
overwhelmingly on working mums.
The Government is fixing this. Under the new
Employment Leave Act, which replaces the Holidays

Act, workers will continue to earn annual leave while
on parental leave, and when they take annual leave
after returning to work, they will be paid in full. These
changes take effect from 1 July 2027, ahead of the
wider reforms, so that parents see the benefit as soon
as possible.

In the year to June 2025, when this policy took
effect, only around 1 in 5 of those eligible continued
to contribute to their KiwiSaver while on paid leave
with their new baby, meaning 4 in 5 missed out on the
matching contribution.

A re-elected National Government will protect that
legislation and oppose any efforts to water down the
rights of working mums and dads to take a holiday with
their new child, without being financially punished.
A re-elected National Government will:
Protect full holiday pay for parents returning from
parental leave, by the parental leave provisions of the
Employment Leave Act and ensuring they take effect
as legislated from 1 July 2027.

KwiSaver Paid Parental Leave TopUp
Right now, the Government matches any KiwiSaver
contributions made by someone on paid parental
leave, as if they were receiving an employer
contribution on their weekly parental leave payments.

National believes strong families are the cornerstone
of a more prosperous society, and that starts with
supporting every family to save for their future and
build their own financial security.
Under National’s policy, from 1 July 2027, the
Government will provide a KiwiSaver contribution to
people on paid parental leave even if the person is not
contributing themselves. This contribution will be made
at the default rate applied against the amount of paid
parental leave a person is receiving.
Fiscal impact
The cost of this policy is modelled as the cost of
applying the full employer contribution on paid
parental leave payments, less ESCT, and the cost of
the current policy to match contributions ($3.8 million
in 2024/25). This table has been updated since the
KiwiSaver policy announcement to reflect staged
extensions to paid parental leave.

In reality, this comes at a time of financial pressure for
many families as they adjust to life on a single income
and more expenses, so many parents choose not to
contribute while on paid parental leave.

Fiscal Year
PPL KiwiSaver contribution ($m)

2027/28

2028/29

2029/30

2030/31

Total

$20.9

$26.5

$34.1

$40.4

$121.9
